name: Andrew Huberman
domain: neuroscience-based health and performance protocols: sleep, light exposure, focus, dopamine and motivation, exercise, nutrition, supplements, stress, hormones and mental health

sources.title: Dopamine: baselines, peaks, and how to keep motivation without crashing
sources.originalTitle: Controlling Your Dopamine For Motivation, Focus & Satisfaction
sources.summary: Huberman explains dopamine as a motivation and craving currency with a baseline plus peaks, where big peaks drop the baseline afterward. He covers intermittent reward schedules, attaching reward to effort, cold exposure, caffeine/yerba mate, and cautions on stacking stimulants and supplements.

principles.text: After a dopamine peak, baseline dopamine drops below where it started, in proportion to how high the peak was.
principles.quote: what actually happens is that your Baseline level of dopamine drops and I will explain the precise mechanism for that

principles.text: Enjoyment depends on the peak relative to baseline and your recent experience, not on dopamine 'hits'.
principles.quote: how much dopamine you experience from something depends on your Baseline level of dopamine when you arrive there and your previous dopamine Peaks

principles.text: Use intermittent, unpredictable reward schedules; vary how much dopamine-boosting stimuli you layer onto activities you want to keep enjoying.
principles.quote: the key thing is to make sure that the peak in dopamine if it's very high doesn't occur too often and if something does occur very often that you vary how much dopamine you experience

principles.text: Don't chronically stack stimulants, pre-workouts, or phone/music onto workouts and study; it undercuts long-term motivation and drive.
principles.quote: chronically trying to spike your dopamine in order to enhance your motivation focus and drive will absolutely undermine your motivation focus and drive in the long run

principles.text: Attach reward to effort itself rather than a reward afterward: tell yourself the friction is the good part.
principles.quote: don't Spike dopamine prior to engaging an effort and don't Spike dopamine after engaging an effort learn to spike your dopamine from effort itself

principles.text: Cold water exposure raised dopamine about 2.5x with a sustained rise rather than a crash, and calm focus afterward; use caution about safety.
principles.quote: it was actually a sustained rise in dopamine that took a very long time up to 3 hours to come back down to Baseline

sources.title: Huberman's foundational weekly fitness protocol: endurance, resistance and recovery
sources.originalTitle: Fitness Toolkit: Protocol & Tools to Optimize Physical Health
sources.summary: Huberman lays out a flexible weekly template covering long zone 2 cardio, one moderate-intensity and one HIIT session, and resistance training for legs, torso and arms. He adds rep-range cycling, heat/cold contrast kept apart from training, and slow breathing for recovery.

principles.text: Get roughly 180-200 minutes of zone 2 cardio per week for longevity and health.
principles.quote: الحصول على 180 إلى 200 دقيقة من تمارين القلب في النطاق الثاني أسبوعيًا له آثار إيجابية هائلة على طول العمر وعلى الصحة العامة

principles.text: Train every major muscle group hard at least weekly; exact days matter less than spacing.
principles.quote: وهذا يعني تدريب ساقيك بقوة مرة واحدة على الأقل في الأسبوع، وجذعك بقوة مرة واحدة على الأقل، وذراعيك مرة واحدة على الأقل في الأسبوع.

principles.text: Alternate months of heavier low-rep work (4-8) with lighter moderate-rep work to keep progressing.
principles.quote: أتبع بشكل عام برنامجاً لمدة شهر تقريباً، أي ثلاثة إلى أربعة أسابيع، حيث أؤدي كل تدريبات المقاومة في نطاق يتراوح بين أربع إلى ثماني تكرارات.

principles.text: For each muscle group, pick one lengthened-under-load exercise and one peak-contraction exercise.
principles.quote: لكل مجموعة عضلية، حاول العثور على تمرين تضع فيه تلك العضلة في وضع تمدد تحت ثقل.

principles.text: Keep deliberate cold exposure on a separate day from lifting or endurance training, since it can blunt adaptations.
principles.quote: يمكنه بالفعل تعطيل أو منع بعض التكيفات التي تسعى لتحقيقها من خلال تمارين القوة والتحمل

principles.text: End each training session with 3-5 minutes of slow deliberate breathing to speed recovery.
principles.quote: من 3 إلى 5 دقائق من التنفس البطيء المتعمد.

sources.title: Focus Toolkit: tools to improve focus and concentration
sources.originalTitle: Focus Toolkit: Tools to Improve Your Focus & Concentration
sources.summary: Huberman models focus as an arrow: epinephrine is the shaft (alertness), acetylcholine the arrowhead (spotlight), dopamine the engine. He lays out mostly zero-cost tools to raise and train focus: sleep, 90-minute bouts, 40 Hz binaural beats, cold exposure, a 13-minute refocusing meditation, NSDR, visual anchoring, caffeine, and select supplements.

principles.text: Focus needs epinephrine (alertness), acetylcholine (spotlight) and dopamine (drive); each tool targets one of these.
principles.quote: these three neurochemicals together, acetylcholine, epinephrine and dopamine really allow you to get focused, to focus very precisely

principles.text: Sleep modulates focus; no tool overcomes chronic sleep deprivation, so get good sleep about 80% of nights.
principles.quote: There is simply no tool that's going to allow you to overcome chronic sleep deprivation and allow you to remain focused, no pill, no device, no supplement, no protocol whatsoever.

principles.text: Work in focus bouts of 90 minutes or less with a 5-10 minute warmup, then deliberately defocus afterward.
principles.quote: the ideal duration is about 90 minutes, not exactly 90 minutes, but we can reliably say 90 minutes or less

principles.text: Use 40 Hz binaural beats for about five minutes before work, or throughout when distractible.
principles.quote: 40 HZ binaural beats have been shown in a number of peer reviewed studies to increase focus and concentration.

principles.text: Deliberate cold exposure for 1-5 minutes raises epinephrine and dopamine and boosts focus for an hour or more.
principles.quote: it should be uncomfortably cold, but safe to stay in for one to five minutes.

principles.text: A daily 13-minute breath meditation that repeatedly refocuses attention trains focus circuits; avoid it within four hours of bedtime.
principles.quote: I recommend that you not do it within the four hours prior to your bedtime.

sources.title: Master Your Sleep & Be More Alert When Awake: light, adenosine, caffeine and NSDR
sources.originalTitle: Master Your Sleep & Be More Alert When Awake
sources.summary: Huberman explains sleep as driven by adenosine buildup and the circadian clock, which light sets best. He gives a practical light schedule (morning and evening sun, dim light late at night), notes caffeine tolerance varies, and introduces NSDR and a few sleep supplements.

principles.text: Get sunlight into your eyes outdoors soon after waking, for a few minutes, to anchor your cortisol and melatonin rhythms.
principles.quote: ما يجب عليك فعله هو تعريض عينيك لضوء الشمس في أقرب وقت ممكن من استيقاظك.

principles.text: Windows and windshields cut sunlight's effect enormously; go outside without sunglasses when it's safe to do so.
principles.quote: أن مشاهدة ضوء الشمس من خلال نافذة، أو زجاج أمامي للسيارة ، أو نافذة جانبية للسيارة أقل فعالية بخمسين مرة

principles.text: Viewing sunlight near sunset helps protect your brain and body from the harmful effects of artificial light later at night.
principles.quote: التعرض للضوء في وقت لاحق من اليوم عند غروب الشمس أو حول ذلك الوقت يمكن أن يساعد في حماية آليات دماغك وجسمك من الآثار السلبية للضوء في وقت متأخر من اليوم.

principles.text: After about 8 pm keep light exposure low, and avoid bright light between 11 pm and 4 am; prefer dim, low-placed lights over overhead lights.
principles.quote: ويجب أن تحرص على دخول أقل قدر ممكن من الضوء إلى عينيك، سواء كان اصطناعياً أو ضوء شمس، بعد الساعة الثامنة مساءً تقريباً.

principles.text: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors; tolerance and best cutoff time vary, so test it yourself rather than following a universal rule.
principles.quote: يعمل الكافيين كمضاد للأدينوزين.

principles.text: Non-sleep deep rest (meditation, yoga nidra, hypnosis) trains the nervous system to calm down and helps reset alertness and sleep onset.
principles.quote: الراحة العميقة غير المرتبطة بالنوم، أو ما سنشير إليه لاحقاً بـ NSDR

sources.title: Deliberate cold exposure: how to use cold for resilience, dopamine, metabolism and recovery
sources.originalTitle: Using Deliberate Cold Exposure for Health and Performance | Huberman Lab
sources.summary: Huberman explains how cold drives norepinephrine, epinephrine and dopamine release, and how to use cold showers or immersion for mental resilience, metabolism, recovery, and mood. He covers timing against circadian temperature, the Søberg principle, and palm cooling for performance.

principles.text: Choose water that is uncomfortably cold, makes you want out, but that you can safely stay in.
principles.quote: the environment that you place yourself into should place your mind into a state of whoa, I would really like to get out of this environment, but I can stay in safely.

principles.text: Build resilience by counting mental 'walls' (adrenaline surges) you push past, not just by time or colder temps.
principles.quote: my favorite protocol for building mental toughness AKA grit, AKA resilience, is to take into account that some days, just getting into the ice bath or cold shower represents a wall

principles.text: Aim for about 11 minutes total deliberate cold per week, split into 2 to 4 sessions, to raise metabolism.
principles.quote: I recommend that you get at least 11 minutes total per week

principles.text: Cold water immersion produced large, long-lasting rises in norepinephrine and dopamine without raising cortisol.
principles.quote: the plasma or serum levels of norepinephrine in the blood increased 530%.

principles.text: To maximize metabolic benefit, end on cold and let your body rewarm itself, ideally to the point of shivering.
principles.quote: So the Søberg principle is if you want to increase your metabolism, end with cold

principles.text: If your main goal is strength or hypertrophy, avoid cold immersion for about 4 hours after training.
principles.quote: it is probably best to avoid cold water immersion and ice bath immersion in the four hours immediately following that strength and or hypertrophy training.

sources.title: Tools for Managing Stress & Anxiety: physiological sigh, adrenaline, social connection
sources.originalTitle: Tools for Managing Stress & Anxiety
sources.summary: Huberman frames stress as a generic mobilizing system that helps in the short term and harms when chronic. He gives tools by time scale: the physiological sigh and exhale-emphasized breathing in real time, deliberate adrenaline and gaze dilation to raise stress threshold, and social connection plus selective supplements for long-term stress.

principles.text: The physiological sigh (double inhale, long exhale, 1-3 times) is the fastest real-time way to calm down.
principles.quote: the physiological sigh is the fastest hardwired way for us to eliminate this stressful response in our body quickly in real time.

principles.text: Longer or more vigorous exhales slow the heart rate; longer or stronger inhales speed it up.
principles.quote: if you want to calm down quickly, you need to make your exhales longer and or more vigorous than your inhales.

principles.text: Short-term stress and adrenaline are useful for immune defense; breathing or cold exposure can trigger it deliberately.
principles.quote: when adrenaline is released in the body, you are in a better position to combat infections.

principles.text: Raise stress threshold by dilating your gaze while the body is highly activated, so the mind stays calm.
principles.quote: by deliberately going from tunnel vision to broader panoramic vision, literally seeing more of your environment all at once.

principles.text: Losing good sleep signals a shift from acute to chronic stress, so learn to switch the stress response off.
principles.quote: When you are no longer able to achieve good sleep, you are now moving from acute stress to chronic stress.

principles.text: Social connection is a key buffer against long-term stress.
principles.quote: The data really points to the fact that social connection and certain types of social connection in particular are what are going to mitigate or reduce long-term stress.

sources.title: Rational supplementation: foundational, sleep, hormone and focus stacks, tested one ingredient at a time
sources.originalTitle: Developing a Rational Approach to Supplementation for Health & Performance | Huberman Lab Podcast
sources.summary: Huberman frames supplements as a layer above behaviors and nutrition, not a replacement for them. He recommends one broad foundational formula, then single-ingredient trials, isolated one week at a time, for sleep, hormone support and focus. He pairs this with dosing cautions and blood testing.

principles.text: Behaviors are the base layer, then nutrition, then supplements, then prescription drugs.
principles.quote: Better Living Through Chemistry still requires Better Living

principles.text: Foundational supplements (vitamins, minerals, enzymes, adaptogens, pre/probiotics) are the one category where multi-ingredient formulas make sense.
principles.quote: this is the one category of supplements for which I think it's appropriate and in fact advantageous to have multiple ingredients in a given supplement

principles.text: For targeted goals, use single-ingredient formulations and test them one at a time for about a week.
principles.quote: if there's an overriding theme of today's conversation it's really about learning how to isolate variables in the realm of supplementation

principles.text: For middle-of-the-night waking, inositol at 900 mg can shorten time to fall back asleep.
principles.quote: myoinositol typically taken as 900 milligrams of myoinositol myoinositol can help shorten the amount of time that it takes to fall back asleep

principles.text: Verify hormone supplements with blood tests, before and after about 4 to 8 weeks.
principles.quote: the best way to know whether or not fedojia or any of these other supplements is impacting your hormone levels in the direction that you want

principles.text: Aim for at least 1 gram of EPA per day (up to about 3 g) from fish oil for brain and body health.
principles.quote: ingesting one to three grams of EPA in particular in the form of either fish oil capsules or liquid can be beneficial

sources.title: Sleep Toolkit: light, temperature, caffeine, supplements and timing tools to optimize sleep
sources.originalTitle: Sleep Toolkit: Tools for Optimizing Sleep & Sleep-Wake Timing
sources.summary: Huberman lays out a practical sleep toolkit organized around three critical periods of the 24-hour day. It covers morning and evening sunlight, avoiding bright light at night, temperature manipulation, caffeine timing, a supplement stack (magnesium threonate, apigenin, theanine, plus glycine/GABA/inositol), NSDR/hypnosis, and using temperature minimum to shift your schedule.

principles.text: Get bright sunlight in your eyes within 30-60 minutes of waking to set cortisol, wakefulness and the sleep timer.
principles.quote: View bright sunlight within the first 30 to 60 minutes after waking.

principles.text: Delay caffeine 90-120 minutes after waking and keep it under 100 mg after 4 p.m. (ideally stop by 2-3 p.m.).
principles.quote: I highly recommend that everybody delay their caffeine intake for 90 to 120 minutes after waking.

principles.text: Dim lights and place them low between 10 p.m. and 4 a.m.; little light at night disrupts sleep.
principles.quote: avoid bright artificial lights of all colors and in particular overhead bright artificial lights between the hours of 10:00 p.m. and 4:00 a.m.

principles.text: Keep the bedroom cool; a 1-3 degree core temperature drop gates sleep. Hot bath or sauna in the evening, then cool off.
principles.quote: every night when you actually sleep, your body is dropping by 1 to 3° and that drop in temperature is required.

principles.text: Sleep stack 30-60 min before bed: 145 mg magnesium threonate, 50 mg apigenin, 100-400 mg theanine; drop any that don't suit you.
principles.quote: 145 mg of magnesium threeonate, 50 5 0 mg of apigenin, and again, you could just take the apigenin on its own, and 100 to 400 mg of theanine

principles.text: Shift your clock using temperature minimum (about 2 hours before usual wake time): light, exercise or caffeine before it delays, after it advances.
principles.quote: If you view bright light, exercise, or drink caffeine, or all of the above in the 2 to 4 hours before your temperature minimum, that will delay your clock.

sources.title: Optimal Protocols for Studying & Learning: Self-Testing, Focus, Sleep and Spacing
sources.originalTitle: Optimal Protocols for Studying & Learning
sources.summary: Huberman argues learning is about offsetting forgetting, and that self-testing soon after first exposure beats rereading by a wide margin. He covers the two-step plasticity process (focus, then sleep), habits of top students, NSDR, gap effects, emotion and interleaving.

principles.text: Treat studying as offsetting forgetting, not just absorbing information.
principles.quote: Rather than think about studying to learn and retain information. I want you to think about studying to offset the natural process of forgetting

principles.text: Test yourself rather than rereading; testing is the best studying tool, not just evaluation.
principles.quote: reading and rereading material and re-re-re-rereading material is far less effective than reading material and then thinking about that material, testing yourself on that material

principles.text: Self-test soon after first exposure, ideally the same or next day, then again after a long delay.
principles.quote: Test yourself on the material that you were just exposed to very soon after your first exposure to it because that offsets the natural forgetting of new material

principles.text: Prefer open-ended, short-answer self-tests over multiple choice, which only trains familiarity.
principles.quote: The best tests are open-ended, short answer, very minimal prompt tests

principles.text: Learning is two steps: alert, focused attention first, then neuroplastic change during deep sleep, so sleep well the first night.
principles.quote: Neuroplasticity and learning, that is converting your studying efforts into retention of knowledge, is a two-step process.

principles.text: Train focus with 5 to 10 minutes of daily mindfulness or a visual focusing exercise, and expect strain to feel productive.
principles.quote: the strain that you feel in forcing yourself to learn how to focus, that is good

sources.title: Fasting & time-restricted eating: how to time your eating window for fat loss and health
sources.originalTitle: Effects of Fasting & Time Restricted Eating on Fat Loss & Health | Huberman Lab Podcast #41
sources.summary: Huberman explains time-restricted feeding using Satchin Panda's work. When you eat sets fed or fasted conditions that drive circadian clock genes, liver health, inflammation, fat loss and hormones. He covers window length (about 8 hours), placement, protein timing, ways to speed the move to a fasted state, and what breaks a fast.

principles.text: When you eat matters as much as what you eat; eating sets fed or fasted conditions in your body.
principles.quote: when you eat is as important as what you eat. I'll repeat that, when you eat is as important as what you eat

principles.text: Avoid all calories for the first hour after waking and for 2-3 hours before bed to protect sleep-related fasting.
principles.quote: for the first hour after you wake up and potentially for longer to not ingest any food, okay, the second major pillar that's well supported by research is that for the two and ideally three hours prior to bedtime

principles.text: An eight-hour window is a solid default, but people underestimate their window, so aim 1-2 hours shorter than your target.
principles.quote: if you'd like to be on a 10 hour feeding window, you should probably select an eight or a nine hour feeding window, because the way it plays out is that people almost always eat outside of their eating window

principles.text: Keep the window at the same time daily; drifting on weekends is like jet lag and offsets benefits.
principles.quote: it is effectively like jet lagging your system. It is effectively like traveling a couple times zones over eating there for a few days and coming back

principles.text: For muscle maintenance or growth, eat protein early in the day, before about 10 AM if you wake at 7.
principles.quote: if your main interest is maintaining and, or building muscle, then it can be beneficial to ingest protein early in the day

principles.text: Speed the fed-to-fasted transition with a 20-30 minute light walk after eating; sodium in water can ease the fast.
principles.quote: you can accelerate that considerably by taking a 20 or 30 minute just light walk, it doesn't have to be speed walking.

sources.title: Huberman on muscle growth, strength and recovery: set volume, lactate, CO2 test, supplements
sources.originalTitle: Science of Muscle Growth, Increasing Strength & Muscular Recovery
sources.summary: Huberman explains that muscle growth and strength are driven by the nerve-to-muscle connection. He covers training volume (5 to 15 sets per muscle per week at 30 to 80% of 1RM), lactate as a signal to heart, liver and brain, recovery tests (grip strength, CO2 tolerance), and supplements such as creatine, beta-alanine and electrolytes. He warns that cold and NSAIDs after training blunt adaptation.

principles.text: Train at 30-80% of 1RM near failure; about 5 sets per muscle per week maintains, 10-15 builds.
principles.quote: it's very clear that moving weights or using bands or using body weight, for instance in the 30% to 80% of one-rep maximum. That is going to be the most beneficial range in terms of muscle hypertrophy and strength.

principles.text: The better you can isolate a muscle with your brain, the fewer sets you need; poor control needs more.
principles.quote: If you can generate high-intensity muscular contractions using your brain, using your neurons, it will take fewer sets in order to stimulate the muscle to maintain itself and to stimulate the muscle in order to grow or get stronger.

principles.text: Spend about 10% of exercise in the burn zone; lactate buffers acidity, fuels work, and signals heart, liver and brain. Keep breathing.
principles.quote: every once in a while, about 10% of the time you should exercise to the point of intensity where you start to feel that so-called burn.

principles.text: For a testosterone boost, do six sets of 10 on big compound lifts with 2 minutes rest; ten sets of 10 does not raise it.
principles.quote: six sets of 10 repetitions even if it requires lightening the weight on one set to the next, with about two minutes 120 seconds rest in between sets.

principles.text: Test recovery on waking with grip strength and a CO2 blow-off time; a 15-20% drop means you are not recovered.
principles.quote: If they're starting to drop by anywhere from 15% to 20%, you're veering in the direction of not recovering.

principles.text: Avoid whole-body cold, antihistamines and NSAIDs within about 4 hours of training; they blunt adaptation.
principles.quote: cold after resistance training seems to short circuit some of the benefits of that resistance training.

sources.title: Optimizing testosterone and estrogen: breathing, light, cold, training, supplements
sources.originalTitle: The Science of How to Optimize Testosterone & Estrogen
sources.summary: Huberman explains how sex steroids are made and regulated, then gives levers for balancing testosterone and estrogen. Nasal breathing and apnea reduction, early bright light, cold exposure, heavy training, and foundational nutrients come first, with cautious notes on supplements and menopause compounds.

principles.text: Fix breathing first: apnea raises cortisol and lowers testosterone and estrogen, so breathe through your nose awake and asleep.
principles.quote: breath-holding in sleep leads to buildup of carbon dioxide and leads to increases in cortisol, which then decrease testosterone and decrease estrogen in negative ways across all sexes

principles.text: View bright light (ideally sunlight) early in the day and avoid bright light at night to support dopamine and sex hormones.
principles.quote: it means getting anywhere from 2 to 10 minutes of bright light exposure in your eyes early in the day

principles.text: Heavy lifting (about 1 to 8 reps) stopping short of failure raises testosterone for up to a day or two; lift before cardio.
principles.quote: weight training with heavy loads, so anywhere from one-rep maximum to somewhere in the six to eight repetition range, in males or females, increases testosterone significantly

principles.text: Cold exposure may raise gonadal hormones via rebound vasodilation, though the mechanism is indirect and understudied.
principles.quote: there's a rebound in vasodilation after cooling, so cooling causes vasoconstriction, and then after the cooling, there's a rebound vasodilation and there's more infusion of blood into the gonads

principles.text: Make sure zinc, magnesium and vitamin D3 are adequate, and check blood work before taking hormone-active supplements.
principles.quote: make sure you're getting adequate zinc, magnesium, and D3 unless you want these steroid hormone levels to be reduced for whatever reason

principles.text: The goal is a healthy ratio of testosterone to estrogen; more is not better.
principles.quote: more is definitely not better

sources.title: Huberman's daily protocol: light, caffeine timing, focus blocks, exercise, food, NSDR and sleep
sources.originalTitle: Maximizing Productivity, Physical & Mental Health with Daily Tools
sources.summary: Huberman walks through his 24-hour routine with the science behind each step: morning sunlight and walking, delaying caffeine, 90-minute focus blocks timed to temperature minimum, exercise structure, meal composition, NSDR/hypnosis, afternoon light, and a sleep-supporting evening with specific supplements.

principles.text: Get outdoor light in your eyes soon after waking (2-10+ min, longer if overcast) to time cortisol and set circadian rhythm.
principles.quote: getting sunlight in your eyes first thing in the morning is absolutely vital to mental and physical health

principles.text: Walk outdoors in the morning to generate optic flow, which lowers amygdala activity and anxiety while staying alert.
principles.quote: forward ambulation walking or biking or running and generating optic flow in particular has this incredible property of lowering activity in the amygdala

principles.text: Delay caffeine 90-120 minutes after waking to avoid an afternoon crash from adenosine rebound.
principles.quote: i purposely delay my caffeine intake to 90 minutes to 120 minutes after i wake up

principles.text: Do a 90-minute focused work block with no phone or internet, placed 4-6 hours after your temperature minimum (about 2 hours before usual wake time).
principles.quote: you can be reasonably sure that your best work is going to be done anywhere from four to six hours after your temperature minimum

principles.text: Position your screen at or above eye level; looking up raises alertness while looking down promotes sleepiness.
principles.quote: how open and upward directed your eyes are will increase your levels of alertness

principles.text: Eat lower-carb, protein-rich meals earlier for alertness and starchy carbs at dinner to raise serotonin and aid sleep.
principles.quote: starches cause the release of serotonin in the brain and lend themselves to a state of sleepiness

sources.title: Nutrients for brain health: omega-3s, choline, creatine, and how to rewire food preference
sources.originalTitle: Nutrients For Brain Health & Performance | Huberman Lab Podcast #42
sources.summary: Huberman lists foods and supplements that support neuron structure (EPA omega-3s, phosphatidylserine, choline, creatine, anthocyanins, glutamine) with doses. He then explains the three signals driving food choice (taste, gut nutrient sensing, learned belief) and how pairing foods can shift preference.

principles.text: Get at least 1.5 g/day of EPA omega-3s, ideally 2-3 g, from fish, plants or supplements.
principles.quote: everybody should be striving to get a minimum threshold of at least a gram and a half of EPAs per day one way or the other.

principles.text: Aim for roughly 500 mg to 1 g of choline daily, mainly from egg yolks, to support acetylcholine and focus.
principles.quote: most people should probably strive to get somewhere between 500 mg and a gram of choline per day, so 1,000 mg.

principles.text: Creatine monohydrate at 5 g/day supports cognition, especially for people who eat no meat.
principles.quote: creatine supplementation of 5 g per day, that's creatine monohydrate, has been shown to improve cognition in people that aren't getting creatine from animal sources

principles.text: Eat dark berries daily for anthocyanins: about 60-120 g of fresh blueberries.
principles.quote: somewhere between 60 to 120 g of fresh blueberries each day is the way that you can get sufficient anthocyanins

principles.text: Have two to four servings of low-sugar fermented foods daily to support gut health.
principles.quote: ingest two to four servings of fermented foods that are low in sugar each day.

principles.text: Take artificial sweeteners away from foods that raise blood glucose, since pairing disrupts insulin management.
principles.quote: if you're going to consume artificial sweeteners it's very likely best to consume those away from any food that raises blood glucose levels.

sources.title: Andrew Huberman on dopamine peaks and troughs, daily energy protocols, and friendship
sources.originalTitle: Andrew Huberman: You Must Control Your Dopamine! The Shocking Truth Behind Cold Showers!
sources.summary: Huberman explains dopamine as the currency of motivation that gets depleted after big peaks. He shows how to manage energy with NSDR, morning light, hydration, exercise, food and cold exposure. He also covers neuroplasticity, porn and dopamine, and why a daily good-morning text to a friend is among the most powerful social protocols.

principles.text: Big dopamine peaks are followed by a trough below baseline; the trough's depth tracks the peak's height, and chasing more only deepens it.
principles.quote: this trough below baseline, as Anna Lembke taught us with Dopamine Nation, that trough is a state that can last a long time.

principles.text: Compulsive behaviors usually resolve with a 30 to 60 day abstinence; wait out the trough rather than re-stimulating.
principles.quote: Most all addiction, most all compulsive behavior can be cured, essentially, through a period of abstinence lasting somewhere between 30 and 60 days

principles.text: Use NSDR/yoga nidra (10-20 min) to replenish dopamine and offset poor sleep.
principles.quote: NSDR, non-sleep deep rest, aka yoga nidra, can increase the baseline levels of dopamine in a brain area called the basal ganglia

principles.text: Start the day with hydration, then bright light (even overcast) and movement, ideally before caffeine, to lift mood, focus and sleep quality.
principles.quote: bright light in the morning, especially from sunlight, increases daytime mood, focus, and alertness, and it will improve your sleep later that night.

principles.text: Cold exposure works by releasing catecholamines; use the minimum dose that gives the alertness effect, not more.
principles.quote: Do it the minimum amount, so that you get the effect that you're seeking, which is to be more alert and motivated.

principles.text: Send a daily good-morning text to a friend; one reliable connection counters isolation.
principles.quote: One of the most powerful things that anyone can do, believe it or not, is to have someone each morning that they text good morning to.

sources.title: Controlling cortisol rhythm: high morning, low evening, and fixing two burnout patterns
sources.originalTitle: How to Control Your Cortisol & Overcome Burnout
sources.summary: Huberman reframes cortisol as an energy-deploying hormone, not just a stress hormone, and says the 24-hour rhythm (high early, low in the 4 hours before and 2 hours after sleep) underlies mood, sleep and health. He gives morning tools to amplify the peak, evening tools to keep cortisol low, and distinct fixes for two burnout patterns.

principles.text: Want cortisol high shortly after waking and low in the hours before and early in sleep; this rhythm anchors everything else.
principles.quote: You want your cortisol high early in the day, shortly after waking, and you want your cortisol low in the hours right before sleep and in the first hours of sleep.

principles.text: Get bright light, ideally sunlight, in your eyes within the first hour (ideally 30 min) of waking to boost the cortisol awakening response.
principles.quote: The protocol is to get bright light, ideally from sunlight, into your eyes within the first hour of waking. Ideally, within the first 30 minutes.

principles.text: A bigger morning cortisol peak sets up lower cortisol at night via negative feedback, helping you fall and stay asleep.
principles.quote: the higher that first peak in cortisol is early in the day, the better you're setting yourself up for low levels of cortisol later in the evening and at night

principles.text: Habitual caffeine users barely raise cortisol but extend its life; delaying caffeine 60-90 minutes can flatten the afternoon crash.
principles.quote: This is where the recommendation that I've been making for some years now of delaying your caffeine by anywhere from 60 to 90 minutes comes about.

principles.text: In the evening, dim overhead lights, favor red or amber light, and cut caffeine by about 2 p.m. to keep cortisol low.
principles.quote: I recommend a cut off of about 2 p.m.

principles.text: Use the physiological sigh and non-sleep deep rest to lower arousal; do behavioral steps before supplements like ashwagandha (300 mg) in the evening.
principles.quote: the fastest way to calm down in real time is going to be the so-called physiological sigh

sources.title: Huberman on cortisol bookending, top-down willpower, learning, stress and presence
sources.originalTitle: Why You’re Tired, Stressed & Unfocussed (and how to fix it) - Dr Andrew Huberman
sources.summary: Huberman explains bookending the day with high morning cortisol and low nighttime cortisol, and building top-down impulse control. He covers a learning protocol (alertness, errors, sleep, self-testing), physiological sighs, present-tethered awareness, a 4-step trauma framework, and a weekly cardio structure.

principles.text: Make the first hour of the day high cortisol and the last hour low cortisol; light, caffeine, exercise up front, dim lights at night.
principles.quote: Make the first hour of your day high cortisol and the last hour hour of your day low cortisol.

principles.text: Build top-down impulse control by choosing the harder option in small things all day; you are training the circuit, not the task.
principles.quote: what it proves is that it's the circuit. It's not what you're doing. You're getting the reps into the circuit.

principles.text: Learn by being alert, making genuine errors, then sleeping and self-testing; the error gap is the plasticity signal.
principles.quote: The error between what you currently do and what you're trying to do. The error is the signal that the neurons, the nerve cells need to change.

principles.text: To calm down fast, do deliberate long exhales, ideally two inhales then a full exhale (physiological sigh).
principles.quote: It's the fastest and most effective way to calm down fast. Better if you can do two big inhales first

principles.text: To be present, ask trivial questions about your immediate physical environment, then choose what to do or think next.
principles.quote: First, you ask trivial questions about your immediate environment that can only be answered accurately by focusing on the present.

principles.text: Daily nicotine pouches only rescue withdrawal; as a performance aid use it rarely, at most twice a week.
principles.quote: If you want nicotine to be a performance aid, you use it occasionally

sources.title: Morning light and the nervous system: Huberman's light, sleep and calming protocols with Rangan Chatterjee
sources.originalTitle: DO THIS In The Morning To Boost Energy, Improve Sleep & REDUCE FATIGUE! | Andrew Huberman
sources.summary: Huberman explains how bright light reaching the eyes early in the day sets the circadian clock, cortisol timing and nighttime melatonin, and why bright light late at night disrupts it. He adds free tools for calming and focus: the physiological sigh and panoramic vision.

principles.text: Get bright light, ideally sunlight, in your eyes within 30-60 minutes of waking, on most days.
principles.quote: التعرض لضوء ساطع، ويفضل ضوء الشمس، خلال 30 دقيقة إلى ساعة من الاستيقاظ

principles.text: Go outside for 5-10 minutes each morning; even an overcast sky beats indoor lighting.
principles.quote: ولكن بشكل عام، الخروج لمدة 5 إلى 10 دقائق كل صباح أمر مهم للغاية. حتى لو كان الجو غائماً، يظل الأمر مهماً.

principles.text: Avoid bright light, including screens, between 10 pm and 4 am; use dim, low-positioned lamps, firelight or candlelight.
principles.quote: بشكل أساسي، الوقت الذي يجب فيه تجنب الضوء هو ما بين العاشرة مساءً والرابعة فجراً.

principles.text: Don't wear blue-blocking glasses in the morning or during the day; blue wavelengths set your clock. Use them only late in the day.
principles.quote: بمعنى آخر، لا ترتدِ نظارات حجب الضوء الأزرق في الصباح وطوال اليوم.

principles.text: Use the physiological sigh for fast stress relief: two inhales through the nose, then a long exhale through the mouth.
principles.quote: هي القيام بشهيقين متتاليين عبر الأنف. الأول هو شهيق طويل وعميق، ثم في الشهيق الثاني لن تتمكن إلا من إدخال كمية ضئيلة من الهواء، يتبعها زفير طويل وكامل عبر الفم.

principles.text: Widen your gaze into panoramic vision without moving head or eyes to calm arousal subtly, without losing awareness.
principles.quote: ما عليك فعله هو فقط محاولة الرؤية دون تحريك رأسك أو عينيك. ما تحاول فعله هو توسيع نظرتك بحيث ترى المزيد من المساحة من حولك

sources.title: Toolkit for Sleep: Huberman's 12-point list for better sleep
sources.originalTitle: Toolkit for Sleep (Neural Network newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's condensed sleep protocol: anchor the circadian clock with morning and afternoon sunlight, keep consistent wake times, limit caffeine, alcohol and bright night lights, keep the bedroom cool, and use NSDR or select supplements as needed. Sleep is the foundation of health, but don't obsess over perfection.

principles.text: View sunlight outdoors within 30-60 min of waking and again in late afternoon before sunset.
principles.quote: View sunlight by going outside within 30-60 minutes of waking. Do that again in the late afternoon, prior to sunset.

principles.text: Scale sunlight time to cloud cover: 10 min bright, 20 min cloudy, 30-60 min very overcast.
principles.quote: On bright cloudless days: view morning and afternoon sun for 10 min; cloudy days: 20 min; very overcast days 30-60 min.

principles.text: Wake at the same time daily and go to bed when you first feel sleepy; pushing past sleepiness can cause 3 am waking.
principles.quote: Pushing through the sleepy late evening feeling and going to sleep too late (for you) is one reason people wake at 3 am and can’t fall back asleep.

principles.text: Avoid caffeine within 8-10 hours of bedtime.
principles.quote: Avoid caffeine within 8-10 hours of bedtime

principles.text: Limit artificial light at night, especially bright overhead lights between 10 pm and 4 am.
principles.quote: only use as much artificial lighting as is necessary for you to remain and move about safely at night.

principles.text: Keep the bedroom cool and dark; the body must drop 1-3 degrees to fall and stay asleep.
principles.quote: Your body needs to drop in temperature by 1-3 degrees to fall and stay asleep effectively.

sources.title: Improve Your Sleep: QQRT fundamentals, light, temperature, caffeine and falling-asleep protocols
sources.originalTitle: Improve Your Sleep (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's newsletter distills sleep protocols from the Matthew Walker guest series. It frames sleep as Quantity, Quality, Regularity and Timing (QQRT), then covers light/dark, temperature, meal and caffeine timing, a wind-down routine, avoiding alcohol, and tactics for trouble falling asleep.

principles.text: Judge sleep by QQRT: quantity (7-9 hours), quality, regularity and timing with your chronotype.
principles.quote: The typical adult needs sleep **7 to 9 hours of sleep per night**.

principles.text: Keep bed and wake times within about 30 minutes every day, weekends included, to anchor your circadian clock.
principles.quote: Aim for **consistent bedtimes and wake times** with a ± 30 minutes margin of error, whether it’s the **weekend or a weekday.**

principles.text: Get 10-15 minutes of morning sunlight, even on overcast days, and dim lights in the evening.
principles.quote: Upon waking, go outside for **10-15 minutes of morning sunlight**.

principles.text: Core body temperature must drop to fall asleep: keep the room cool and take a warm bath or shower before bed.
principles.quote: To fall asleep, **core body temperature must decrease** by approximately 2-3°F (1°C).

principles.text: Caffeine only masks sleepiness; take it early and not within 8-10 hours of bedtime.
principles.quote: Caffeine does not reduce the need for sleep; it only temporarily masks sleepiness.

principles.text: If you can't fall asleep in about 20-25 minutes, leave bed to relax, and avoid compensating after a bad night.
principles.quote: If it’s taking longer than **~20-25 minutes** to fall asleep or back asleep, leave your bed and go elsewhere in the house to engage in a relaxing activity.

sources.title: Huberman's top 10 sleep Q&A: practical protocols from the Matt Walker series
sources.originalTitle: Your Top Questions on Sleep, Answered (newsletter)
sources.summary: Andrew Huberman summarizes the 10 most popular audience sleep questions from his guest series with Dr. Matt Walker. Covers racing thoughts, sleeping position, 3:30 a.m. waking, banking sleep, aging, menopause, dreams, supplements, and the single most important tip: sleep regularity and timing.

principles.text: Use meditation, body scans/NSDR, long-exhale breathing, or a mental walk to quiet racing thoughts at sleep onset.
principles.quote: Body scans – where your focus moves progressively from one part of the body to another. (Non-sleep deep rest, or NSDR, typically includes a body scan and can be very effective in helping you fall asleep.

principles.text: Avoid sleeping on your back; monitor snoring and see a doctor if confirmed, since sleep apnea is widely undiagnosed.
principles.quote: **Avoid sleeping on your back**, as it increases the likelihood of **snoring** or that your airway could collapse, causing a “hypoxic event.”

principles.text: Remove visible clocks from the bedroom; checking the time at night trains your brain to keep waking at that time.
principles.quote: Checking the time when you wake up at night can train your brain to continue waking at that time.

principles.text: You can't fully repay sleep debt on weekends; only about 25% of lost hours are recouped, though you can bank sleep before anticipated loss.
principles.quote: You can’t accumulate a sleep “debt” and then pay it off later, such as on the weekend. The body can **only recoup ~25% of the lost hours**.

principles.text: When awake at night, don't try hard to fall asleep; embrace rest and use NSDR to fall back asleep.
principles.quote: **Don’t try too hard!** Getting back to sleep can be frustrating. Instead of trying hard to fall asleep, which can often be counterproductive, take a more relaxed approach.

principles.text: Fix behaviors and light/temperature before supplements, and keep a consistent sleep and wake schedule, even on weekends.
principles.quote: Keep your sleep schedule regular by keeping your sleeping and waking times consistent (**even on weekends!**).

sources.title: Using Light for Health: Huberman's zero-cost sunlight and lighting protocol
sources.originalTitle: Using Light for Health (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's newsletter distills his light protocols: view sunlight within the first hours of waking, get afternoon sun, use bright overhead light for daytime focus, dim lights and avoid bright light at night, and sleep in a very dark room. He also covers red light and afternoon skin sunlight for hormones.

principles.text: View morning sunlight within the first hours of waking: 5-10 min on sunny days, 15-20+ min if overcast.
principles.quote: On a **sunny morning**, get outside for **5-10 minutes.**

principles.text: Morning sunlight raises early-day cortisol and sets the circadian clock, preparing you for sleep that night.
principles.quote: Viewing sunlight within the first hours of waking (as soon as you can, even if through cloud cover) **increases early-day cortisol release**

principles.text: Don't view morning light through a window or windshield; sunglasses and blue blockers reduce the effect.
principles.quote: trying to do all this through a windshield or window won’t work; too many of the relevant wavelengths are filtered out.

principles.text: Get afternoon sun to cue the evening transition to sleep and act as a second circadian anchor.
principles.quote: Sunlight viewed in the late afternoon/evening communicates to the brain’s circadian clock that it is evening and time to begin the process of transitioning **to sleep that night**.

principles.text: For daytime focus, use bright overhead lights and a desk near a window, then dim and reduce blue light in late afternoon.
principles.quote: In the morning and until the midafternoon, use **bright overhead lights** to facilitate the release of dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine

principles.text: Avoid bright light at night; use red or very dim light if you must get up, and sleep in a very dark room.
principles.quote: So, if you need to get up in the middle of the night (to use the bathroom or check on children, etc.), try using **no light or very dim light.**

sources.title: Dopamine toolkit: managing baseline, peaks, and motivation (newsletter)
sources.originalTitle: Tools to Manage Dopamine and Improve Motivation and Drive (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman explains dopamine as the molecule of wanting and motivation, then lists ways to keep baseline healthy (morning sun, tyrosine, avoiding late-night light and melatonin, caffeine) and to manage peaks (random intermittent rewards, subjective control, spotlighting, not stacking stimulants, supplement microspiking).

principles.text: Dopamine drives wanting and motivation, not having; serotonin relates to well-being about what you already have.
principles.quote: The simplest way to think about dopamine is that when our dopamine levels are elevated, we tend to focus our attention on outward goals — the things we want — and we feel motivated to pursue them.

principles.text: View early morning sunlight for 10-30 minutes daily to raise baseline dopamine; a brief cold shower adds to it.
principles.quote: Viewing early morning sunlight** for 10-30 minutes daily.

principles.text: Avoid bright light between 10 p.m. and 4 a.m., since it reduces circulating dopamine via the habenula; keep it very dim if needed.
principles.quote: Avoid viewing bright lights between 10 p.m.-4 a.m**.

principles.text: Eat tyrosine-rich foods, avoid melatonin supplements (except for jet lag), and use caffeine (100-400mg) early, not close to sleep.
principles.quote: Tyrosine is an amino acid and a building block of dopamine — a diet rich in tyrosine will sustain your body’s natural dopamine production.

principles.text: Use random intermittent reward timing: celebrate some wins, not every one, and tie winning to the effort process itself.
principles.quote: The key is to **celebrate your wins, but do not celebrate every win**.

principles.text: Don't layer too many dopamine sources (preworkout, music, nootropics, etc.); stacking causes a crash and undermines long-term drive.
principles.quote: But stacking all these dopamine-triggering sources causes a crash afterward, ultimately undermining our longer-term motivation and continued drive.

sources.title: Foundational Fitness Protocol: weekly plan covering strength, hypertrophy, endurance and recovery
sources.originalTitle: Foundational Fitness Protocol (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's newsletter outlines a weekly template that trains every major fitness goal, with resistance training periodized monthly between heavier and lighter schedules. It also covers session length, breathing, stretching, ice-bath timing, fasted vs fed training, handling illness or stress, and performance supplements.

principles.text: Alternate monthly between a heavy low-rep schedule and a moderate higher-rep schedule for strength and hypertrophy.
principles.quote: Schedule A: ~4-8 repetitions (heavier weights) and 3-4 sets per exercise with 2-4 minutes rest between sets

principles.text: Use two exercises per muscle: one at the shortened position, one under load at the lengthened position.
principles.quote: Exercise #2 should focus on resistance occurring for the muscle group when it is in a lengthened position

principles.text: Keep weight workouts to 50-60 minutes of hard work after warmup, 75 minutes max.
principles.quote: Keep weight workouts to 50-60 minutes of hard work after a warmup, 75 minutes maximum. This assists effectiveness and recovery.

principles.text: Avoid ice baths right after resistance training; wait 6-8 hours or do them before.
principles.quote: If you do ice baths on weight training days, wait 6-8 hours, or do them before training.

principles.text: Improve flexibility with 30-60 second static stretches, 3x/week to daily, with long exhales.
principles.quote: Hold each major muscle group in a static stretch for 30-60 seconds and repeat between 3x/week and daily.

principles.text: Use physiological sighs between sets and slow breathing afterward to downshift and aid recovery.
principles.quote: After a training session, use 3-5 minutes of deliberate slow breathing to “downshift” the nervous system, relax the mind and body and aid muscle recovery.

sources.title: Cold exposure protocol: 11 min/week, dopamine, resilience, metabolism and recovery
sources.originalTitle: The Science and Use of Cold Exposure for Health and Performance (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's newsletter on deliberate cold exposure. Aim for uncomfortably cold but safe water, about 11 minutes total per week across 2-4 sessions. Benefits include sustained dopamine, adrenaline and focus, top-down resilience training, and metabolic effects. Covers timing, shivering, workout recovery trade-offs and safety.

principles.text: Pick a temperature that is really cold and makes you want out, yet is safe to stay in. Colder means shorter exposure.
principles.quote: The key is to aim for a temperature that evokes the thought, “This is really cold (!), and I want to get out, BUT I can safely stay in.”

principles.text: Baseline protocol: 11 minutes of deliberate cold per week total, split into 2-4 sessions of 1-5 minutes.
principles.quote: Consider doing deliberate cold exposure for 11 minutes per week TOTAL. NOT per session, but rather, 2-4 sessions lasting 1-5 mins each distributed across the week.

principles.text: Cold releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, raising alertness, energy and focus that carry over after the exposure.
principles.quote: Cold causes their levels to stay elevated for some time and their ongoing effect after the exposure is to increase your level of energy and focus

principles.text: Cold causes a prolonged dopamine release, lifting mood, energy and focus even from short bouts.
principles.quote: Even short bouts of cold exposure can cause a lasting increase in dopamine and sustained elevation of mood, energy, and focus.

principles.text: Choosing cold as a stressor trains prefrontal top-down control, building resilience that transfers to real-world stress.
principles.quote: deliberate cold exposure is great training for the mind.

principles.text: Do cold early in the day, not near bedtime, since the post-cold rise in body temperature promotes wakefulness.
principles.quote: I suggest using deliberate cold early in the day and not too close to bedtime.

sources.title: Deliberate heat exposure: sauna protocols for cardiovascular health, mood, and growth hormone
sources.originalTitle: Deliberate Heat Exposure Protocols for Health and Performance (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's newsletter distills his heat exposure episode into three sauna protocols: cardiovascular health, general health/mood/stress, and growth hormone release. It covers temperature and duration targets, hydration, timing for sleep, and safety cautions including sperm count, pregnancy, and infrared saunas.

principles.text: For cardiovascular health, sauna at 80-100°C for 5-20 minutes, 2-7 times per week; more often seems better.
principles.quote: Heat the sauna to a temperature in the range of **80-100 ℃; 176-212 ℉.**

principles.text: For general health, mood and stress resilience, do about 1 hour of sauna per week split into 2-3 sessions.
principles.quote: use sauna for a total of **1 hour per week**, but not all at once. Rather, split that into **2 to 3 sessions.**

principles.text: Heat is a hormetic stressor: regular sauna lowers cortisol and activates heat shock proteins and DNA repair/longevity pathways.
principles.quote: Studies have found that the regular use of sauna can [decrease cortisol levels]

principles.text: To boost growth hormone, do rare, long sauna days (once a week or less): four 30-minute sessions with cool-downs, in a semi-fasted state.
principles.quote: use the sauna in a **semi-fasted state** (having not ingested food for 2 to 3 hours prior).

principles.text: Hydrate well (16 oz water per 10 minutes in the sauna) and use sauna in the afternoon/evening to aid sleep onset.
principles.quote: Drink at least **16 ounces of water for every 10 minutes** you spend in the sauna.

principles.text: Safety: start with cooler temperatures; pregnant women and children under 16 should not sauna; heat can reduce sperm count for ~45-60 days.
principles.quote: in general, pregnant women and children younger than 16 should not sauna.

sources.title: Breathwork Protocols: physiological sigh, box breathing, cyclic hyperventilation, and heart rate
sources.originalTitle: Breathwork Protocols for Health, Focus and Stress (newsletter)
sources.summary: Andrew Huberman explains how deliberate breathing patterns shift brain-body state. He covers reducing overbreathing, the CO2 tolerance test, the physiological sigh for fast calming, cyclic hyperventilation for alertness, and using inhale/exhale emphasis to raise or lower heart rate.

principles.text: Most people overbreathe; nasal breathing and pauses between breaths reduce it and protect focus and calm.
principles.quote: Overbreathing causes excessive exhalation, thereby reducing carbon dioxide (this is termed “hypocapnia”) and decreasing oxygen delivery to the brain and other tissues.

principles.text: Use the physiological sige (double nasal inhale, long mouth exhale) as the fastest real-time calming tool.
principles.quote: It is — to my knowledge, the fastest way to calm down in real time.

principles.text: Practice 5 minutes of cyclic physiological sighs daily to lower stress, improve sleep and mood, and reduce resting heart rate.
principles.quote: cyclic physiological sighs, practiced daily for 5 minutes, reduce overall stress, promote relaxation, improve sleep, lower resting heart rate and enhance mood.

principles.text: Cyclic hyperventilation boosts alertness and focus via adrenaline; avoid it near water or while driving.
principles.quote: And never, ever perform cyclic hyperventilation near or in any body of water or while driving.

principles.text: Test CO2 tolerance with a slow full exhale, then do 2-3 minutes of box breathing 1-2x per week to improve diaphragm control.
principles.quote: practice 2-3 minutes of box breathing, 1-2x per week, to improve your diaphragmatic control and learn to increase your CO2 discard rate.

principles.text: Longer exhales lower heart rate; longer, more vigorous inhales raise it, usable anytime without formal breathwork.
principles.quote: To increase your heart rate: deliberately inhale longer and more deeply/vigorously than you exhale. To decrease your heart rate: exhale longer and more vigorously than you inhale.

sources.title: Improve Working Memory and Attention: Dopamine, NSDR, Cold Exposure, Binaural Beats and Supplements
sources.originalTitle: Improve Working Memory and Attention (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman explains working memory as dopamine-dependent and gives two self-tests as a proxy for baseline dopamine. He lays out behavioral tools first (NSDR, deliberate cold, binaural beats), then cautious supplement and prescription options with dosing guidance.

principles.text: Working memory depends on attention and the neuromodulator dopamine; capacity supports task-switching and focused productivity.
principles.quote: Working memory requires attention and is critically dependent on the neuromodulator dopamine.

principles.text: Do NSDR/yoga nidra 2-3x per week for 10-20 minutes; it has been shown to raise dopamine in key brain regions.
principles.quote: Consider incorporating this practice **2-3x per week** in **10-to-20-minute sessions**.

principles.text: Do 1-3 minutes of deliberate cold exposure 30-60 minutes before a work bout needing working memory.
principles.quote: try incorporating a deliberate cold exposure of 1-3 minutes in duration **30-60 minutes prior** to a work bout requiring working memory.

principles.text: Pick a cold temperature that is uncomfortable but safe for 60-180 seconds; for most people 40-50°F works, though it is individual.
principles.quote: The ideal water **temperature is highly individual**, a temperature you can safely stay in for 60-180 seconds but is uncomfortable enough that it takes some mental effort to get in and makes you want to get out.

principles.text: 13-30 Hz binaural beats may help working memory but data is mixed; people with lower baseline dopamine benefit most from raising it.
principles.quote: Those with initially lower dopamine apparently benefit more from increasing it than those with already high levels of dopamine at the outset, which makes logical sense.

principles.text: Try behavioral tools before dopamine-boosting supplements like L-tyrosine or Mucuna pruriens; find the minimal effective dose and consult a doctor.
principles.quote: Try the above behavioral tools first, before adding **supplements to boost dopamine**.

sources.title: Neuroplasticity Super-Protocol: 9 steps to teach and learn anything faster
sources.originalTitle: Teach and Learn Better With a Neuroplasticity Super-Protocol (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's newsletter distills the science of neuroplasticity into a nine-step behavioral protocol for learning. It covers getting alert and focused, doing fast repetitions, embracing errors, inserting micro-rests, random rewards, limiting sessions to 90 minutes, then NSDR and deep sleep to consolidate. Steps 1, 2 and 9 are non-negotiable.

principles.text: Get alert before learning, using deep breathing with an empty-lung hold.
principles.quote: One simple way to become more alert is 25-30 deep breaths (inhales through the nose, and exhales through the mouth).

principles.text: Build focus by staring at a point for 30-60 seconds before the task; mental focus follows visual focus.
principles.quote: Mental focus follows visual focus. To increase your level of focus on the task you are about to do, stare at a point on a wall or screen, or object for 30-60 seconds before starting

principles.text: Expect and embrace errors; they increase alertness and set up the next attempt (~15% error rate may be optimal).
principles.quote: Provided they don’t comprise safety, errors during learning are terrific because they increase activation of the neural circuits that increase alertness.

principles.text: Insert random 10-second micro-rests (about one per 2 minutes) during learning to get faster neural replay.
principles.quote: randomly introduce 10 second pauses during learning. “How often?” I get asked. A ratio of approximately 1 pause per every 2 minutes of learning is good

principles.text: Cap intense learning bouts at ~90 minutes, spaced hours apart, and follow with NSDR within an hour.
principles.quote: Within 1 hour of completing a learning bout, do a short NSDR protocol.

principles.text: Sleep is where learning rewiring actually happens; the learning bout is only the trigger.
principles.quote: Think of the learning bout as the “trigger” or stimulus for the possibility that we might learn, but sleep and NSDR are when the actual learning- the neural circuit rewiring, occurs.

sources.title: Using caffeine for mental and physical performance: dose, timing, sleep and abstinence tools
sources.originalTitle: Use Caffeine for Mental and Physical Performance (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's newsletter on caffeine: how to find your dose (1-3 mg/kg), time it around sleep and afternoon crashes, hydrate with salt, and use abstinence to boost athletic performance. He also warns about dopamine stacking and explains how caffeine reinforces behaviors, so pair it with habits you want to build and avoid pairing it with ones you want to quit.

principles.text: Start with 1-3 mg caffeine per kg body weight; go lower if sensitive.
principles.quote: Dose: Start with 1 to 3 mg of caffeine per kilogram body weight. If sensitive, start lower.

principles.text: Avoid caffeine within 10-12 hours of bedtime, since it disrupts deep and REM sleep even if you fall asleep.
principles.quote: To protect your sleep, its typically best to avoid caffeine for least 10-12 hours before bedtime.

principles.text: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and has a quarter-life of about 12 hours for most people.
principles.quote: for most people, caffeine has a quarter-life of approximately 12 hours. So, if you consume caffeine at noon, about 25% of it is still active in your body by midnight.

principles.text: Drink equal volumes of water with caffeine, ideally with a pinch of salt or electrolytes, to avoid jitteriness.
principles.quote: Consume equal volumes of water with your caffeine to avoid jitteriness, blurry vision or a low blood sugar feeling.

principles.text: Abstain from caffeine for days before a big physical challenge, then dose about 30 minutes before the start.
principles.quote: To experience the maximum performance-enhancing effects of caffeine, abstain from caffeine for a few days (3 to 20 days).

principles.text: Don't habitually stack dopamine boosters; spikes are followed by a dip below baseline, and re-spiking lowers baseline further.
principles.quote: The worst thing you can do in the below-baseline phase is to try and spike your dopamine again with pharmacology, as that will drive your baseline down even more.

sources.title: Build or break habits: Huberman's three-phase day and 21-day habit blocks
sources.originalTitle: Build or Break Habits Using Science-Based Tools (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman lays out a two-part habit framework. Split each waking day into three phases that match your neurochemistry, and alternate 21-day blocks of building habits with 21-day blocks of testing which stuck. He also gives a simple rule for breaking habits: notice the behavior, then do a positive action right after.

principles.text: Do effortful, focus-demanding habits in the first 8 hours after waking, when dopamine, adrenaline and cortisol are high.
principles.quote: Set 1-4 habits for completion in Phase 1. These should be the habits that require energy and focus.

principles.text: Use a flexible time window (e.g. before noon) rather than a fixed clock time for Phase 1 habits.
principles.quote: Setting a window for completion (e.g., 45 min of focused reading, work, etc. in Phase 1) rather than a precise start and stop time lends flexibility to your schedule.

principles.text: Hours 9-15 after waking suit looser, creative, low-focus habits like brainstorming, play or Zone 2 cardio.
principles.quote: Leverage your naturally higher serotonin levels and lower adrenaline, and engage in habits that don’t require you to overcome much limbic friction.

principles.text: Phase 3 (hours 16-24) is for resetting your capacity for habits through sleep: avoid bright lights and sleep cool and dark.
principles.quote: This is when we reset our ability to overcome limbic friction by, you guessed it, resting and sleeping.

principles.text: Pick six new habits per day for 21 days, aim for four to six, and never compensate by doing more than six.
principles.quote: Do not fret about only doing four out of six of the new habits per day, and never compensate by doing more than six per day.

principles.text: Alternate 21 days of habit formation with 21 days of tracking without adding new habits, to see what actually stuck. Habit strength depends on limbic friction and context-dependence.
principles.quote: The strength of a habit is dictated by how much limbic friction you need to overcome to perform the behavior and how much context-dependence there is

sources.title: Gut microbiome: 6 tools to increase diversity and support brain and body health
sources.originalTitle: 6 Key Tools to Improve Your Gut Microbiome Health (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman summarizes six levers for gut microbiome diversity, drawing on his conversation with Stanford's Justin Sonnenburg: fermented foods, targeted prebiotics/probiotics, sleep, avoiding processed foods, caution with artificial sweeteners, and not over-sanitizing. Emphasis is on consistency and whole, plant-fiber-rich foods.

principles.text: Eat low-sugar fermented foods consistently; they raise microbiome diversity and lower inflammation.
principles.quote: consistently incorporate fermented foods into your daily diet to achieve better outcomes for gut microbiome health and inflammation reduction.

principles.text: Buy refrigerated fermented foods with live active cultures; shelf-stable ones are pasteurized.
principles.quote: Find these products in the refrigerator section to ensure there are live active cultures.

principles.text: Use low levels of pre/probiotics normally and higher levels after antibiotics, stress or travel; excess can cause brain fog.
principles.quote: the excessive intake of probiotics has been linked to the induction of brain fog; therefore, if you experience these symptoms, you could try to reduce the level of supplements that you are ingesting.

principles.text: Prioritize quality sleep (generally 6-9 hours) because the gut microbiome is tied to stress.
principles.quote: achieving the proper quality (deep) and duration (generally 6-9 hours) of sleep each night is essential to manage stress and, in turn, to ensure gut microbiome health.

principles.text: Favor whole foods, plant fiber and fermented foods over processed foods, whose emulsifiers disrupt the gut.
principles.quote: To enhance the health of your gut microbiome, prioritize a diet rich in whole foods, plant-based fiber, and fermented foods.

principles.text: Consider trimming artificial sweeteners to see if you notice an effect; stevia is probably fine.
principles.quote: Potentially, try removing some artificial sweeteners from your diet to see if you notice an effect and also consider that artificial sweeteners might be capable of influencing your gut microbiome.

sources.title: Water: Hydration Targets, Tap Water Filtering and Water Types
sources.originalTitle: Optimize Your Water Quality and Intake for Health (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman explains how to hydrate well: roughly 80 oz in the first 10 hours after waking, more with exercise, heat, sauna or caffeine, and electrolytes. He also covers filtering tap water and which water types are worth drinking, dismissing claims that water changes body pH.

principles.text: Drink about 80 oz of fluid in the first 10 hours after waking, spread out as practical.
principles.quote: Eighty ounces in the first 10 hours of your day, spread out as is practical, is just fine.

principles.text: Even mild dehydration hurts physical performance, alertness and focus, and can cause brain fog.
principles.quote: Dehydration (even mild dehydration) negatively impacts physical performance, alertness and cognitive focus, and thereby can cause “brain fog.”

principles.text: Front-load water in the daytime and cut fluids 2-3 hours before sleep to reduce night urination.
principles.quote: Reduce fluid intake in the evening and in the 2-3 hrs before sleep.

principles.text: During exercise, drink body weight in lbs divided by 30 oz every 15-20 minutes, more in heat or sauna.
principles.quote: Body weight (in lbs.) divided by 30 = number of ounces to consume every 15-20 minutes

principles.text: Offset caffeine with about twice the fluid, ideally with electrolytes; thirst lags true hydration status.
principles.quote: your **perception of thirst lags behind the body’s true hydration status**. So not being thirsty does not mean you don’t need more fluid.

principles.text: Filter tap water since it contains contaminants; options range from free settling to whole-house systems, and don't boil it.
principles.quote: do not opt for boiling tap water as a filtration method because high heat can actually make contaminants worse.

sources.title: Toolkit for Setting & Achieving Goals: 6 goal-setting steps and 7 pursuit tools
sources.originalTitle: Toolkit for Setting and Achieving Goals (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's newsletter lays out a protocol for choosing one ambitious goal, defining it in a 12-week measurable plan, and sustaining pursuit. Tools cover visualizing failure, visual targeting, phone removal, random rewards, handling mid-goal slumps, and timing work to circadian attention peaks.

principles.text: Pick one priority goal; pursuing many habit overhauls at once usually fails all of them.
principles.quote: Pursuing too many goals simultaneously often leads to failure of all goals. Instead, **set a priority goal**

principles.text: Make the goal lofty and give it a 12-week window with set hours, days, session length and time window.
principles.quote: I’d suggest a **12-week** time period is appropriate for most goals.

principles.text: Don't announce a new goal; positive feedback activates reward circuits and reduces motivation to do the work.
principles.quote: receiving positive feedback on a newly set goal can **undermine your success**.

principles.text: Visualize failure on unmotivated days for 1-3 minutes; it recruits adrenaline to raise arousal and focus.
principles.quote: It will recruit neurochemicals, like adrenaline, to boost your levels of arousal and focus.

principles.text: Use a visual target: hold gaze on one point for 30-90 seconds to increase alertness and motivation.
principles.quote: Hold it in your gaze for 30-90 seconds.

principles.text: Use random intermittent rewards (coin flip) rather than constant or finish-line-only rewards to sustain motivation.
principles.quote: Use **random, intermittent rewards** (like a slot machine) to maintain motivation.

sources.title: Defeat Jet Lag: shifting your clock with light, meals, exercise and caffeine
sources.originalTitle: Defeat Jet Lag (newsletter)
sources.summary: Huberman's newsletter explains how to cut jet lag by pre-shifting your circadian clock before travel and timing light, meals, exercise and caffeine at the destination. The key tool is timing bright light relative to your home-time temperature minimum, roughly two hours before usual wake-up.

principles.text: Pre-shift for eastward travel: wake 30-45 min earlier for two days, with bright light on waking, early caffeine and movement.
principles.quote: Starting two days before you leave, try waking up 30 to 45 minutes prior to your usual wake-up time and view bright sunlight or bright artificial light as soon as you wake up.

principles.text: For westward travel, shift light, caffeine and workouts about 45 minutes later and get bright light after sunset.
principles.quote: You’ll also want to make sure that you get bright light exposure to your eyes from artificial lights in the one to two hours after sunset.

principles.text: Your temperature minimum is about two hours before usual wake-up; light after it advances your clock, light before it delays it.
principles.quote: If you get bright light exposure to your eyes in the one to two hours after your temperature minimum, you will adjust your circadian clock such that it will make you want to go to sleep earlier in the subsequent nights and wake up earlier in the subsequent mornings.

principles.text: Use your home-time temperature minimum at the destination; wear dark sunglasses in that window for the first days to avoid shifting the wrong way.
principles.quote: It would be better to wear dark sunglasses during the two to three hours before your temperature minimum for the first two days in London.

principles.text: Eat on the local meal schedule on arrival to entrain your clock; fasting 14-16 hours before local breakfast can help.
principles.quote: Eating is a strong mechanism for entraining (setting) your circadian clock.

principles.text: Carry a 5,000-10,000 lux light for cloudy days, wear red-lens glasses after sundown, and keep exercise early in the local day.
principles.quote: What you can do, however, is travel with a portable bright light device (you’ll want one with 5,000-10,000 lux brightness) to use to shift your clock.

sources.title: Tim Ferriss Show #660: Huberman's five daily foundations, weekly training split, supplements, and fertility
sources.originalTitle: Tim Ferriss Show #660 transcript: Dr. Andrew Huberman
sources.summary: Huberman lays out five foundations to re-up every 24 hours (sleep, nutrients, movement, light, relationships), then details his weekly training split, sleep and performance supplements, gut and fertility tips, and his changed stance on supervised psychedelics.

principles.text: Re-up five foundations every 24 hours: sleep, nutrients, movement, light, relationships; nothing else works without them.
principles.quote: you have to re-up on each and every one of those five things every 24 hours.

principles.text: Train different adaptations on different days: endurance, leg strength, heat/cold, torso, VO2 max, with workouts under about 60 minutes.
principles.quote: there’s an optimal training schedule for me that allows me to target one specific thing each day.

principles.text: Keep resistance sessions under 60 minutes; longer raises cortisol and hurts sleep and recovery.
principles.quote: if you start training for longer than 60 minutes with resistance training, cortisol levels go up, you start feeling lousy, you’re not sleeping well

principles.text: Front-load the day: hydrate heavily, get sunlight and movement early; sip your last fluids at night to avoid waking to urinate.
principles.quote: you want to hydrate pretty heavily first thing in the morning, and then over the day you can titrate off that liquid.

principles.text: Sleep stack: magnesium threonate, theanine, apigenin, occasionally 900 mg myo-inositol; if only two, mag threonate and apigenin.
principles.quote: So it’s magnesium threonate, spelled T-H-R-E-O-N-A-T-E, theanine, and apigenin.

principles.text: Take at least 1 g/day of EPA for mood; fermented foods (3-4 servings low-sugar) support gut health.
principles.quote: Minimum one gram per day of EPA.

sources.title: Andrew Huberman on peptides, training split, psychedelics and cortisol bookending (Tim Ferriss Show)
sources.originalTitle: Tim Ferriss Show transcript: Dr. Andrew Huberman on peptides, performance and protocols
sources.summary: Huberman describes his Dorian Yates-style low-volume, high-intensity split plus cardio, and explains the cortisol principle of high morning and low night levels. He reviews peptide categories (GLPs, GH secretagogues, BPC-157, pinealon) with a skeptical, risk-aware lens, and shares his MDMA plus psilocybin experience.

principles.text: Bookend the day: high cortisol in the morning and low at night supports melatonin and sleep; the principle matters more than any single tool.
principles.quote: you want to bookend the day with high cortisol in the morning whenever your morning happens to be.

principles.text: Train each muscle group hard once a week directly, with a second indirect hit from other training, using low-ish volume to failure.
principles.quote: you train each body part directly once per week, it gets hit indirectly a second time per week, you give it plenty of rest

principles.text: Structure a week of 3 resistance days and 3 cardio days: long slow, max-effort intervals, and moderate sessions.
principles.quote: this arrangement of three times per week of resistance training, three times a week of cardio, you're training everything directly once a week and indirectly a second time

principles.text: Compound movements must anchor high-intensity training; isolation work alone does not replace them.
principles.quote: There's no world where you can just do isolation movements this way.

principles.text: Peptides are mostly overhyped except GLPs and anecdotally pinealon; fix sleep, light and caffeine first, and prefer clean compounded sourcing over gray market.
principles.quote: I don't think you need pinealon until you've tried everything else

principles.text: Raise REM without drugs by warming the sleep environment in the final two hours; alpha GPC (900 mg) allows late workouts without caffeine.
principles.quote: you can heat up your sleeping environment in the final two hours of your sleep. You'll get much more REM.

sources.title: Diary of a CEO: Huberman's 10 daily protocols from Protocols
sources.originalTitle: Diary of a CEO transcript: Andrew Huberman's 10 daily protocols
sources.summary: Huberman walks through ten daily practices in sequence: hydration, morning light, early exercise, cold exposure, physiological sighs, evening light, a dark sleep environment, focused learning, and personal development. The through-line is a high morning cortisol peak that sets up low cortisol and good sleep at night. He also covers a short supplement stack, walking after meals, and his views on peptides and prayer.

principles.text: Aim for a high cortisol peak early in the day; it sets up low cortisol and better sleep at night.
principles.quote: You want this peak in cortisol as high as possible in the first 60 minutes of your day.

principles.text: Get daylight in your eyes early in the day, outdoors rather than through glass; use a 10,000 lux light if there is no sun.
principles.quote: But you want daylight in your eyes in the first hours of your day. Go out on your balcony if that's all you can do.
