- Andrew does NSDR or Reverie hypnosis most days in the early afternoon. It replenishes him and has improved his ability to fall and stay asleep.
- Afternoon or evening intense exercise raises body temperature and delays the circadian clock, so you want to sleep later. Exercise early in the day, within 0-4 hours of waking, doesn't shift the clock much.
- He cites research suggesting exercise right after waking, 3 hours after waking, or 11 hours after waking, but says it's hard to be prescriptive.
- Get low-angle sunlight in the eyes in the late afternoon or around sunset, for 5-30 minutes depending on cloud cover.
  - It acts on the evening oscillators and sets a second anchor point for the clock.
  - It partly (not fully) inoculates against the harm of artificial light at night.
  - The brain distinguishes morning from evening light by the yellow-blue-orange ratio.
- During the day, bright overhead lights help alertness.

chunks.heading: Evening and night: light, temperature and sleeping environment
chunks.text:
- Light at night:
  - Between 10 p.m. and 4 a.m., avoid bright artificial light of any color, especially overhead light.
  - Very little light is enough at night to disrupt the clock and suppress melatonin, the reverse of the morning, when you need a lot.
  - Photosensitive cells sit in the lower retina, which views the upper visual field, so overhead lights mimic daytime sun. Use low lamps and floor lights.
  - Dim screens. Candlelight is about 3-10 lux and moonlight is low. Desk or overhead lights are 100-1,000 lux. Supermarket and gas-station fluorescents are the worst.
  - Andrew has worn sunglasses at night in those places.
  - Blue blockers aren't necessary, because bright light of any color wakes you.
- Temperature:
  - Core temperature must drop 1-3 degrees for sleep onset, and a rise of the same size wakes you.
  - Avoid cold showers at night.
  - A hot bath, hot tub or sauna for no more than 20-30 minutes, followed by getting out, triggers a compensatory drop that helps sleep. It can also help if you're wired from caffeine or late exercise.
  - Keep the bedroom cool, lowering it at least 3 degrees. An Eight Sleep or a fan also works.
  - Heat leaves through glabrous skin: palms, soles and the upper face. Putting a hand or foot out from the blankets cools you.
  - Andrew doesn't wear socks to bed, though they help people who wake with cold feet.
- Alcohol and THC can help people fall asleep, but they degrade sleep architecture. Andrew doesn't drink, since alcohol just knocks him out and the sleep is disrupted.
- CBD and THC edibles may lower anxiety for some people.

chunks.heading: Sleep supplements and dosages
chunks.text:
- Andrew's order of operations: behavior first, then nutrition, then supplements, then prescription drugs. Check with a physician before adding or removing a supplement.
- The base stack, taken 30-60 minutes before bed, especially if you haven't eaten for about 3 hours:
  - Magnesium threonate: 145 mg.
  - Apigenin: 50 mg.
  - Theanine: 100-400 mg.
- You need not take all three, and some people need none.
  - About 5% report that magnesium threonate upsets their gut. If it does, skip it.
  - Some find theanine causes vivid or anxious dreams, so they leave it out.
- Single-ingredient products let you titrate and add or remove one component at a time.
- Extras Andrew adds:
  - Every third or fourth night: 2 g glycine plus 100 mg GABA. More often and the stack seems to work less well.
  - Every other night, on the nights without glycine and GABA: 900 mg myo-inositol with the base stack.
- Inositol helps him fall asleep and fall back asleep after waking in the night. It also seems to give a lasting anxiety-lowering effect, so he feels "buffered" against stress. He notes it may suit people who are fasting or low-carb.
- He prefers this stack to melatonin, because commercial doses are far above physiological levels and melatonin interacts with the testosterone, estrogen and puberty systems. Occasional use for jet lag is probably fine; chronic use, especially in kids, is potentially problematic.

chunks.heading: Falling back asleep, NSDR and sleep-environment tools
chunks.text:
- NSDR (non-sleep deep rest) scripts and yoga nidra are free on YouTube. They help with falling asleep, staying asleep and falling back asleep.
- Reverie (self-hypnosis from Stanford's David Spiegel):
  - It has a fall-back-asleep session. Andrew says that 99 times out of 100 he's asleep within minutes.
  - It costs $14.99/month, $99.99/year, or $249 once, with a 7-day free trial. It is currently Apple-only.
  - This is clinically supported self-hypnosis, not stage hypnosis.
- If he wakes at night, he goes to the bathroom with dim lights and returns to bed, then uses Reverie if needed.
- Eye masks help if not too tight and the room is cool enough. The upper face is a heat-exchange area, so a warm room plus a mask wakes you.
- Ear plugs: some people love them; Andrew hears his own heartbeat and finds them unhelpful.
- Raise the foot of the bed 3-5 degrees (or the feet with a pillow) for deeper sleep via lymphatic washout. If you have acid reflux, do the opposite and raise the head side by 3-5 degrees.
- Sleep apnea is dangerous and common in heavy-set people, including very muscular ones. It is linked to cardiovascular, sexual and cognitive problems.
- Nose-breathing in sleep helps:
  - Tape your mouth shut with medical tape. This also reduces snoring.
  - Practice nasal breathing during low-intensity cardio (mouth closed, or a held sip of water). It gradually dilates the nasal passages.
  - He cites James Nestor's book *Breath* on this.

chunks.heading: Consistency, compensatory sleep and shifting your clock
chunks.text:
- Keep wake times within plus or minus one hour on weekends. If you sleep in, do it by at most an hour, then use an afternoon nap instead of sleeping until 11 or noon.
- After a bad night:
  - Still delay caffeine 90-120 minutes. Caffeine especially disrupts compensatory sleep.
  - Use NSDR or Reverie to partly offset the loss. He says nothing fully compensates for lost sleep.
- Temperature minimum is about 2 hours before your usual wake time. For a 7:00 a.m. riser it is 5:00 a.m.
  - Bright light, exercise or caffeine in the 2-4 hours before it delays the clock, so you want to sleep and wake later.
  - Bright light, exercise, socializing or food in the hours after it advances the clock, so you want to sleep and wake earlier.
- To become an early riser:
  - Move bedtime and wake time earlier by 30-60 minutes each night over about a week.
  - On waking, get light (artificial if the sun's not up), exercise and breakfast even without hunger.
  - Eating on local time is one of the fastest ways to adapt to jet lag or shift work.
- Use the same logic to pre-shift before travel.
- Shift work:
  - Stay on one shift for about 2 weeks at a time and avoid swing shifts.
  - If you must be awake in the middle of the night (feeding a baby, caring for someone), use red light, which hasn't been shown to disrupt the cortisol rhythm.
- Jet lag can also come from being woken at night.
- Andrew says early risers show cognitive and grip-strength benefits, especially night owls who shift deliberately.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman argues learning is about offsetting forgetting, and that self-testing soon after first exposure beats rereading by a wide margin. He covers the two-step plasticity process (focus, then sleep), habits of top students, NSDR, gap effects, emotion and interleaving.

chunks.heading: Core principle: study to offset forgetting, not to "learn"
chunks.text:
- Andrew argues that most of what people believe about the best way to study is wrong, and the best learning practices "are not intuitive."
- He says preferred learning styles (auditory vs visual, reading vs slides, group vs solo) mostly melt away in the research. What matters is whether a method accesses memory in a way that offsets forgetting.
- His reframe: don't think "study to retain," think "study to inoculate against forgetting."
- Most information the brain meets each day is discarded. Learning is about making the right things stick.
- He says he wishes he had known this in elementary school, high school and college.

chunks.heading: How learning works: neuroplasticity in two steps
chunks.text:
- Neuroplasticity is the nervous system's ability to change with experience. It happens in three ways:
  - Strengthening existing synaptic connections.
  - Weakening existing connections.
  - Neurogenesis (new neurons), which is rare in adult humans and only a trivial share of learning. It occurs mainly in the olfactory bulb and the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus.
- Weakening or removing connections is not "forgetting" or "getting worse." Much motor-skill refinement from infancy to adulthood is removal of connections, and the remaining ones become more robust and reliable.
- Step 1 is alert, focused attention during exposure. Focus and attention cue the nervous system that something is important and must change.
- Step 2 is the actual rewiring, which happens during deep sleep and sleep-like states, especially REM sleep, which predominates in the latter half of the night.
- He describes a "first night effect": material is mostly consolidated in the first night's sleep after learning.
  - A poor first night doesn't doom the material forever.
  - But late-night caffeine and all-nighters work against learning.

chunks.heading: Getting alert and focused
chunks.text:
- Sleep well the night before. He calls sleep "without question the best nootropic."
- Use a silent script such as "I need to learn this" to ramp up focus. Don't passively wait for the material to pull attention out of you.
- Effortful focus is a skill. Constantly pulling your mind back is meant to feel difficult.
  - The strain reflects release of neuromodulators like epinephrine.
  - He treats that strain as a cue to the nervous system that plasticity is needed.
  - If learning felt seamless, circuits wouldn't need to change.
- Behavioral tools to improve focus:
  - 5-10 minutes of daily mindfulness meditation, citing Wendy Suzuki's lab at NYU. He says it improves focus and memory and recall.
    - Sit or lie down, close your eyes, focus on your breath, and bring attention back each time it drifts.
    - Missing a day is no big deal. Timing doesn't matter, though late-night sessions disrupt sleep for some people.
  - An eyes-open version: stare at a visual target 1-3 ft away for 1-3 minutes (up to 10), blinking as needed, and keep bringing attention back.
- Supporting basics: good hydration and an amount of caffeine that makes you alert but not shaky.
- People with clinically diagnosed ADHD should talk to their doctor about prescription options. Great sleep matters especially for them.
- He recommends NSDR (non-sleep deep rest) or yoga nidra for 10-20 minutes to restore mental and physical vigor and enhance plasticity.
  - Use it in the morning, the afternoon, or in the night if you can't sleep.
  - It's especially useful if you haven't slept enough.

chunks.heading: Habits of the most effective students
chunks.text:
- He cites a survey of close to 700 medical students (self-report, correlational) that identified about 10 habits of highly effective students.
- The top habits he highlights:
  - They schedule set times to study.
  - They remove distractions: phone away, and they tell friends and family they are unreachable.
  - They study alone.
  - They study about 3-4 hours a day, split into 2-3 sessions rather than one block, at least 5 days a week.
  - They teach other students the material.
- On teaching peers, he says to ignore the worry that you're giving competitors a free advantage. Teaching tests and builds your own mastery.
  - He cites the lab saying "watch one, do one, teach one," for anything that is safe to do that way.
- Scheduling:
  - Study at regular times if you can.
  - Allow about 2-3 days for the brain to entrain to a consistent study schedule.
  - Attention is limited but renewable. Adenosine builds the longer you're awake, which is why sleep restores focus.
- The best students also had a long-term, abstract, aspirational motivation, such as how success would change their lives and families.
  - He says that pull helps when you don't love the material.
- He says material you struggle with is often what you later remember most fondly. Effortful study is the most effective study.

chunks.heading: Testing is the best way to study
chunks.text:
- The central claim: testing is "one of the best ways to build our knowledge, to retain our knowledge, and again to offset forgetting."
  - It is not just for evaluating what you know.
- A 1917 study had children read biographies.
  - One group reread them repeatedly.
  - Another group read them once and then recalled them from memory.
  - The recall group vastly outperformed the rereading group, in both the amount and the accuracy of what they remembered.
- A more modern set of experiments compared four groups:
  - Study-study-study-study.
  - Study-study-study-test.
  - Study-test-test-test.
  - Each group was then given a final test days, weeks or a year later.
  - Performance on the final test rose with the number of earlier tests taken.
- The confidence trap:
  - The study-four-times group felt most confident.
  - The study-once, test-three-times group felt least confident.
  - The actual results were the reverse.
  - Re-exposure builds a feeling of familiarity, not mastery.
- You can get quiz answers wrong and still benefit, as long as you see the correct answers afterward. Even scoring 40-50% or less still beats rereading.
- Why it works: getting things wrong, noticing the gap and correcting it cues the nervous system to lock in what you have right and fix what you have wrong. That differs from passive re-exposure.
- He uses the distinction between familiarity (recognition) and recollection (being able to recall and use the material).
  - He points to a review in the journal Hippocampus on this.
- His own example: in a hard undergraduate neuroanatomy lab course, he lay on his bed with his eyes closed and mentally "flew through" the nervous system.
  - He entered through the ear, the eye and the dorsal brain surface, and traced tracts.
  - When he hit a gap he looked it up in the textbook, then resumed.
  - He says this is why he still has strong mastery of neuroanatomy.
  - Today, after reading a paper, he often takes a walk and mentally rehearses its key points and graphs.
- Self-testing can take whatever form suits you best. The principle is recalling the material and finding your gaps.

chunks.heading: When and how to test yourself
chunks.text:
- Test soon after first exposure, the same day or the next day. This beats waiting and then testing right before the exam.
  - The best group: expose, test soon after, then a long delay, then the final test.
  - The middle group: expose, delay, test, delay, test.
  - The worst group: expose, long delay, then two tests back to back.
- A prerequisite to testing is a first exposure to the material.
- One self-test on new material roughly halves forgetting.
  - He says it improves retention by about 50%.
  - He cites studies across music, math, language and motor learning, with benefits measured out to a year later.
- Don't walk out of class and straight onto your phone. Take a few seconds to a few minutes right after exposure to test yourself on what you just heard.
  - Finding that you're confused is useful. It tells you what to review.
- Format:
  - Open-ended, short-answer or long-answer questions with minimal prompts are the best, because they require recall.
  - Multiple choice is weaker because it lets you rely on recognition.
  - The exception is multiple-choice questions with plausible trick answers, as on the GRE, LSAT or MCAT.
- Testing for learning should be separate from grading.
  - He notes students dislike pop quizzes and penalize teachers for them in evaluations.
  - The better approach is to announce at the outset that regular quizzes are part of the method, or to test yourself every day.
- He points to the literature on testing: "Testing Enhances Learning: A Review of the Literature" and "Test-Enhanced Learning."

chunks.heading: Gap effects, emotion and interleaving
chunks.text:
- Gap effects:
  - Take pauses of about 5-10 seconds, up to 30 seconds, during learning.
  - During those pauses the hippocampus replays the material at roughly 20-30 times the normal rate, as it does in REM sleep.
  - Use them in learning of any kind, including music and motor skills.
- Emotion and neuromodulators:
  - Emotionally charged material is remembered more durably, because epinephrine and norepinephrine (and others) wire experiences into circuits.
  - Extreme stress produces one-trial learning, which is the basis of PTSD.
  - With a dull teacher or source, deliberately raise your own internal intensity and interest.
  - He cites James McGaugh's review of a medieval practice of throwing people into cold water after teaching them, to boost adrenaline and consolidate memory.
  - He doesn't say you must do cold exposure after learning, but a cold shower or plunge while mentally testing yourself is an option. He points to his deliberate cold exposure newsletter for best practices.
  - Caffeine modestly raises epinephrine and probably helps a little.
- Interleaving:
  - Mix in related but undemanding anecdotes or bits of information, which act as more than a pause.
  - They give the hippocampus more repetitions.
  - They let the brain link new knowledge with existing or distantly related knowledge.
  - He doesn't mean mixing two hard subjects like math and history in one session, which would be overwhelming.

chunks.heading: Levels of skill
chunks.text:
- Andrew distinguishes four levels:
  - Unskilled: limited understanding or ability to use information.
  - Skilled: can recognize and use information in basic or advanced ways.
  - Mastery: close to the full depth of knowledge, usable flexibly.
  - Virtuosity: mastery so deep that you can invite uncertainty and spontaneity, as great musicians and athletes do.
- He says most people would be content with skill and mastery.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman explains time-restricted feeding using Satchin Panda's work. When you eat sets fed or fasted conditions that drive circadian clock genes, liver health, inflammation, fat loss and hormones. He covers window length (about 8 hours), placement, protein timing, ways to speed the move to a fasted state, and what breaks a fast.

chunks.heading: Time-restricted eating: what it is and why timing matters
chunks.text:
- Andrew uses "time-restricted feeding" as the umbrella term. Fasting and eating are two sides of one coin, and everyone already fasts during sleep.
- His core idea: what and when you eat "set conditions" in the brain and body. These conditions are either fed or unfed (fasted), and the body cares about the condition, not about whether you are currently chewing.
- He says "when you eat is as important as what you eat" for liver health and mental health. In his framing, eating is a timing cue for the body's 24-hour clock, second only to light.
- Calories in versus calories out is the foundation for weight change. A 12-month Stanford study (Gardner et al., JAMA 2018) found no significant weight difference between a healthy low-fat and a healthy low-carb diet. Hormones, exercise and context still shape the "calories out" side.
- He flags that mouse and human results can diverge. Higher fasting blood glucose predicts mortality in humans and non-human primates, but the reverse held in mice.

chunks.heading: The mouse study behind the eight-hour window
chunks.text:
- Satchin Panda's 2012 mouse study compared four groups: normal chow ad libitum, normal chow time-restricted, high-fat diet ad libitum, and high-fat diet time-restricted.
- Mice on the same high-fat diet and same calories, but restricted to about eight hours of their active phase, maintained or lost weight and improved health markers. Mice with round-the-clock access gained weight and became obese and sick.
- Time-restricted feeding also reversed some existing damage, including fatty liver.
- Andrew notes the eight-hour window was set by lab logistics (a grad student's schedule), not biology. "The eight hour feeding windows are not holy."
- Eating around the clock raises inflammatory markers (TNF alpha, IL-6, IL-1). Restricting the window lets them fall.
- About 80% of genes in the brain and body run on a 24-hour schedule. Regular feeding times tighten the rhythm of clock genes (PER, BMAL, CRY1). Chaotic feeding scrambles them.
- Light is the primary entrainer of these clocks and food is the second most powerful.

chunks.heading: Foundational rules for setting up a feeding window
chunks.text:
- No food or calories for at least the first 60 minutes after waking. Longer is better.
- No food or liquid calories for 2 to 3 hours before bed.
- The sleep-related fast is especially valuable. Sleep fasting goes with autophagy and with clearing debris from the brain and organs. Andrew says to build the eating window around protecting it.
- Ideal for pure fasting benefit: eat in the middle of the day, for example 10 AM to 6 PM. He calls it ideal but impractical for most social schedules.
- His pragmatic version is roughly noon to 8 PM, with the last bite or sip of calories by 8 PM and bed between 10 PM and 1 AM. He says this allows lunch and dinner with others and still captures the sleep fast.
- A window pushed to 2 or 3 PM through 10 or 11 PM means you are still digesting for roughly the first six hours of sleep. That loses much of the sleep-fast benefit.
- Digestion takes about 5 to 6 hours. Stopping eating is not the same as being fasted.
- How fast you reach the fasted state depends on three things:
  - Meal size: bigger takes longer.
  - Fat content: more fat slows gastric emptying.
  - Liquid versus solid: liquid calories clear faster.
- Fibre and fat blunt and prolong glucose rises. Pure sugars spike them.

chunks.heading: How long the window should be
chunks.text:
- Eight hours is Andrew's anchor. Humans studies, including Panda and Krista Varady's trial in obese adults, show that an 8-hour window produced mild caloric restriction and weight loss without calorie counting. It also lowered blood pressure. Studies exist in obese adults, non-obese adults and some children.
- People underestimate their real window. Data from Panda's My Circadian Clock app (food photo logs from thousands of people) shows actual windows are usually one to two hours longer than people think. So aim for a shorter window than you want: for a 10-hour target, plan 8 to 9 hours; for 6 hours, plan 7 to 8.
- Short windows of 4 to 6 hours improve insulin sensitivity, beta cell function, blood pressure, oxidative stress and evening appetite. But they either do nothing for body weight or increase it, apparently because people overeat inside the window.
- One meal per day has very few studies. People tend to maintain or lose weight and may under-eat, which matters for training, hormones and fertility. Andrew says it is fine if it works for you, as long as you do not under-eat.
- Practical shifting: move the window by about an hour per day over 1 to 10 days, then hold the new schedule for at least 30 days, ideally indefinitely. Going straight from three meals over 16 hours to 8 hours can leave you hungry and irritable while leptin and the hypocretin/orexin system adjust.
- Consistency matters. Window drift on weekends, say 2 hours later, acts like jet lag for the clock genes. The effects of that can take two to three days to recover from. "We don't want to be overly neurotic," but regularity matters as much as length.
- Andrew personally uses roughly an 8 to 10 hour window and does not fuss over it. He likes it because he does not negotiate with food: "I don't eat half the croissant." A time rule removes the portion-control decisions (the basal ganglia go/no-go circuitry is metabolically demanding).

chunks.heading: Muscle, hormones and who should not squeeze the window
chunks.text:
- Aoyama et al. (Cell Reports, 2021, mice and humans): protein early in the day supports muscle maintenance and hypertrophy, via protein synthesis pathways regulated by the clock gene BMAL. Andrew's rough cutoff is to get some protein before about 10 AM if muscle is the main goal.
- This held regardless of when the resistance training was done. It does not mean later protein is bad.
- If muscle is your priority, a late-shifted window is less ideal. He mentions this cuts against his own habit of not eating until noon to 2 PM.
- Elite cyclist study (Mauro et al.): about 4,800 calories per day eaten in an 8-hour window versus a longer window, same calories. Free testosterone dropped significantly, but cortisol fell more than in controls, which may offset the testosterone effect. Inflammatory markers did not rise.
- Baseline testosterone matters: a 10 to 20% drop is more consequential if you start low. Andrew recommends blood work.
- For hard training, high psychological stress, or heavy workloads, he would not go shorter than 8 hours. The body does not distinguish physical from mental stress.
- Reproduction: leptin from body fat signals the brain to maintain ovulation and fertility. Cutting calories or window length too far can lower sperm counts and disrupt cycles. Women trying to ovulate regularly or conceive should avoid very short windows.
- Mouse data suggest male-female differences in response, with human data still awaited. Some people do not do well on time-restricted eating, and for them smaller meals spread through the day may be better.

chunks.heading: Speeding the shift from fed to fasted
chunks.text:
- Glucose clearing:
  - A 20 to 30 minute light walk after eating speeds gastric emptying and glucose uptake.
  - Air squats or pushups also help.
  - High-intensity interval training lowers blood glucose when done in the second half of the day and raises it when done early. The early rise reflects nutrient shuttling to muscle and is not bad. Andrew prefers training early. Late HIIT is only worthwhile if caffeine or stimulation do not wreck sleep.
- Glucose disposal agents (use with caution):
  - Metformin (prescription) and berberine (over the counter, with effects "almost identical" to Metformin).
  - Berberine without carbohydrates gave Andrew a splitting headache from hypoglycemia. Response varies by person and time of day. Some people take it before high-carb meals.
  - Cinnamon is a mild disposal agent. Lemon or lime juice can lower blood glucose through acidity. Half a lime in water helps if a sweet food is overwhelming.
  - A continuous glucose monitor (CGM) is the best way to see the effects.
- Cell signaling logic: eating or having high glucose raises mTOR (cell growth). Fasting raises AMPK, sirtuins, FOX-O, ATF and ketones (repair, autophagy). This is about conditions, not about which food. "Anytime you eat any food, doesn't matter if it's plant-based, animal-based... you are biasing your system towards... cell growth."

chunks.heading: Health effects and fat loss specifics
chunks.text:
- Gut: in time-restricted eating, the mucosal lining and microbiome improve. Lactobacillus (high levels correlate with metabolic disorders) falls and Acetobacter rises. Helps some people with IBS and colitis.
- Liver: non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is now common in adults and children. A recent Cell Reports Medicine study found low brown fat, not the gut microbiome, correlates with it. Time-restricted eating and cold exposure (1 to 3 minutes, 2 to 4 times per week, or about 10 minutes) both appear to raise brown fat. Andrew says time-restricted eating may help prevent and "potentially" reverse fatty liver.
- Fat versus lean loss: with 60+ days of time-restricted eating and a caloric deficit, mouse and human data point to more of the loss coming from fat. Hepatic lipase rises (promoting lipolysis) and CIDEC (a lipolysis inhibitor) falls. "You're removing the brake and you're pressing on the accelerator of fat loss." He says no feeding schedule is holy, since a calorie deficit still drives weight loss.
- Longer fasts: alternate-day fasting and 5:2 regimens appear safe, with no bone loss, and can cause rapid weight loss and lower blood glucose. But adherence is hard, and weight and glucose rebound after stopping are unstudied. No quality peer-reviewed studies yet on long fasts for dementia.

chunks.heading: What breaks a fast, and fasting tactics
chunks.text:
- Answer: it depends on context, because the real readout is blood glucose and metabolic state, not the clock. He suggests a CGM if you want a definitive answer.
- Fine during a fast: water, tea, black coffee, caffeine pills.
- A Panda-lab finding he cites: even 1 gram of sugar after dinner can disrupt expression of circadian genes tied to the sleep fast. A half glass of wine a couple hours after dinner breaks the fast.
- Context examples: one peanut after a big carb meal an hour ago can break a fast, while a handful deep in a fast may not. A soda breaks it unless you just ran an ultramarathon. Pizza breaks it. Pure fat probably does not after five or more hours of strict fasting (so-called fat fasting, MCTs).
- Sweeteners: evidence is mixed. Artificial sweeteners can cause a brief glucose rise and then a dip, which may drive hunger. Stevia and monk fruit have little data. He considers moderate use unlikely to "take you out of the fast." Heavy use may harm the microbiome, and some people get appetite spikes from sweet taste.
- Toothpaste does not break a fast unless swallowed.
- Salt for fasting symptoms: if shaky, lightheaded or unable to concentrate during a fast, try about a half teaspoon of sea salt or a small pinch in water, optionally with lemon or lime. Neurons run on sodium, potassium and magnesium. Caffeine increases water and sodium excretion. Skip heavy salt if you have hypertension, and talk to a doctor.
- Sauna: with a CGM, Andrew found sauna spikes blood glucose as high as a meal and then drops back. This is because dehydration concentrates blood sugar. He still uses the sauna 3 to 4 times per week before sleep and is not worried.
- Tools he mentions: the free My Circadian Clock site (Panda lab) for logging food, and the Zero app for tracking feeding and fasting windows. He has no affiliation with either.
- For anyone diabetic or making major dietary changes, he says to consult a physician.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman explains that muscle growth and strength are driven by the nerve-to-muscle connection. He covers training volume (5 to 15 sets per muscle per week at 30 to 80% of 1RM), lactate as a signal to heart, liver and brain, recovery tests (grip strength, CO2 tolerance), and supplements such as creatine, beta-alanine and electrolytes. He warns that cold and NSAIDs after training blunt adaptation.

chunks.heading: Muscle as a nervous system output: neural control and energy
chunks.text:
- Andrew frames muscle around the nervous system: "the whole reason why you have a brain is so that you can move." Muscle matters for movement, metabolism, posture (breathing, even alertness) and aesthetics.
- He says muscle size and quality raise metabolism. The ability to jump and to get up off the floor quickly is one of the most predictive markers of biological aging.
- Control runs through three nodes:
  - Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex drive deliberate movement.
  - Lower motor neurons in the spinal cord send axons to muscle and release acetylcholine, the only way muscle contracts.
  - Central pattern generators run reflexive, rhythmic movement such as walking.
- Flexors and extensors are reciprocally inhibited (bicep/tricep, hamstring/quadriceps, abs/lower back). Activating one inhibits its antagonist.
- He argues hypertrophy is driven by the nerve-to-muscle connection, not by something that happens only inside the muscle.

chunks.heading: Lactate and "the burn": a hormonal signal for heart, liver and brain
chunks.text:
- Glucose or glycogen breaks down to pyruvate, which yields a little ATP. With oxygen, pyruvate goes to the mitochondria and yields 28 to 30 ATP. Muscle is the most metabolically expensive tissue after brain.
- Without enough oxygen in the muscle, pyruvate picks up hydrogen and becomes lactate. Andrew stresses humans make lactate, not lactic acid, and that the common belief that lactate causes the burn is backwards.
- Lactate has three roles:
  - It buffers acidity, so it suppresses the burn rather than causing it.
  - It is a fuel that lets contraction continue.
  - It is a hormonal signal to the heart, liver and brain, with positive effects. In the brain it acts partly through astrocytes.
- Protocol: take about 10% of your effort in a workout (any modality: weights, running, cycling, swimming) to the point of the burn, if you can do it safely. Don't spend the whole session there; it would impair recovery.
- Keep breathing through the burn. Holding your breath makes it feel worse and blunts lactate's buffering and fuel role.
- He says exercise-driven neurogenesis in humans has little evidence (the data are strong in mice). The brain benefit more likely comes from blood-borne signals such as IGF-1 and lactate, which improve connections between neurons.

chunks.heading: Henneman size principle, strength vs. hypertrophy, and the mind-muscle connection
chunks.text:
- Motor units are recruited from low to high threshold, which conserves energy. More units are recruited as effort continues.
- Andrew says it is a misreading that you need the heaviest weights to reach high-threshold units. Loads from 30% to 80% of one-rep max (1RM) can drive both strength and hypertrophy when sets are taken close to failure.
- Hypertrophy happens when stress, tension and/or damage trigger protein synthesis that thickens myosin. His analogy: the balloons on a bouquet of strings get bigger.
- Strength means distributing work across many muscles and the whole nervous system, moving progressively greater loads. Hypertrophy means isolating a muscle and making it do the work, with hard, almost cramping local contractions.
- Self-test: try to contract a muscle hard with no weight (for example the calf, or the lat by pulling the elbow behind the body). If you can nearly cramp it, you have a high potential to grow and strengthen it, and you need fewer sets. Poor control means more sets.
- For a pure strength or performance goal, avoid isolating single muscles.

chunks.heading: Training volume, intensity, rest and session design
chunks.text:
- Biasing: 75% to 90% of 1RM biases toward strength. About 30% to 50% with many more reps biases toward hypertrophy and muscle endurance. In between, he says it doesn't matter much.
- Take sets to failure or near it, but only about 10% of sets or workouts should go to true failure. Most sets stop short of failure, so you can do more volume without fatiguing the nervous system.
- Weekly sets per muscle (they can be split across sessions):
  - About 5 hard sets per week maintains muscle.
  - 5 to 15 sets per week suits most untrained and moderately trained people (he cites a 2 to 20 range for beginners).
  - Experienced lifters can benefit from up to about 25 to 30 sets per week, but some people who generate a lot of force respond to as few as 4 to 8.
- Keep sessions to 45 to 60 minutes; beyond roughly 60 minutes cortisol and inflammatory pathways rise.
- Rep speed for hypertrophy and strength: anywhere from 0.5 to 8 seconds per rep appears to work.
- Rest between sets for strength and hypertrophy: 2 to 6 minutes can work. Walking or standing still helps clear lactate.
- Pre-exhaustion: doing an isolation exercise first (for example leg extensions before squats) makes the compound lift target that muscle more, at the cost of weight lifted and possibly form.
- Flexing the target muscle hard for about 30 seconds between sets can improve hypertrophy and the nerve-to-muscle connection. It lowers performance on the next set, so skip it when the goal is strength or moving weight.
- Explosiveness and speed: use roughly 60% to 75% of 1RM, move the weight as fast as safely possible, and stop before failure (as sets near failure the bar slows). Gains here are mostly neural.
- Andrew suggests periodizing training over 1 to 6 months and adjusting, since neuromuscular gains are fastest early on.
- Cooling the palms between sets (palmer cooling) lets you hold reps and add sets at a given weight.

chunks.heading: Testosterone-boosting resistance protocol (Duncan French)
chunks.text:
- Per Andrew, work by Duncan French (UFC Performance Center) found a clear testosterone rise with 6 sets of 10 reps, 120 seconds rest, on big compound movements (squats, deadlifts, chin-ups).
- Lighten the weight between sets if needed.
- 10 sets of 10 did not raise testosterone and tilted toward catabolic, cortisol-like effects.
- Do it as a stand-alone session, at most twice per week.
- Hypertrophy or explosive training under 60 minutes also raises testosterone. Sessions over about 75 minutes at high intensity tend to lower testosterone and raise cortisol.

chunks.heading: Measuring recovery, and what blunts adaptation
chunks.text:
- Andrew says the adaptation happens during recovery, not training, and gives three morning checks of nervous-system recovery:
  - HRV (needs a device; higher variability is good).
  - Grip strength: squeeze a hand tool or a floor scale and compare with your rested baseline. A 10% to 20% drop is a warning.
  - CO2 tolerance test:
    - Do 4 deep nose inhales with full exhales.
    - On the 5th, inhale as deeply as you can through the nose and fill the belly.
    - Exhale through the mouth as slowly as possible (like through a tiny straw) and time it until you truly can't exhale more.
- CO2 exhale-time zones:
  - 20 to 25 seconds or less: probably not recovered.
  - About 30 to 60 seconds: green zone.
  - 65 to 120 seconds: nervous system recovered.
  - A drop of 15% to 20% from your own norm means you are veering toward not recovering.
- To start recovery, finish training with about 5 minutes of deliberate parasympathetic engagement, such as non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) or 10 physiological sighs (double inhale through the nose, long exhale). Some athletes also use physiological sighs between sets to refocus.
- Cold exposure (whole-body or neck-down) within about 4 hours after resistance training lowers inflammation and soreness but can interfere with pathways like mTOR that drive repair and growth. It is fine if the goal is quick recovery or endurance.
- Antihistamines and NSAIDs can blunt gains from endurance and resistance training, so be cautious within 4 hours before or after exercise. NSAIDs also mask pain, which is a useful warning signal.
- The aim is inflammation during and just after training as the stimulus, then lower inflammation later.
- Baseline anti-inflammatory trio per Galpin: above 1,000 mg EPA per day (omega-3), vitamin D, and magnesium malate (for delayed onset muscle soreness).
- Soreness isn't required for gains. If a muscle is still sore, Andrew's takeaway is that it isn't recovered.

chunks.heading: Supplements, protein and leucine, and training around cognitive work
chunks.text:
- Electrolytes: sodium, potassium and magnesium are essential for neurons to fire and for nerve-to-muscle communication. Needs rise with sweat, caffeine, heat and diuretics. Water alone won't do it.
- Creatine:
  - He cites examine.com for the supporting studies.
  - Dose, by body weight: about 5 g/day around 180 lb, 10 to 15 g if 220 to 230 lb, and 3 to 5 g (or 1 to 3 g) if lighter.
  - Loading isn't required.
  - Benefits include more power output, less fatigue, more cell hydration and possible cognitive benefit.
  - It can raise DHT, which may worsen hair loss in some men.
- Beta-alanine: 2 to 5 g per day, for efforts of about 60 to 240 seconds (sets of 8 to 15 reps, rowing, intervals). Andrew hasn't tried it himself.
- Arginine and citrulline: may help long-duration endurance via vasodilation, but can trigger cold sore (HSV-1) outbreaks.
- Protein: aim for 700 to 3,000 mg leucine per meal, preferably from whole foods. Animal proteins are denser in essential amino acids per calorie; vegans may want to supplement leucine. Two to four meals per day is enough, not six or seven.
- Hard exercise (roughly 30 to 60 minutes near failure or with intervals) can reduce brain oxygenation afterwards, so manage intensity and duration if you need to think that day.
- Train at a consistent time. Your body then anticipates focused effort at that time, so on non-training days that same clock time may be good for deep cognitive work.
- Training time of day (morning vs. afternoon) doesn't matter much for strength or hypertrophy. The afternoon may be slightly better for performance.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman explains how sex steroids are made and regulated, then gives levers for balancing testosterone and estrogen. Nasal breathing and apnea reduction, early bright light, cold exposure, heavy training, and foundational nutrients come first, with cautious notes on supplements and menopause compounds.

chunks.heading: Why Andrew frames hormone optimization around ratios and salutogenesis
chunks.text:
- Andrew separates the pathogenic model (exercise and eat well to avoid heart disease, dementia, bad body composition) from the salutogenic model (do behaviors to move toward energy, endocrine and metabolic well-being). He argues the best mindset holds both.
- He cites Alia Crum's Stanford work: hotel cleaners told their work counted as exercise showed greater health benefits than uninformed colleagues. His takeaway is that knowing why a behavior is good for you changes physiology.
- Estrogen and testosterone are the "sex steroids" and are present in everybody. Their ratio, not the absolute level of either, drives effects on mood, anxiety, reproduction and libido.
- Estradiol is the active form of estrogen in both sexes. Testosterone is made mainly by the testes (some by the adrenals); estrogen mainly by the ovaries.
- Aromatase converts testosterone to estrogen. It is made by body fat and, at low levels, by the testes themselves.
- Levels vary hugely between people and across life. Estrogen rises sharply at puberty and falls at menopause (roughly age 45-60). Testosterone is said to fall about 1% per year, but some men in their 90s still have pubertal levels.
- He gives no target numbers and recommends blood work with a physician, ideally an endocrinologist.

chunks.heading: How testosterone, competition, sex and parenting interact
chunks.text:
- Testosterone lowers the amygdala's threshold for stress and anxiety. Andrew says it makes "effort feel good" and promotes novelty-seeking, foraging and competitiveness.
- Competing raises testosterone whether you win or lose. Winning adds dopamine, and dopamine drives pituitary signals that lead to more testosterone later.
- Testosterone drives sex-seeking in all sexes. In females, estrogen drives receptivity, and testosterone peaks just before ovulation.
- Men need estrogen for libido. If estrogen is pushed too low, libido is lost, even with high testosterone.
- Sex itself raises testosterone and dopamine. Prolactin then rises after ejaculation and sets the refractory period.
- Escasa et al. (2011): watching pornography raised testosterone about 10%, while real sex raised it about 70%.
- Ejaculation does not lower testosterone. Abstinence or sex without ejaculation for a week or more raised it up to 400%.
- Expecting fathers show about a 50% drop in testosterone, a roughly three-fold drop in cortisol and doubled estradiol, which Andrew attributes to prolactin. Extra body fat is laid down in both parents. Ongoing contact with the baby's smell influences how long this lasts.
- Illness and the inflammatory cytokine IL-6 lower libido, testosterone and estrogen, and also interfere with sex steroid receptors. IL-10 is the anti-inflammatory counterweight. Keeping IL-6 low supports these hormones.
- DHEA raises both testosterone and estrogen. Where it goes depends on your starting ratio and how much aromatase you have. With high aromatase or low testosterone, it may mostly become estrogen.

chunks.heading: Pheromones: what is established in animals and what is not in humans
chunks.text:
- A pheromone is a chemical released by one member of a species that affects others. He says human pheromones remain controversial because no clear vomeronasal organ has been found.
- Animal examples he lists:
  - Lee-Boot effect: females housed together without males develop longer estrus cycles.
  - Whitten effect: male presence changes female cycling.
  - Bruce effect: a pregnant female aborts or reabsorbs her litter if the sire is replaced by a novel male for about 48 hours.
  - Vandenbergh effect: a novel male accelerates female puberty, and older females delay it.
- Human evidence he points to: Stern and McClintock (1998). Armpit sweat from donor women was diluted in alcohol so it had no detectable odor, then swabbed under other women's noses. It changed the timing and pattern of their menstrual cycles, though not clean synchronization.
- Partners can pick out their boyfriend's washed t-shirt among hundreds at far above chance levels.
- Andrew notes that animals use the flehmen response to capture pheromones with the mouth. He calls the perfume industry's pheromone claims "well-established and well-documented" as a business.
- Whether human miscarriage relates to the Bruce effect is an open question.

chunks.heading: Breathing, apnea and sleep as the foundation for sex hormones
chunks.text:
- Apnea (breath-holding or under-breathing, mostly in sleep) is consistently associated with lower estrogen in people with ovaries and lower testosterone in people with testes. Andrew says the direction of causation is unclear.
- Mechanism he describes: CO2 buildup raises cortisol. Cholesterol is shunted toward cortisol rather than toward testosterone or estrogen, and deep sleep also supports gonadal cell turnover.
- He found at least four quality studies showing that reducing or eliminating apnea raised testosterone in males and improved estrogen-to-testosterone ratios in females.
- Tools he lists:
  - Nasal breathing during the day, unless eating, speaking or at maximum effort.
  - Nasal breathing during cardio below maximum effort. The sinuses dilate over time, so it gets easier. Swimmers, fighters and martial artists have reasons to breathe differently.
  - Taping the mouth shut at night (as James Nestor describes), using tape you can still open through if needed.
  - CPAP for severe sleep apnea.
- He cites "Jaws" (Sandra Kahn and Paul Ehrlich) on chronic mouth breathing changing the jaw and face. He also notes that being very overweight worsens apnea.
- The physiological sigh (a double inhale followed by a long exhale) is what the body does spontaneously after an apnea episode, and it can also be done deliberately to offload CO2.

chunks.heading: Light viewing, dopamine and seasonal biology
chunks.text:
- In seasonal breeders such as foxes, rabbits and ferrets, coat color and breeding status track day length. Tyrosine is the shared precursor for dopamine and melanin pigmentation.
- Light to the eyes raises dopamine. Dopamine drives GnRH, then LH and FSH, then testosterone and estrogen.
- Humans are not seasonal breeders, but mood and hormones tend to run higher in spring and summer. Susceptibility to winter lows has a strong genetic component.
- Protocol:
  - View bright light, ideally sunlight, in the first hour after waking, for about 2 to 10 minutes.
  - Sunglasses do not substitute for it, though prescription glasses and contacts are fine. If sunlight is unavailable, use bright artificial light.
  - Never look at anything painfully bright.
  - Avoid bright light in the middle of the night. He cites two papers (in "Cell" and "Neuron") showing it suppresses dopamine. He suspects much of sleep deprivation's hormone effect comes from night light, which he says no study has tested yet.
- Light raises both hormones in parallel and keeps your existing ratio. He says you cannot raise "the wrong one".
- Order of priorities: breathing, light and sleep come before supplements.

chunks.heading: Cold, heat and the gonads
chunks.text:
- Cold exposure may raise testosterone and estrogen, but he says the effect is likely not the cold itself. His best guess is rebound vasodilation after vasoconstriction.
- Cooling the neurons that control blood vessels reduces blood flow. The re-warming then delivers more blood and more GnRH, LH and carrier proteins to the gonads. He calls this his most plausible explanation, not a proven mechanism.
- Examples he mentions: 1 to 10 minute ice baths, cold showers, cold-water swims, and ice-pack underwear sold online (he did not buy any).
- No studies test the gonad-cooling products directly. He says there is no firm evidence behind the folk claims about room temperature and a child's sex.
- Too much heat is bad for sperm. Sperm proteins are heat sensitive, which harms fertility independent of any effect on testosterone or estrogen.

chunks.heading: Exercise protocols for testosterone
chunks.text:
- Heavy resistance training raises testosterone in males and females for about a day, sometimes up to 48 hours.
  - Use heavy loads, roughly 70-95% of maximum, in sets of about 1 to 6-8 reps.
  - Stop short of failure. Training to failure was not the best for testosterone in the studies he cites.
- Studies he names: Ratamess et al. (2005), on androgen receptor content after heavy resistance exercise, and Izquierdo et al. (2006), on training to failure versus not to failure. Duncan French is an author on several.
- He thinks the signal comes from recruiting high-threshold motor units, and he admits the mechanism is not well understood.
- Combined sessions: lift heavy first, then do cardio. Endurance first lowered testosterone during the lifting. On separate days there was no interaction.
- High-intensity interval training and sprinting increase testosterone.
- Endurance work beyond about 75 minutes starts to lower testosterone, presumably via cortisol. Intensity matters, so he says a 3-hour hike is unlikely to hurt but 3 hours of hard running probably would.
- He says cyclists caught doping with testosterone may use it partly to avoid cortisol-driven drops in testosterone, and he is not recommending it.

chunks.heading: Menopause options and supplements for estrogen
chunks.text:
- Standard care is hormone therapy (oral, patch or pellet), with variable success. He flags caution when there is a breast cancer background, since many such cancers are estrogen-dependent. Tamoxifen and anastrozole were developed for that reason.
- Alternatives with human trials, from examine.com:
  - Black cohosh: 13 peer-reviewed studies, mostly 6+ months and double-blind, in women aged 45-64. It gave consistent but modest improvements in estrogen and symptoms, above placebo.
  - Panax ginseng: reduced some symptoms, mostly libido-related, with unreliable effects otherwise.
  - Maca (increases dopamine): minor effects.
  - Valeriana officinalis: some improvement in hot flashes and insomnia in 100+ subject trials.
  - Pueraria mirifica (Kwao Krua Kao): four studies, each comparable to estrogen replacement for symptoms. He calls it "particularly interesting" and cautions about hormone-related compounds generally.
- He is not a physician and says to talk to your doctor first.

chunks.heading: Nutrients and supplements for testosterone and the HPG axis
chunks.text:
- Housekeeping nutrients: vitamin D3, zinc and magnesium. Wrzosek et al. (2020) links deficiencies to impaired HPA/sex steroid function. He takes all three himself, but says to check doses on examine.com and get blood work.
- Opioids sharply lower testosterone and estrogen by disrupting receptors on hypothalamic GnRH neurons, and can cause gynecomastia in men and ovarian disruption in women.
- Creatine raises DHT, possibly via 5-alpha reductase. People prone to hair loss may notice it.
- Total testosterone is typically cited as about 300-900, with supraphysiological levels around 1,200-1,600. Most testosterone is bound to SHBG or albumin, which shuttle it to tissues, and he argues against demonizing them. Albumin carries it across the blood-brain barrier.
- Free-testosterone supplements he mentions:
  - Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia Jack): 400-800 mg per day, with possible side effects of alertness and insomnia if taken late.
  - Boron: a couple of grams per day, with no known side effects.
  - Stinging nettle: possible effects on prostate and liver.
- Ecdysteroids such as turkesterone (Isenmann et al., 2019, "Archives of Toxicology"): in a 10-week study with strength training, they gave above-placebo gains in muscle mass and strength. The authors called for banning them in sport; Andrew presents that as their view.
- Fadogia agrestis can raise LH and so testosterone and estrogen, in the existing ratio. Its side-effect profile is undocumented, so he stresses blood work.
- hCG is a prescription LH mimic, originally extracted from pregnant women's urine. It stimulates the gonads and is used for fertility or pituitary issues.
- He did not cover Bulbine natalensis because its evidence is mostly rat or sponsored studies and it shows liver toxicity concerns.
- The tissues with the most cell turnover (breast, prostate, testes) are cancer-prone and androgen- or estrogen-sensitive. He says "more is definitely not better".
- The menstrual cycle's feedback loop is delicate, so hormone manipulation can disrupt it. He advises blood tests and cycle monitoring.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman walks through his 24-hour routine with the science behind each step: morning sunlight and walking, delaying caffeine, 90-minute focus blocks timed to temperature minimum, exercise structure, meal composition, NSDR/hypnosis, afternoon light, and a sleep-supporting evening with specific supplements.

chunks.heading: Daily protocol: waking, light, caffeine and fasting
chunks.text:
Andrew structures his day around the 24-hour rhythm because every cell and organ is modulated on that cycle. He stresses he does not insist others copy his schedule, only that the protocols map onto a day.

- **Log wake time.** He writes down when he wakes (about 6:00-7:00 a.m.). His body-temperature minimum falls about 2 hours before average wake time (wake at 8:00 means minimum around 6:00). He tracks the time of the minimum, not the temperature itself.
- **Morning walk outdoors.** Forward motion creates optic flow, which lowers activity in the amygdala (fear/threat/anxiety). He cites a *Neuron* paper (Macé et al., functional ultrasound imaging in mice) and a *Journal of Neuroscience* paper on lateral eye movements and amygdala deactivation. For him the walk is "not about exercise," it is about being "alert but not anxious." Indoors works, but less well.
- **Morning sunlight.** Get outside, ideally without sunglasses, even under cloud cover. Minimum about 2 minutes; 10 minutes is better; 30 is great. On a very bright, clear day about 60 seconds can suffice. Never stare at the sun. Skip it no more than one day in a row.
- **Hydration.** 16-32 oz of water with roughly half a teaspoon of sea salt, since neurons need sodium, potassium and magnesium.
- **Delay caffeine 90-120 minutes after waking.** Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors; drinking it immediately leads to an early/mid-afternoon crash when it wears off. Delaying removed his afternoon crash.
- **Fasting for focus.** He eats nothing until about 11 a.m.-noon. Fasting raises adrenaline (epinephrine), which helps focus and learning. What "breaks a fast" depends on insulin sensitivity, recent meals and glycogen status.
- **What he consumes while fasted.** Water, yerba mate or guayusa tea, and Athletic Greens with lemon. Yerba mate and guayusa increase GLP-1, which aids fat mobilization. He prefers non-smoky mate and reuses leaves for a day or two.

chunks.heading: Focused work block: 90-minute ultradian cycles
chunks.text:
Andrew does one deep 90-minute work block in the morning, and a second one in the afternoon. Together that is about 3 hours of deep work, which he thinks matches most people's actual total.

- **Timing.** Place it about 4-6 hours after the temperature minimum (wake at 6:30 gives a minimum at 4:30, so about 8:30-10:30 a.m.). That is the steepest part of the rising body-temperature curve. He says exact optimum varies by person. People who are naturally sharp early should keep using that.
- **Screen height.** Put the screen at eye level or slightly above. Eyes directed upward raise alertness; downward gaze and drooping lids promote sleepiness. Upright posture is more alerting than reclining.
- **Eliminate distraction.** He uses the Freedom app to block the internet, turns the phone fully off (not just airplane mode, sometimes leaving it in the car), and avoids bathroom breaks in the block. The bladder has a direct neural link to brainstem alertness areas. He sets a 90-minute timer.
- **Low-level white noise.** Played at low volume, not through headphones. He cites studies showing it engages attention/cognition/memory areas and increases dopamine-associated brain activity.
- He calls the state "the tunnel" and says the work feels like "a workout for the mind," likely tied to dopamine and norepinephrine release. He admits he is not perfect about it.

chunks.heading: Exercise structure
chunks.text:
- **About 60 minutes (plus or minus 15), 5 days per week**, with 2 full rest days. Going much longer than an hour can be detrimental via cortisol.
- **Three-to-two split in 10-12 week blocks.** For 10-12 weeks do 3 strength/hypertrophy sessions and 2 endurance sessions, then flip to 3 endurance and 2 strength.
- **80/20 intensity rule.** About 80% of resistance work should stop short of failure and about 20% can go to failure. Similarly, about 80% of endurance work should stay below the lactate "burn" and about 20% should push into it. Lactate is its own brain fuel, and the burn is not lactic acid.
- **Why.** Exercise increases brain blood flow, BDNF, and anti-inflammatory signaling (lowering IL-6, raising IL-10). Resistance training releases bone-derived hormones such as osteocalcin that support neuron health. In humans, new-neuron creation from exercise is not well supported, so he emphasizes health of existing neurons.
- **Fasted training.** He trains fasted when possible, citing Satchin Panda's *The Circadian Code* for cellular and liver benefits. If hungry, he has water with electrolytes (half teaspoon sea salt plus a 99 mg potassium tablet, or an electrolyte product like LMNT). He is not a fan of energy drinks pre-workout.
- **Occasional aid.** On rare days, 300 mg alpha-GPC (supports acetylcholine) for physical and cognitive performance.

chunks.heading: Food, hormones and supplements
chunks.text:
- **Lunch (around noon, about 80% full).** Large volumes divert blood to the gut and cause lethargy. He eats protein, vegetables, nuts and healthy fats, low carb. Starches only if he trained that day, because starch raises serotonin and causes sleepiness. About 25% of people have genes that let them tolerate lots of carbohydrate without sedation; he does not.
- **Post-lunch walk of 5-30 minutes** improves nutrient utilization and gives more outdoor light information.
- **Omega-3s.** At least 1,000 mg per day of EPA (not 1,000 mg of fish oil) has been shown in over a dozen studies to be about as effective as prescription antidepressants for depression. He takes fish oil; algae-based options exist for non-fish eaters.
- **Selenium for thyroid.** A few Brazil nuts per day. He also notes iodine matters.
- **Cholesterol for hormones.** Sex steroids are made from cholesterol, so he eats butter (keeping portions modest).
- **Testosterone/estrogen options.** 400 mg/day Tongkat Ali (a ginseng) to raise free testosterone by lowering SHBG effects, and Fadogia agrestis to raise luteinizing hormone. He notes the evidence is limited and to check with a doctor.
- Allowing 12+ hours per day without eating is beneficial.

chunks.heading: NSDR and hypnosis in the afternoon
chunks.text:
- **Non-sleep deep rest (NSDR)** is his umbrella term for meditation, yoga nidra and hypnosis, all deliberate shifts toward deeper relaxation.
- **Daily 10-minute hypnosis after lunch and the walk,** using the Reveri app (reverie.com), based on research by David Spiegel at Stanford. He cites a *Cerebral Cortex* paper (Jiang et al.) showing hypnosis engages executive networks, the default mode network and the insula (interoception). It is not stage hypnosis.
- Unlike a nap, he exits "focused" with no grogginess. It can also increase plasticity and be directed toward goals like focus, creativity, pain reduction, anxiety or sleep.
- After NSDR, he drinks water and does a second 90-minute work block around 2:30-3:00 p.m. Combined with delayed caffeine, he avoids the afternoon slump.
- **Napping.** Keep naps to 90 minutes or less; 10-20 minutes is often better. Know whether naps disrupt your night sleep.

chunks.heading: Evening light, dinner and sleep
chunks.text:
- **Afternoon/evening sunlight (about 4-5 p.m.)** for 5-30 minutes lowers retinal sensitivity to later light and keeps the melatonin rhythm appropriate (a *Scientific Reports* study). Light between 10-11 p.m. and 4 a.m. disrupts dopamine, learning, memory, immune function and mood.
- **Blue blockers.** He does not wear them. If used at all, wear them only late at night, not in the afternoon. Bright light of any wavelength still activates the relevant retinal cells. For headaches from screens, look into the distance (over 20 feet) periodically.
- **Dinner with starchy carbs** (rice, pasta) plus protein and vegetables boosts serotonin, aiding the transition to sleep. Low-carb dieters often struggle to fall asleep. He avoids refined sugar, citing Robert Lustig.
- **Skip serotonin/dopamine precursor supplements** (5-HTP, tryptophan): they made him fall asleep fast, then wake after 3-4 hours.
- **Heat to cool down.** A hot bath, shower or sauna 20 minutes before bed accelerates the later temperature drop of 1-3 degrees. For growth hormone, 20 minutes in the sauna, 10 minutes out, repeat.
- **Bedroom.** Very dark and cool, with warm blankets, so you can dump heat through palms, feet and face during non-REM sleep.
- **Sleep stack (30-60 min before bed).** 300-400 mg elemental magnesium threonate or bisglycinate (promotes GABA), 50 mg apigenin (from chamomile), and 100-200 mg theanine. He avoids melatonin: doses are too high, possible effects on sex hormones, a role in suppressing puberty onset, and it does not keep you asleep. Check with a physician first; some get GI upset from magnesium.

chunks.heading: Night waking and weekends
chunks.text:
- **Waking at 2:30-3 a.m. after a very early melatonin pulse** (you are tired at 8:30 but stay up): go to bed earlier, or get somewhat more bright light around 7-8 p.m. to delay melatonin.
- **If you wake up, keep lights dim** and turn them off fast. Use NSDR/yoga nidra, hypnosis or long-exhale breathing: "It's very hard to control the mind with the mind. Look to the body."
- **Consistency.** Even after a late night, wake at your regular time. After a bad night, do not go to bed much earlier the next day; stay up to your normal time.
- **Weekends.** He takes one full unstructured day off per week. Daily non-negotiables: morning sunlight and regular sleep.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman lists foods and supplements that support neuron structure (EPA omega-3s, phosphatidylserine, choline, creatine, anthocyanins, glutamine) with doses. He then explains the three signals driving food choice (taste, gut nutrient sensing, learned belief) and how pairing foods can shift preference.

chunks.heading: Omega-3s, phosphatidylserine and choline as the structural nutrients for neurons
chunks.text:
- Andrew's framing: much of the brain (beyond water) is fat, and neuron membranes are built from structural fat, not belly storage fat. The foods you eat supply the building blocks of the neurons that let you think.
- Two "modulatory" foundations come first: regular, ample sleep, and 150-180 minutes per week of cardiovascular exercise (heart health feeds the brain's oxygen and glucose supply). Resistance training is a bonus on top.
- **Omega-3 (EPA):** most people get enough omega-6 but not enough omega-3. He says to aim for at least 1.5 g of EPA per day, ideally 2-3 g. He says 1-3 g/day of EPA has mood benefits on par with some antidepressant treatments, and can allow lower antidepressant doses for people already on them.
- Sources: mackerel, salmon, herring, oysters, sardines, anchovies, and caviar ("the heavyweight champion of EPAs per unit volume"). Plant sources include chia seeds, walnuts and soybeans. Alternatives are liquid or capsule fish oil, krill oil, or algae-based EPA.
- **Phosphatidylserine:** found in meat, fish and, to some extent, cabbage. In at least three studies, 300 mg/day modestly improved cognition, and in at least five it reduced cognitive decline. He calls the effects "modest" but real.
- **Choline** (for acetylcholine, the "electrical highlighter pen" for focus and alertness): the main food source is egg yolks, with smaller amounts in fish, potatoes, nuts, seeds, grains and fruit. He suggests 500 mg to 1 g per day from food and supplements combined.
- Hydration plus sodium, magnesium and potassium are also required for neurons to fire.

chunks.heading: What Andrew takes himself
chunks.text:
- Liquid fish oil (1-2 tablespoons per day, often lemon-flavored), switching to capsules when traveling. The target is 2-3 g of EPA per day, not just 2-3 g of fish oil. He takes less if he has eaten fish.
- Alpha-GPC at 300 mg, about 2-3 times per week, early in the day because it can be mildly stimulating (far less than a double espresso). Studies on offsetting cognitive decline used 600-1,200 mg/day. He considers 900 mg sounds very high for himself.
- Creatine monohydrate at 5 g per day, for a long time, as a "baseline insurance policy." He has no phosphatidylserine habit yet. He eats limited meat and does not seek out meat for creatine.
- Glutamine in small amounts regularly, since college, originally for immune support.
- He tells people to check with their doctor first, and notes supplement quality varies (he points to Thorne).

chunks.heading: Creatine, anthocyanins and glutamine for cognition
chunks.text:
- **Creatine:** can fuel the brain and may support frontal circuits tied to mood and motivation (emerging evidence for mild depression). Benefit appears at 5 g/day or more and is especially clear in people who eat no meat, with some evidence for meat-eaters too. Caveats: water retention varies by person, and creatine may raise DHT, which could matter for people prone to hair loss. He cites a 2021 review (Roschel).
- **Anthocyanins** (blueberries, blackberries, black currants, thin-skinned dark berries): one study in people aged 65+ used about 428-598 mg of anthocyanins daily for 12 weeks and found improved verbal learning and memory. Effects on DNA damage and LDL oxidation are also reported (review: Afzal, 2019). Supplement range: about 5.5-11 g of blueberry extract, with the higher end seeming more beneficial. Food range: 60-120 g of fresh blueberries per day.
- **Glutamine:** found in cottage cheese, beef, chicken, fish, dairy, eggs, beans, cabbage, spinach and parsley. Supplemental doses typically run 1-10 g/day. It may reduce sugar cravings by engaging glutamine-sensing gut neurons that signal satiety.
- Glutamine may offset cognitive effects of low oxygen (altitude, and likely sleep apnea) by reducing inflammation. He flags apnea as a serious health issue linked to cognitive decline and amyloid burden (Sharma 2018; Quaresma review).

chunks.heading: Three signals that drive food preference
chunks.text:
- Andrew describes the brain's "yum, yuck or meh" analysis as three channels:
  1. Taste in the mouth: five tastes (bitter, sweet, umami, salty, sour) are converted into electrical signals that travel to the brainstem and then the insular cortex.
  2. Subconscious gut signals about nutrient content.
  3. Learned association between a taste and its metabolic payoff, which is where belief and conditioning come in.
- **Taste is central:** Charles Zuker's lab at Columbia showed that sweet and bitter are represented by separate neuron populations. Silencing the sweet neurons removes the preference for sweet. Activating them makes animals prefer bitter or plain water. Preference is a central brain phenomenon, not just a tongue phenomenon.
- Normally these systems are correlated, but they can be uncoupled and re-paired.
- The insula handles interoception, meaning the internal sense of how you feel (fullness, anxiety, alertness).

chunks.heading: Gut neuropod cells, hidden sugars and gut health
chunks.text:
- Diego Bohorquez (Duke) found neuropod cells in the gut lining. They sense amino acids, sugars and fatty acids and signal via the nodose ganglion to trigger dopamine release, driving you to seek more of that food. This happens subconsciously.
- Robert Lustig's "hidden sugars" in processed foods are described as engaging these mechanisms so you want more, even without an obviously sweet taste.
- Gut health: rather than relying on supplemental probiotics or prebiotics, he favors 2-4 servings per day of low-sugar fermented foods (for example sauerkraut, natto). He cites Stanford work from Justin Sonnenburg and Chris Gardner published in Cell. A healthy gut environment lets these neurons signal appropriately for healthy food seeking.
- Time-restricted feeding recap: begin the eating window at least 1 hour after waking, end it at least 2-3 hours before bed, and keep it at roughly the same time each day because it affects clock genes.

chunks.heading: What the brain is actually seeking, and the artificial sweetener warning
chunks.text:
- Work from Ivan de Araujo (Mount Sinai) and Dana Small (Yale) showed the reward is not just taste, dopamine, or even a rise in blood glucose. Using 2-deoxyglucose, which stops neurons from metabolizing glucose, the reward disappeared. Andrew's summary: what you subconsciously seek is for your neurons to be metabolically active.
- Food preference is partly hardwired and partly "soft-wired," like language, so it can be changed.
- **Artificial sweeteners alone:** initially not rewarding (no dopamine rise), but with repeated use dopamine can eventually rise, so people may come to like or crave them.
- **Sweeteners paired with carbohydrate:** the Dalenberg/Small paper (Cell Metabolism, March 2020), "short-term consumption of sucralose with but not without carbohydrate impairs neural and metabolic sensitivity to sugar in humans," showed that taking sucralose along with carbs impairs metabolic sensitivity to sugar. After that pairing, drinking the sweetener alone triggered an outsized insulin release. In a study of children, insulin responses were large enough to make them pre-diabetic and the study was halted.
- Andrew's takeaway: he does not say artificial sweeteners are bad. He says to consume them away from foods that raise blood glucose. If you want a diet soda, "be my guest," but not with a meal.
- He also mentions a Nature paper suggesting some sweeteners can disrupt the gut microbiome, with mixed results depending on the sweetener.

chunks.heading: How to learn to like healthy foods (belief and pairing)
chunks.text:
- The protocol: if you want to eat more of a food because it is good for you but you find it "meh" or mildly "yuck," pair it in the same meal with foods that fuel your brain metabolically. For a ketogenic eater, that means ketone-supporting foods. You do not need to hide the flavor.
- Timeline: based on the human sucralose conditioning data, the food should taste at least better within about 7 days, and certainly within about 14 days.
- Limits: this will not override truly noxious foods, which are hardwired avoidance. It works for neutral-to-mildly-unpleasant foods.
- Belief matters: Alia Crum's Stanford work found that people told a milkshake was high-calorie and nutrient-rich had larger insulin and blood glucose responses than those told it was low-calorie, even though it was the identical shake. He calls this a belief effect, distinct from placebo.
- Eating progressively sweeter, highly palatable food shifts the dopamine system toward needing it. Eating less sweet, less palatable food can reset what feels rewarding.
- Food preference circuits stay rewirable even in people with type 2 diabetes or metabolic disorders (de Araujo, Small, "Rethinking Food Reward," Annual Review of Psychology, 2019).
- He suggests that much "food war" certainty (carnivore versus plant-based) partly reflects reinforcement of whatever one eats regularly, though he does not take a side on that debate.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman explains dopamine as the currency of motivation that gets depleted after big peaks. He shows how to manage energy with NSDR, morning light, hydration, exercise, food and cold exposure. He also covers neuroplasticity, porn and dopamine, and why a daily good-morning text to a friend is among the most powerful social protocols.

chunks.heading: Dopamine is a wave pool, and the trough follows the peak
chunks.text:
- Andrew uses an analogy from endocrinologist Kyle Gillette: dopamine is a reservoir, like a wave pool. If you generate big waves, they crash out of the pool and deplete it.
- After a big surge from cocaine, amphetamine, pre-workout stacks, excess caffeine or intense media, dopamine drops below baseline.
- In the trough, the same thing feels less good, and you need more of it for the same output.
- The trough's depth and duration scale with how high the peak was, not how long it lasted.
- People in the trough usually reach for something to re-trigger dopamine, which pushes them deeper. Andrew compares it to a glucose spike followed by a crash below baseline.
- He says dopamine is "the universal currency of motivation-seeking and reward." The brain isn't built to release it in huge amounts without preceding effort.
- Andrew cites Anna Lembke's *Dopamine Nation* seesaw model.
- He describes a "forward center of mass" state (term from a former Navy SEAL), versus flat-footed or back on your heels. His advice is to master the transitions between these states, because you can't be full tilt all the time.
- Burnout, he says, is "trying to be forward center of mass for too long."
- Most people do well to come off the gas pedal a little, especially when a peak comes from pharmacology or an extreme circumstance.

chunks.heading: Getting out of the dopamine trough: abstain, then return to baseline
chunks.text:
- Andrew says most addiction and compulsive behavior can be reset with abstinence lasting roughly 30-60 days. To a person craving the thing, that sounds like horror.
- For burnout from work plus stimulants (he mentions tech and finance people on Adderall), the answer is to accept feeling low for about a week. Then you feel a bit less low and return to baseline, and only then can you go forward again.
- He sees a clinical use case for ADHD medication in people who need it. Others have driven themselves into a trough and are chasing anything to get out, when what they need is to stay away from all of it and wait.
- Rewards in smaller things, like time with dogs, help.
- The chocolate test (from Lembke): abstain from chocolate for a week, then taste your favorite piece. It tastes great, but the brain quickly shifts to wanting more rather than savoring.
- Healthy habits aren't a problem, but the same logic applies. Loud music, pre-workout and a hard workout are fine occasionally, but you should also be able to train without them.
- Stacking catecholamine drivers 7 days a week leaves you "cooked" in the afternoon.
- Know your own baseline. Andrew can work about 12 hours a day, five or six days a week, with one full day off (Sunday). Pushing to 15-hour days or 7 days a week makes him "run aground."
- He says you can deviate from your groove by about 15-20%, but anything more extreme leads to trouble.
- Andrew worries far less about energy drinks, loud music or workouts than about high-intensity pornography used regularly, or prescription stimulants taken without need. He says the latter is "a recipe for burnout, depression, or worse."

chunks.heading: Daily energy protocol: NSDR, hydration, sunlight, movement
chunks.text:
- **Sleep:** Not everyone needs 8-9 hours. Andrew got about 6 hours 45 minutes the night before the interview. If you wake unrested, don't push through; do a non-sleep deep rest.
- **NSDR (non-sleep deep rest):** 10, 20 or 30 minutes lying down with eyes closed, long exhale breathing and a body scan (feet, then legs, then hands, and so on). It is similar to yoga nidra. Free scripts are on YouTube: Andrew's own, Kelly Boys (a female voice), and Kamini Desai.
  - The instruction is to stay awake, but falling asleep is fine if you set an alarm.
  - Andrew cites a study showing yoga nidra raised baseline dopamine in the basal ganglia by about 60%.
  - He also says there's some evidence it speeds learning, and that his lab is gearing up with Matt Walker's lab to study the mechanism.
  - He did a 10-minute one on the way to the interview, and uses it in the afternoon when depleted.
- **Hydration:** 16-32 oz of water on waking.
- **Morning light:** Get bright light, ideally sunlight, in your eyes first thing. Face east and take sunglasses off. Glasses and contacts are fine. Even through cloud cover it's far brighter than indoor light.
  - It triggers a healthy cortisol peak that supports alertness, immunity and mood, and improves sleep that night.
  - You don't need to see the sun itself, only the light it emits.
  - On very dark winter days (UK, Scandinavia), use bright artificial light in the morning and through the day. SAD lights are a special case at 10,000 lux or more.
  - If you wake before sunrise, you have to wait.
- **Exercise:** Some movement in the morning, even 5 minutes of skipping rope, jogging in place or a walk. Everyone should do at least 2-3 days a week of resistance training plus cardiovascular training. Timing is flexible (morning, lunch or evening), as long as caffeine or pre-workout doesn't wreck sleep.
  - Andrew finds that finishing his workout before 9 a.m. gives him more energy all day. A mid-to-late-morning workout leaves him sleepy in the afternoon.
- **Caffeine:** Some people get light and exercise before caffeine. Andrew fully supports anyone who wants coffee or tea first thing.

chunks.heading: Circadian entrainment, shift work and chronotype
chunks.text:
- Body temperature rises in the morning, which makes you more alert. In the early afternoon it peaks, which is a common source of post-lunch sleepiness.
- To fall asleep, body temperature must drop about 1-3°. A cool room with warm blankets helps, as does sticking a foot out.
- Entrainment: if you hate mornings, force yourself up and exercising at 6 a.m. for 3 days in a row. By day four you naturally start waking around then.
- The suprachiasmatic nucleus is driven by sunlight to the eyes, physical activity, meal timing and social engagement. Light, exercise, caffeine, hydration and an early meal shift your clock earlier. By 10-11 p.m. you start feeling sleepy, then you need the discipline to put the phone in another room.
