- He says even short bouts can cause a lasting rise in dopamine and sustained elevation of mood, energy and focus. He notes this is not true of every stress.

chunks.heading: Resilience and the "counting walls" approach
chunks.text:
- Embracing cold as a self-directed challenge builds "top-down control" by the prefrontal cortex over deeper brain centers that regulate reflexive states.
- He says this is the basis of "resilience and grit", and that the skill carries over to real-world stressors, helping you stay calm and clear. In short, "deliberate cold exposure is great training for the mind."
- Counting walls:
  - Before or during cold, your mind pushes back ("I really don't want to do this," "Get me out of here"). Each of these is a "wall".
  - The walls are adrenaline pulses, and they trigger the adaptive response. Without difficulty there is no stimulus to adapt to.
  - Staying in despite the urge to exit means you've traversed the wall.
  - Set a goal of walls to traverse (e.g., 3-5 per round), or go by time.
  - He prefers walls because it transfers better to life stressors, which can't simply be timed, and it strengthens mind-body connection.
- To make cold a stronger resilience stimulus without lowering the temperature, keep moving your limbs while hands and feet stay in the water. Staying still lets a thermal layer insulate you, and moving breaks it up so the water feels much colder. He compares it to slowing a weight lift to remove momentum.

chunks.heading: Metabolism, shivering and the Søeberg principle
chunks.text:
- Cold increases metabolism short-term because the body burns calories to raise core temperature, but he says the total calories burned are not significant.
- The bigger benefit is the conversion of white fat (energy storage) to beige or brown fat, which are highly metabolically active. This helps cold adaptation (feeling more comfortable in cold) and triggers further, sustained metabolic increases.
- He stresses calories in versus calories out still governs weight: "There is no escaping the laws of thermodynamics."
- The Søeberg Principle (from Dr. Susanna Søeberg) is to force your body to reheat on its own, or "End With Cold."
- Shivering may enhance the metabolic effect: it releases succinate from muscles and further activates brown fat thermogenesis.
- To increase shivering, during or right after cold:
  - Don't huddle or cross your arms.
  - Don't towel off.
  - Let your body reheat and dry naturally.
- He admits this is tough. Unless it's a hot sunny day, he takes a hot shower and towels off after cold, knowing he is likely limiting the metabolic effect.

chunks.heading: Recovery and timing around training
chunks.text:
- He cites a meta-analysis finding cold water immersion can be a highly effective recovery tool after high-intensity or endurance training.
- Short immersions (under 5 minutes) improved muscle power and perceived recovery and reduced muscle soreness, partly via lower circulating creatine kinases.
- Cold water immersion (not cold showers) can blunt hypertrophy, strength or endurance gains if done within roughly 4 hours after training.
- He suggests waiting 6-8 or more hours after training, or doing cold before training.
- The exception is when you only want recovery without adaptation, such as in competition mode.

chunks.heading: Time of day
chunks.text:
- Cold is followed by the body heating up, and body temperature increases tend to wake you while decreases push you toward sleepiness.
- He suggests using deliberate cold early in the day, not close to bedtime.
- Late is better than never, but not if it disturbs sleep. If it affects sleep, move it earlier or skip it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman's newsletter distills his heat exposure episode into three sauna protocols: cardiovascular health, general health/mood/stress, and growth hormone release. It covers temperature and duration targets, hydration, timing for sleep, and safety cautions including sperm count, pregnancy, and infrared saunas.

chunks.heading: Safety limits and who should skip sauna
chunks.text:
- Andrew says heat exposure is only beneficial when it isn't too hot. Too-high temperatures are "extremely dangerous."
- Pregnant women and children younger than 16 should not use sauna.
- He advises starting slow, with cooler temperatures that don't significantly raise heart rate. Hyperthermia and dehydration are always possible.
- Men trying to conceive should know that repeated deliberate heat exposure can reduce sperm count. Counts rebound after stopping sauna or hot baths, but this takes about 45-60 days.
- Men who want to avoid this can put a cool or cold pack on while in the sauna. That isn't possible in a hot bath.

chunks.heading: Ways to get deliberate heat and the infrared caveat
chunks.text:
- Options include dry saunas, steam saunas, hot tubs, hot showers, or wearing warm layers on a brief jog to raise body temperature.
- He recommends picking whatever method fits your schedule and budget and can be done routinely.
- Infrared saunas: there is currently insufficient evidence that they have effects beyond a standard sauna. Most also don't reach the heat range (80-100 °C) he lists for positive health effects.

chunks.heading: Cardiovascular health and Protocol #1
chunks.text:
- Regular sauna use is linked to a lower risk of fatal cardiovascular events and stroke (Laukkanen et al.). Longer and more frequent sessions were associated with lower long-term cardiovascular disease risk. Other clinical groups have linked sauna to lower "all-cause mortality."
- Heat triggers some of the same responses as cardio: heart rate and blood flow rise, and blood vessels vasodilate as the body works to cool down.
- **Protocol #1 (cardiovascular):**
  - Temperature: 80-100 °C (176-212 °F), adjusted to personal tolerance.
  - Duration: 5-20 minutes per session.
  - Frequency: 2-3x per week, or up to 7x per week. More often appears better for cardiovascular health.

chunks.heading: Mood, stress response and Protocol #2
chunks.text:
- Heat drives release of dynorphins and endorphins. Dynorphins first cause discomfort and agitation but set the stage for endorphins to have enhanced effects on mood and body. This explains the mild, happy euphoria after sauna.
- Heat is a form of hormesis, a mild tolerable stress that helps the body adapt. Regular sauna use has been found to:
  - decrease cortisol levels
  - enhance activation of DNA repair/longevity pathways
  - activate heat shock proteins, which help monitor and possibly repair protein structure within cells
- **Protocol #2 (general health, mood, stress, hormetic pathways):**
  - Total of 1 hour per week, split into 2-3 sessions rather than done all at once.
  - Temperature: 80-100 °C (176-212 °F).

chunks.heading: Growth hormone and Protocol #3
chunks.text:
- Growth hormone supports muscle growth, bone strength, tissue repair and metabolism. It is released at night during sleep and declines with age.
- Specific sauna protocols have been shown to boost growth hormone release dramatically, up to 16-fold in one study.
- **Protocol #3 (growth hormone):**
  - Use sauna infrequently: once per week or less.
  - On that day, do 30 minutes in the sauna, cool off outside for 5 minutes, then 30 minutes more, then cool off.
  - A few hours or more later, repeat, for a total of four 30-minute sauna sessions in one day. Andrew notes "that's a lot!"
  - Do it in a semi-fasted state, with no food for 2-3 hours beforehand. Lower blood glucose encourages growth hormone release, as it does for daily release during sleep.
  - More frequent sauna has other effects but blunts the growth hormone increase.
  - To add metabolic gains, alternate sauna with deliberate cold exposure during the rest periods.

chunks.heading: Hydration and timing
chunks.text:
- Hydrate well before and after sauna, since sweat contains water and electrolytes.
- He recommends drinking at least 16 ounces of water for every 10 minutes spent in the sauna.
- Body temperature fluctuates with circadian rhythm. Using sauna in the afternoon or evening lets the body's natural cooling align with the "post-cooling sauna effect," which helps with falling asleep at night.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andrew Huberman explains how deliberate breathing patterns shift brain-body state. He covers reducing overbreathing, the CO2 tolerance test, the physiological sigh for fast calming, cyclic hyperventilation for alertness, and using inhale/exhale emphasis to raise or lower heart rate.

chunks.heading: Why breathing matters: the O2:CO2 balance
chunks.text:
- Andrew describes breathing as balancing oxygen and carbon dioxide in the brain and body, not just taking in O2. Oxygen passes from lung alveoli into the blood and hemoglobin carries it to cells.
- Carbon dioxide is not just waste. He says it changes hemoglobin's shape to "liberate bound oxygen" into tissues. During exercise body pH drops slightly, which increases oxygen offloading to muscles.
- The brain is the most metabolically active tissue at rest, so it needs a lot of oxygen. Improper O2:CO2 ratios can create a hypoxic state that hurts cognition and physical function.
- Breathing is regulated by parallel mechanical and chemical pathways that monitor O2 and CO2 constantly.

chunks.heading: Overbreathing, nasal breathing and sleep apnea
chunks.text:
- Healthy resting breathing moves about 6 liters of air per minute, roughly 12 shallow-to-moderate breaths per minute. Most people overbreathe at 15-18 breaths per minute.
- Overbreathing over-exhales CO2 (hypocapnia), which lowers oxygen delivery to the brain and tissues. The brain becomes hyper-excitable, causing difficulty focusing and anxiety.
- To reduce overbreathing outside exercise:
  - Take small pauses between breaths.
  - Breathe through the nose, because nostril resistance extends exhale duration.
- Nasal breathing at rest and during sleep:
  - Allows maximum lung inflation each breath, increasing oxygen delivery.
  - Warms incoming air, which is healthier for the lungs.
  - Produces nitric oxide in the nasal passages, relaxing smooth muscle and improving blood vessel dilation. This helps remove waste, deliver nutrients and relieve sinus congestion.
  - Is linked by Andrew to facial structure benefits (jaw, cheekbones, tooth and jaw structure).
- Mouth breathing has its place during exercise.
- Some people under-breathe at night. Sleep apnea means breaths are too shallow or infrequent, causing temporary hypoxia and waking. It is more common with excess weight, but lean people can have it too.
  - Symptoms: sleepiness, snoring, morning headache, irritability, inattention.
  - Risks: cardiovascular disease and stroke, worsened dementia, impaired cognition, decreased libido.
  - Options: a CPAP machine; medical tape over the mouth during sleep to force nasal breathing; practicing nasal breathing during exercise and the day.

chunks.heading: Test and train CO2 tolerance with box breathing
chunks.text:
- To reduce overbreathing, practice diaphragm control: deliberately expand the stomach "out" on the inhale and let it return "in" on the exhale.
- Andrew uses the carbon dioxide tolerance test, developed by Brian Mackenzie:
  1. Breathe normally for 4-5 breaths.
  2. Inhale once deeply through the nose until the lungs are completely full.
  3. Start a timer and exhale as slowly as possible.
  4. Stop the timer when the lungs are empty and note the duration. He stresses: "it's not about measuring how long you can hold your breath!"
- Use the exhale time to set box breathing durations from a reference table.
- Box breathing is inhale-hold-exhale-hold, each side the same duration, like the sides of a box.
- Practice 2-3 minutes of box breathing, 1-2x per week. Retest after 1-2 weeks and see if each side can be longer.
- Progress means less frequent breaths and healthier breathing patterns. He says this should mean less overbreathing at rest, better exercise performance and reduced anxiety.

chunks.heading: Physiological sigh for fast stress relief
chunks.text:
- Technique:
  1. Two consecutive inhales through the nose: one big inhale, then another with no exhale in between, to maximally inflate the lungs.
  2. Exhale fully through the mouth until the lungs are empty.
- He says it rapidly shifts the autonomic nervous system from arousal and agitation toward calm, and is, "to my knowledge," the fastest way to calm down in real time. Even 1-3 sighs can help.
- Daily practice: his lab, with Dr. David Spiegel of Stanford, published a clinical trial showing 5 minutes a day of cyclic physiological sighing reduces overall stress, promotes relaxation, improves sleep, lowers resting heart rate and enhances mood.

chunks.heading: Cyclic hyperventilation for alertness and focus
chunks.text:
- Forceful, deep, repeated inhales followed by exhales release adrenaline in the brain and body, raising alertness and capacity for focus.
- Protocol:
  1. Deep inhale through the nose, immediately followed by a deep exhale (active or passive) through the mouth.
  2. Repeat 25 times.
  3. Fully exhale until the lungs are empty and hold for 15-30 seconds.
  4. Repeat the round, for up to 5 minutes total.
- Expect tingling or agitation right after. Over the next few minutes, adrenaline rises and focus and attention improve greatly.
- Repeated practice trains staying calm while agitated and leads to a higher stress threshold.
- Safety: use caution if prone to panic attacks or high anxiety. "Never, ever" do it near or in water or while driving, because of passing out, shallow water blackout, drowning or car accidents, especially with extended breath holds.

chunks.heading: Controlling heart rate with the breath
chunks.text:
- Breathing and heart rate are directly linked through respiratory sinus arrhythmia, a normal hard-wired feature involving the vagus nerve, heart, lungs and brainstem.
- Rules:
  - To increase heart rate, inhale longer and more deeply or vigorously than you exhale.
  - To decrease heart rate, exhale longer and more vigorously than you inhale.
- How common practices map:
  - Physiological sighs emphasize exhale: calming.
  - Cyclic hyperventilation emphasizes inhale: activating.
  - Box breathing is balanced.
- Use cases: lower heart rate before sleep, an interview or public speaking; raise it before athletic performance.
- He notes that simply understanding this lets you shift your state anytime without dedicated breathwork.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman explains working memory as dopamine-dependent and gives two self-tests as a proxy for baseline dopamine. He lays out behavioral tools first (NSDR, deliberate cold, binaural beats), then cautious supplement and prescription options with dosing guidance.

chunks.heading: Working memory: what it is and why dopamine drives it
chunks.text:
Andrew defines working memory as holding a limited amount of information "in mind" for a specific goal, such as a phone number, name or address, then letting it go so capacity reopens for other information.

- It requires attention and depends critically on the neuromodulator dopamine.
- Working memory capacity underpins task-switching and moving through the day in a productive, focused way.
- He cites D'Esposito and colleagues: people with a high working memory span (those who can remember longer strings of letters or numbers) have more dopamine available in the prefrontal cortex (PFC). Those with shorter spans have less.
- He cites Goldman et al.: introducing small amounts of dopamine directly into the PFC improved working memory.
- He notes that D'Esposito and colleagues showed dopamine-increasing drugs such as bromocriptine improve working memory in humans.
- People with initially lower dopamine apparently benefit more from raising it than people whose dopamine is already high, which he says makes logical sense.

chunks.heading: Two quick tests to estimate baseline working memory
chunks.text:
Andrew describes two brief tests similar to laboratory assessments. They are a proxy, not a diagnostic tool, and he says not to be alarmed by a low result because many tools improve it.

- **Test one:** a digit or letter span task, available as a written test or in audio format. How many numbers or letters you can remember places you in a low, moderate or high working memory group.
- **Test two:** listen to 6 sentences, then recall a specific word from each.
  - 0-2 correct = low working memory group.
  - 3-6 correct = high working memory group.
  - 3-4 is average.
- Results (low vs. high) serve as a proxy for low or high baseline dopamine, which he says neuroimaging studies support.

chunks.heading: Non-Sleep Deep Rest (NSDR) for dopamine and cognitive performance
chunks.text:
NSDR (or yoga nidra) is deliberate muscle relaxation that lets the brain enter a shallow, sleep-like state.

- Both practices involve listening to a script with breathwork and focused attention on the body while lying down. Andrew notes zero-cost NSDR scripts exist.
- He cites a study in which yoga nidra increased dopamine in key brain regions by up to 60%.
- He says other studies using cognitive performance tasks show both NSDR and yoga nidra improve performance.
- Protocol: **2-3x per week, in 10-to-20-minute sessions.**

chunks.heading: Deliberate cold exposure before a working-memory-heavy work bout
chunks.text:
Cold water exposure (shower or cold tub, 1-3 minutes) greatly increases dopamine and other catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine) for many hours afterward.

- It is uncomfortable in the moment, but afterward you feel alert yet calm and likely have improved focus and attention.
- **Timing:** do 1-3 minutes of cold exposure **30-60 minutes before** a study or work session requiring working memory.
- **Dose:** stay in water up to your neck (hands under as well) for 60 seconds to 3 minutes, in a shower or cold plunge.
- **Temperature:** highly individual. The right temperature is one you can safely stay in for 60-180 seconds, but that is uncomfortable enough that it takes mental effort to get in and makes you want to get out.
  - Check: it quickens your breathing and takes effort to submerge, yet doesn't "burn."
  - For most people 40-50°F is a good range; some may need it warmer.

chunks.heading: Binaural beats during cognitive tasks
chunks.text:
Several studies (he cites Engelbregt et al. and Beauchene et al.) show working memory performance increases when listeners use 13-30 Hz binaural beats while doing mental tasks.

- It is unknown whether the benefit comes from increased dopamine or another route.
- Protocol: listen to binaural beats before or during studying or working. They are available as YouTube videos or apps.
- Andrew stresses the data are mixed: some studies show impressive effects, some lesser, and some no improvement in human subjects.

chunks.heading: Supplements to raise dopamine (after trying behavioral tools first)
chunks.text:
Andrew's order of operations: try the behavioral tools above first, then consider supplements. He says never add or remove a supplement without consulting your doctor. Find your minimal effective dose for any supplement.

- **L-tyrosine:** the amino acid precursor to dopamine, shown to increase working memory. Starting dose: **500 mg per 100 kg of body weight** (100 kg is about 220 lb).
- **Mucuna pruriens ("velvet bean"):** contains 99% L-dopa, the molecular precursor to dopamine.
  - He calls it a "VERY potent" way to increase dopamine and says to discuss with your doctor before using it.
  - Typical dose is 250 or 500 mg, though doses up to 1-5 g are tolerable for some people.
- **Crash risk:** some people experience a bit of a "crash" when the effects of pro-dopamine supplements wear off. That is why he prefers behavioral tools.

chunks.heading: Prescription options for working memory and attention
chunks.text:
Andrew lists prescription drugs that improve working memory and attention: bromocriptine (from the study above) and more commonly known medications such as Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse and modafinil.

- If someone decides to explore them, he says it must be done with a board-certified MD.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman's newsletter distills the science of neuroplasticity into a nine-step behavioral protocol for learning. It covers getting alert and focused, doing fast repetitions, embracing errors, inserting micro-rests, random rewards, limiting sessions to 90 minutes, then NSDR and deep sleep to consolidate. Steps 1, 2 and 9 are non-negotiable.

chunks.heading: The 9-step protocol is a trigger-then-consolidate model of learning
chunks.text:
Andrew's "Neuroplasticity Super-Protocol" (shared in a newsletter dated October 29, 2021, based on a lecture for teachers and students hosted by Logitech) treats a learning bout as the "trigger" for the possibility of learning. The actual rewiring of neural circuits happens afterward, during sleep and NSDR (non-sleep deep rest).

- Behavioral protocol only; pharmacology of accelerated learning is deferred to a future discussion.
- He says behavioral protocols are necessary no matter what else is layered on.
- Not all 9 steps are needed every session. Steps 1 (get alert), 2 (get focused) and 9 (deep sleep) are "non-negotiable".

chunks.heading: Step 1: Get alert with deep breathing before a learning bout
chunks.text:
Neuroplasticity requires alertness, which involves many mechanisms but mainly release of epinephrine (adrenaline) in brain and body.

- Take 25-30 deep breaths: inhale through the nose, exhale through the mouth.
- Exhale all air and hold the breath with lungs empty for 15-60 seconds.
- Inhale once and hold. Don't force the hold; start breathing normally as soon as the impulse to breathe arrives.
- Andrew uses this whether or not caffeine is involved, and says he relies on caffeine himself in the early part of the day.
- Do it prior to the learning bout.

chunks.heading: Step 2: Get focused by fixing your gaze
chunks.text:
"Mental focus follows visual focus."

- Stare at a point on a wall, screen or object for 30-60 seconds before starting (blinking is fine).
- The effort you feel is "top-down" attentional engagement, reflecting neural circuits involving acetylcholine release, among other mechanisms.
- Then move into the task. Expect focus to flicker on and off, especially at the start of a bout.
- Reduce distractions: phone off and out of the room, browser closed or limited to essential tabs, or ideally the internet turned off.

chunks.heading: Steps 3-4: Generate repetitions and embrace errors
chunks.text:
**Repetitions**
- Do the maximum number of repetitions you safely can in a bout. For some skills these are literal repeats (e.g., musical scales); for others, repeating the same process such as reading or doing math problems.
- Repeat the process a bit faster than is reflexive. This keeps the mind from drifting and keeps you alert.

**Errors**
- Errors (provided safety isn't compromised) are useful because they increase activation of circuits that raise alertness. If you do something correctly, there's no reason for the brain to take notice.
- The "stressful" feeling of an error is increased attention, which puts you in a better place for the next attempt.
- Computational modeling suggests an error rate of about 15% may be optimal and can guide task difficulty. He says not to worry much about the exact figure.
- Tactic: when you mess up, immediately do another attempt (and another) while the forebrain is maximally attentive.

chunks.heading: Step 5: Insert random 10-second micro-rests
chunks.text:
A non-obvious way to get more repetitions and learn faster.

- Human studies show that pausing for 10 seconds and doing nothing makes hippocampal and cortical neurons replay the same activity patterns as during the actual activity (reading, music practice, skill training), about 10X faster. That is roughly 10X neural repetitions during the pause.
- These "gap effects" resemble what happens in deep sleep.
- Protocol: randomly introduce 10-second pauses during learning, at roughly 1 pause per 2 minutes of learning, distributed at random ("not every 2 minutes on the minute").

chunks.heading: Step 6: Use random, intermittent reward
chunks.text:
- Reward circuits (all brain-chemical rewards) are tightly tethered to circuits for motivation and the desire to pursue things, including learning.
- To keep motivation high for yourself or others, make rewards random and intermittent. He notes this is what casinos do to keep people gambling.
- "Predictable rewards lose their motivational impact quickly."

chunks.heading: Steps 7-9: Session length, NSDR, and sleep
chunks.text:
**Session limits (step 7)**
- About 90 minutes is the longest period of intense focus and effort toward learning. Shorter bouts are fine.
- Space intense bouts 2-3 (or more) hours apart.
- Most people can't do more than 270 minutes of intense learning per day.

**NSDR after a bout (step 8)**
- Two human studies from the prior two years show shallow naps and/or NSDR enhance the rate and depth of learning.
- Within 1 hour of finishing a bout, do a short NSDR protocol. Options: the Reveri self-hypnosis app (zero cost, research tested), a brief 20-minute nap, or an NSDR script such as Yoga Nidra. He does a 10-minute one daily and also recommends a 30-minute one.

**Sleep (step 9)**
- Get quality, sufficiently long deep sleep that night, the next, and so on. Rewiring occurs during sleep and NSDR.
- Goal: get sleep right at least 80% of the time. It takes work but is worth it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman's newsletter on caffeine: how to find your dose (1-3 mg/kg), time it around sleep and afternoon crashes, hydrate with salt, and use abstinence to boost athletic performance. He also warns about dopamine stacking and explains how caffeine reinforces behaviors, so pair it with habits you want to build and avoid pairing it with ones you want to quit.

chunks.heading: Caffeine dosage: how Andrew sets a personal dose
chunks.text:
- Andrew recommends starting at 1 to 3 mg of caffeine per kilogram of body weight, and lower if someone is sensitive.
- Example: he weighs about 100 kg (220 lb), so a tolerable dose for him is 100 to 300 mg. He often takes more because he is "quite caffeine-adapted."
- He says to check what is actually in the drinks you consume. Coffee and energy drinks can contain anywhere from 50 to 500 mg, and as much as 800 mg depending on size and source.
- He warns against extended consumption of high caffeine levels, which raises the risk of headaches, anxiety, irritability and blood vessel damage.

chunks.heading: Hydration, electrolytes and theanine alongside caffeine
chunks.text:
- Caffeine is a diuretic, causing loss of fluid, sodium and other electrolytes.
- Andrew suggests drinking an equal volume of water with caffeine to avoid jitteriness, blurry vision or a low-blood-sugar feeling.
- Ideally add a small pinch of sea salt, table salt or an electrolyte powder to that water.
- Most people wake up slightly dehydrated, which can cause fatigue and reduce mental and physical performance, so hydrate with water when having morning caffeine.
- If even small doses cause anxiety or jitteriness, he suggests supplementing with theanine. He notes many energy drinks include 100 to 200 mg of theanine for this reason.

chunks.heading: Timing caffeine through the day
chunks.text:
- If you tend to have an afternoon crash, he suggests delaying caffeine for 90 to 120 minutes after waking. Otherwise, caffeine first thing is "A-OK."
- Caffeine on an empty stomach lets a smaller dose produce the same stimulant and performance-enhancing effects.
- Peak focus and alertness occur about 30 minutes after consumption and last about 60 minutes.
- Cutoff: avoid caffeine within 10 to 12 hours of bedtime. For some people 8 hours is fine.

chunks.heading: Caffeine, adenosine and sleep
chunks.text:
- Adenosine builds up during the day and creates sleepiness. Caffeine binds adenosine receptors and blocks its effects, so you feel less tired.
- For most people, caffeine has a quarter-life of about 12 hours, though genetics vary. Caffeine at noon means roughly 25% is still active at midnight.
- Even if you can fall asleep, late caffeine can disrupt deep (slow-wave) sleep and subsequent REM sleep.
- His bottom line: "To protect your sleep, it's typically best to avoid caffeine for at least 10-12 hours before bedtime."

chunks.heading: Mood and mental performance
chunks.text:
- Caffeine raises catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine), which increase motivation, alertness and drive.
- Andrew cites large-scale analyses showing regular caffeine intake improves mood and well-being and is associated with a lower risk of depression.

chunks.heading: Physical performance and the abstinence protocol
chunks.text:
- Research he cites shows caffeine improves reaction time, alertness, focus, coordination, power output and endurance. It also reduces fatigue, increases VO2 max, enhances strength, peak power and muscle contractility, and improves feelings of well-being during exercise.
- **Abstinence protocol:** abstain from caffeine for 3 to 20 days, then take caffeine about 30 minutes before the physical challenge (e.g., a marathon). Effects are more potent after abstinence.
- **Gentler variant:** if full abstinence is too painful, reduce daily caffeine for 1 to 3 weeks, or even a few days, then take your regular dose on the day of the challenge.
- He advises first exploring caffeine's effects during training, then deciding how to use abstinence and "caffeine-pulsing" for specific challenges.

chunks.heading: Dopamine stacking caution
chunks.text:
- Dopamine stacking is combining multiple chemical and behavioral inputs to boost dopamine, e.g., loud music, a highly caffeinated energy drink and l-tyrosine before an intense workout.
- Occasional use is fine, but he says not to make it the norm, especially for people who struggle with motivation.
- A dopamine spike is followed by a dip below baseline before returning to baseline, leaving you unmotivated or melancholy.
- "The worst thing you can do in the below-baseline phase" is to spike dopamine again pharmacologically, since that drives baseline down further.

chunks.heading: Using caffeine as a reinforcer
chunks.text:
- Caffeine is a strong reinforcer. People subconsciously prefer caffeinated foods and drinks, partly because of improved focus, mood and well-being. Caffeine can also increase the number of dopamine receptors in brain reward pathways.
- **To build a habit** (e.g., exercise): deliberately use caffeine with it. It raises dopamine for mood and motivation and makes the experience more pleasant and rewarding.
- **To break a habit** (e.g., sugar cravings): avoid caffeine. Don't pair coffee with dessert, or cravings are doubly reinforced through both sugar and caffeine's effects on dopamine.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman lays out a two-part habit framework. Split each waking day into three phases that match your neurochemistry, and alternate 21-day blocks of building habits with 21-day blocks of testing which stuck. He also gives a simple rule for breaking habits: notice the behavior, then do a positive action right after.

chunks.heading: Two time-of-day frameworks for habit work: the Phase 1/2/3 day structure
chunks.text:
Andrew's habit program starts from the idea that changing habits requires overcoming "limbic friction" (the energy needed to push past anxiety, procrastination and/or fatigue). He says to use the natural rhythms of the brain and body so that engaging in or maintaining a habit is more likely. He splits each 24-hour day-night cycle into three phases counted from the time you wake up. He says the Phase framework and the alternating-blocks framework are aligned with biology and neurochemistry and "work best when combined".

- Phase 1: 0-8 hours after waking
- Phase 2: 9-15 hours after waking
- Phase 3: 16-24 hours after waking

chunks.heading: Phase 1 (0-8 hours after waking): schedule effortful, focus-heavy habits
chunks.text:
- Brain and body are more action and focus oriented in Phase 1, due to elevated dopamine, adrenaline and cortisol levels. This makes it easier to overcome limbic friction.
- Caveat: people are also more prone to distraction and reflexive multitasking at this time. He says "Don't succumb to that."
- Set 1-4 habits for completion in Phase 1. These should be the habits that require energy and focus (for example exercise, writing, studying, focused work).
- Use a window for completion rather than a precise start and stop time. Example: 45 minutes of focused reading or work somewhere in Phase 1. He suggests exercising, writing or studying "after waking but before noon", so it can happen at 8 a.m., 10 a.m. or 11 a.m. but definitely in Phase 1.
- Doing it at the same time each day is fine if you can, but a broader window helps with busy lives.
- He calls Phase 1 terrific for habits where precise execution is needed.

chunks.heading: Phase 2 (9-15 hours after waking): looser, creative and low-friction habits
chunks.text:
- Naturally higher serotonin and lower adrenaline make this the time for habits that don't require overcoming much limbic friction.
- Good fits are behaviors and thinking that can be completed with less focus, especially creative exploration:
  - writing fiction or rough drafts
  - writing music
  - play of any kind
  - experimentation
  - lower-focus physical pursuits such as Zone 2 cardio
- Best for looser things: trying a new recipe, brainstorming, exploring a new approach to some aspect of work, a physical pursuit, relationships or learning.
- He quotes from Episode 53: "A lot of habit formation has to do with being in the right state of mind and being able to control your body and mind."

chunks.heading: Phase 3 (16-24 hours after waking): reset limbic friction through rest and sleep
chunks.text:
- Phase 3 is when the ability to overcome limbic friction is reset, by resting and sleeping.
- In short, to master it:
  - Avoid bright lights.
  - Sleep in a cool, dark room.
  - Explore supplementation if needed, but not melatonin.
- He points to his Toolkit for Sleep (Neural Network Newsletter #3) and Episode 2, "Master Your Sleep & Be More Alert When Awake", for details.

chunks.heading: Forming habits: the 21-day block with 4-6 of 6 habits per day
chunks.text:
- Based on his read of the literature, Andrew suggests picking six new habits to incorporate per day for 21 days.
- Write them down, aim to complete four to six of the six each day, and mark them off on a calendar.
- Do not fret about completing only four out of six on a given day.
- "Never compensate by doing more than six per day." He says a no-compensation system is best.
- Merge this with the Phase 1, 2, 3 structure to be in the best position to succeed.

chunks.heading: Testing whether habits stuck: alternating 21-day blocks
chunks.text:
- To know if you are succeeding, spend the next 21 days tracking your behavior without incorporating any new habits.
- The cycle is 21 days of habit formation, then 21 days of testing to see which habits actually became habits.
- Then return to 21 days of habit formation, using the progress in the previous block to decide whether to add more to the four to six per day list.
- How to judge whether a habit has formed: the strength of a habit is dictated by (1) how much limbic friction you need to overcome to perform the behavior, and (2) how much context-dependence there is.
- Context-dependence means whether you perform the habit no matter what, or only when calm, rested, in the presence of others, caffeinated, and so on. A strong habit happens regardless of context.

chunks.heading: Breaking habits: awareness, then an immediate positive behavior
chunks.text:
- Andrew calls the method "simple (alas, not always easy)".
- Step 1: bring conscious awareness to the fact that you participated in the habit you are trying to break.
- Step 2: when you realize you did it, engage in a positive behavior immediately afterward.
- The specific behavior matters less than the fact that it comes immediately after the habit and is not a negative behavior.
- Examples he gives: ten jumping jacks or pushups, as do-anywhere positive behaviors. They count as positive because they are good for you, not because you necessarily enjoy them.
- He cites "task bracketing" and review articles in peer-reviewed journals as the science behind these approaches (listed in the caption of Episode 53, "The Science of Making & Breaking Habits").

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman summarizes six levers for gut microbiome diversity, drawing on his conversation with Stanford's Justin Sonnenburg: fermented foods, targeted prebiotics/probiotics, sleep, avoiding processed foods, caution with artificial sweeteners, and not over-sanitizing. Emphasis is on consistency and whole, plant-fiber-rich foods.

chunks.heading: Fermented foods are Andrew's first lever for gut microbiome diversity
chunks.text:
- Andrew cites a human study by Dr. Justin Sonnenburg and Dr. Chris Gardner (Stanford). It tested diets high in plant fiber versus diets high in fermented foods.
- Fermented foods increased overall gut microbiota diversity and reduced key markers of inflammation (the "inflammatome").
- Participants ate six servings per day. Higher total amounts did not give further benefit, so Andrew stresses consistently including fermented foods daily over eating large quantities.
- Low-sugar examples he lists: sauerkraut, plain yogurt, kimchi, kombucha, natto, kefir, and even drinking brine.
- Buy them from the refrigerated section so they contain live active cultures. Shelf-stable fermented foods are pasteurized and do not give the same boost.
- Making your own kombucha or sauerkraut at home is a cost-effective option.

chunks.heading: What the fermented-food vs. fiber study found about fiber
chunks.text:
- A high-fiber diet did not increase microbiota diversity in the study.
- It did increase carbohydrate active enzymes, which digest fiber and may improve the microbiome's ability to break down other complex carbohydrates.
- Some participants in the high-fiber group showed reduced inflammation markers.
- Andrew still recommends plant-based, high-fiber foods (vegetables, legumes, whole grains). They offer broad health benefits and supply key nutrients for microbiota already established in the gut.

chunks.heading: Prebiotics and probiotics: dosing and cautions
chunks.text:
- Definitions: prebiotics are fermentable dietary fiber or microbiota-accessible carbohydrates that feed existing gut microbiota. Probiotics are live bacteria or yeasts that can colonize the gut. Synbiotics are mixtures of the two.
- Low levels of prebiotics and/or probiotics, alongside whole quality foods, improve gut microbiome health.
- Higher levels can help recovery and replenishment in dysbiosis, for example after antibiotics, during high stress, when traveling, or when changing your diet.
- Excessive probiotic intake has been linked to brain fog, gas and bloating. If you notice these, reduce the amount you take.
- Supplements are not FDA-regulated, so Andrew advises choosing an independently validated product.
- The gut microbiome is highly individualized, so supplementation affects people differently.

chunks.heading: Sleep protects the gut microbiome through stress
chunks.text:
- The gut microbiome is closely tied to your stress level, through direct links to immune system cells.
- Andrew says getting deep, good-quality sleep for generally 6-9 hours per night is essential for managing stress, and therefore for gut microbiome health.
- He points to his Toolkit for Sleep newsletter and Episode 2 of the Huberman Lab Podcast, "Master Your Sleep & Be More Alert When Awake," for sleep tactics.

chunks.heading: Limit processed foods and favor fiber that feeds short-chain fatty acids
chunks.text:
- Emulsifiers are detergent-like additives common in processed foods. They can disrupt the mucus layer of the GI tract.
- In animal models, emulsifiers reduced microbial diversity, caused low-grade inflammation, and increased body fat, blood sugar and insulin resistance, which are markers of metabolic syndrome.
- The typical Western diet (high fat, low fiber, more processed food) lacks many nutrients microbiota need.
- When microbiota ferment complex plant fiber, they produce short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate. These reduce inflammation, maintain the gut's mucosal barrier, regulate the immune system and modulate metabolism along the GI tract.
- His summary: prioritize whole foods, plant-based fiber and fermented foods.

chunks.heading: Artificial sweeteners: possible disruption, test it yourself
chunks.text:
- Clinical studies have not fully separated out the effect of artificial sweeteners on the gut microbiome.
- Animal models show evidence that they can disrupt it.
- A recent study found that gut neuropod cells distinguish natural from artificial sweeteners. They send the brain a different pattern of signals depending on whether the sugar is nutritive (has calories) or non-caloric.
- Because the Human Microbiome Project showed how individualized the microbiome is, Andrew suggests trying removing some artificial sweeteners and seeing whether you notice an effect.
- Non-caloric plant-based sweeteners like stevia are "probably fine," but few studies have examined stevia and the microbiome.

chunks.heading: Don't over-sanitize your environment
chunks.text:
- Andrew quotes Dr. Sonnenburg: "Exposure to microbes from the environment is likely an important part of educating our immune systems and keeping everything in the proper balance."
- The gut microbiome is also seeded by social contact (shaking hands, hugging, kissing), pets, dirt and grass.
- Over-sanitizing environments or overusing antibiotics can remove sources of beneficial microbiota.
- He still says to avoid disease-causing pathogens and harmful environmental chemicals such as pesticides, but notes many environmental microbes help establish and maintain a healthy gut microbiome.
- Low microbial diversity is a marker of dysbiosis, associated with autoimmune diseases, obesity and cardiometabolic conditions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman explains how to hydrate well: roughly 80 oz in the first 10 hours after waking, more with exercise, heat, sauna or caffeine, and electrolytes. He also covers filtering tap water and which water types are worth drinking, dismissing claims that water changes body pH.

chunks.heading: Hydration baseline and timing
chunks.text:
- Water makes up roughly 60-80% of human cells and tissues. It supports cellular function, acts as a solvent, protein structure and chemical reactions, and can act as an antioxidant against free radicals.
- Even mild dehydration hurts physical performance, alertness and focus, and can cause "brain fog."
- Andrew's baseline: about 8 oz (237 mL) of fluid per hour for the first 10 hours of the day, roughly 80 oz total. It is an average, not a schedule. Example: 16 oz on waking, 8 oz a few hours later, 32 oz later, and so on.
- Why the first 10 hours: the circadian clock regulates kidney and gut cells via the hormone vasopressin. In the first ~10 hours awake the kidney filters fluid efficiently, then output drops overnight.
- He says drinking more by day means more bathroom trips, "but that is not a bad thing." Most people simply don't drink enough during waking hours.

chunks.heading: Reducing nighttime urination
chunks.text:
Waking 1-2 times a night to urinate is not a sign of pathology. If it happens more often, Andrew suggests:
1. Hydrate sufficiently during the day.
2. Cut fluid intake in the evening and in the 2-3 hours before sleep.
3. If you must drink at night, sip slowly. Both the rate and the volume of intake affect the urge to urinate.

chunks.heading: Exercise, heat, sauna and caffeine
chunks.text:
- **Galpin Equation** (additional fluid during exercise, an average, not something to obsess over):
  - Body weight in lbs ÷ 30 = ounces to drink every 15-20 minutes.
  - Body weight in kg × 2 = mL to drink every 15-20 minutes.
- In hot temperatures or heavy sweating, increase those amounts by an additional 50-100%.
- Sauna: drink an extra 8-16 oz for every 20-30 minutes.
- Caffeine is a diuretic. Offset it at 2:1: an 8 oz caffeinated coffee calls for 16 oz of water, ideally with low- or no-sugar electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium) such as LMNT, or simply a pinch of salt.
- Dry environments also raise needs.
- Thirst is a useful signal, but "your perception of thirst lags behind the body's true hydration status." Not being thirsty doesn't mean you don't need fluid, so plan hydration ahead in extreme weather or high-intensity activity.

chunks.heading: Tap water contaminants and how to check yours
chunks.text:
- Standard municipal filtration at scale leaves contaminants that can harm health at high concentrations:
  - **Disinfection byproducts (DBPs)**, left over from municipal disinfection. Some are endocrine disruptors that can impair male and female fertility.
  - **Fluoride**: at ≥0.5 mg/L it can disrupt thyroid function, per the study he cites.
  - **Lead** from pipes into the home or building. Rarer in developed countries but still present in places.
- To find out what is in your water: search your zip code for a local water quality report, or contact the EPA Safe Drinking Water Hotline. CDC has further resources.
- In the U.S. these reports should be free from the city; you shouldn't pay.
- Optional testing: home test kits cost about $25; independent lab analysis about $100+.

chunks.heading: Filtering tap water by budget
chunks.text:
Andrew says it is healthier for most people to filter tap water. Pitcher filters like Brita catch some disinfection byproducts but not smaller particles, notably fluoride.
- Under $100: pitcher filter that includes fluoride filtration (e.g., ClearlyFiltered Pitcher).
- About $400: countertop filter for larger volumes (e.g., Berkey).
- $800+: whole-house filter (e.g., Aquasana).
- Zero cost: let 1-5 gallons sit uncapped at room temperature for about a day. Sediment settles, so pour off the top two-thirds to drink.
- Don't boil tap water to filter it: high heat can make contaminants worse.
- He states he has no affiliation with or compensation from these brands.

chunks.heading: Water types and minerals
chunks.text:
- Water with higher magnesium (ideally 8.3-19.4 mg/L) is more alkaline and absorbs better. He stresses this "has nothing to do with adjusting the pH of your body" and calls brand claims to that effect "pure falsehood," since tissue pH is tightly regulated.
- **Hard water** (more magnesium and calcium): higher pH. Some evidence that more alkaline water can reduce inflammation and blood pressure and lower cardiovascular risk.
- **Distilled / double-distilled**: strips calcium and magnesium. Don't drink it regularly because of those ions' health benefits.
- **Reverse osmosis**: removes many contaminants and is safe to drink, but is expensive and can lack key minerals.
- **Hydrogen-enriched, electrolyzed-reduced, deuterium-depleted**: higher pH than tap. Not studied extensively, but one study showed reduced inflammation and improved health metrics, likely from better cell hydration. A DIY version: dissolve a molecular hydrogen tablet (contains a specific form of magnesium) in a glass of water for 5-15 minutes. If your tap water is already high in magnesium, it is already sufficiently alkaline.
- **Structured water**: no scientific evidence of health benefits currently. Some researchers theorize water is structured within cells with added benefits. He calls this controversial with a growing body of science.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman's newsletter lays out a protocol for choosing one ambitious goal, defining it in a 12-week measurable plan, and sustaining pursuit. Tools cover visualizing failure, visual targeting, phone removal, random rewards, handling mid-goal slumps, and timing work to circadian attention peaks.

chunks.heading: Setting a goal: the six-step framework
chunks.text:
Andrew's six steps for defining a goal before pursuing it:

1. **Choose one priority goal.** Overhauling many habits at once (diet, workout, sleep, meditation, all starting January 1st) often causes all of them to fail. He asks: "What is the one goal I can give the necessary time and energy to pursue right now?"
2. **Make it lofty.** Simple goals don't create enough neural arousal and stress to stimulate real growth and learning, so the goal should be ambitious.
3. **Define specific actions.** Macro-goals like "get fit," "write a book" or "run more" must be broken into action steps, e.g. run three times per week. This significantly improves the odds of achieving them.
4. **Make it measurable on a finite timeline.** He suggests a 12-week period for most goals. Within it, define total hours per week, specific days, the length of each work session, and a time window (e.g. 8 a.m. to 9 a.m.) or constraint (e.g. before 9 a.m.).
5. **Quantify it.** Some goals are easily quantified (running a marathon under a set time); subjective ones (developing a meditation practice) need extra care and clearly outlined actions. For any goal, designate smaller outcomes along the 12 weeks to keep motivation up.
6. **Don't tell the world.** Positive feedback on a newly set goal can activate the brain's reward mechanisms and reduce motivation to pursue it, because you got the reward without the work. Keep it to yourself at first; sharing is more fun after the first milestone.

chunks.heading: Reminders and visualization during goal pursuit
chunks.text:
**Post-it note fallacy**
- A note saying "floss!" or "run today!" stops working after a few days because the brain monitors for what's new and stops "seeing" static reminders.
- A static visual reminder fails to trigger action. Write a new note every few days and post it in a different location.

**Visualize success and failure**
- If motivated before a work session, spend 1-3 minutes visualizing the positive outcomes of goal success as well as goal failure, to sustain motivation through the work bout.
- On unmotivated days, spend 1-3 minutes visualizing the failure of not achieving the goal.
- Humans work hard to avoid feelings of failure, and this exercise recruits neurochemicals like adrenaline to boost arousal and focus.

chunks.heading: Visual targets and removing the phone
chunks.text:
**Visual target strategy**
- Mental focus is strongly anchored to the visual system. Narrow the "cone" of visual attention to a specific object or point in front of you and hold it for 30-90 seconds.
- Dr. Emily Balcetis and colleagues have shown this increases alertness and autonomic arousal, and helps build and sustain motivation.
- When finished working, relax your gaze and look off to the horizon. This "turns off" the release of chemicals associated with alertness and arousal and aids relaxation.

**Phone**
- During work bouts, put the phone out of reach or turn on airplane mode.
- Two costs to avoid: task-switching (checking the phone between bouts of work) and procrastinating (checking it right before starting).

chunks.heading: Intermittent rewards to sustain dopamine-driven motivation
chunks.text:
- Consistently receiving rewards diminishes the reward's power and reduces overall motivation. Rewarding yourself only at the finish line (~12 weeks) also reduces motivation.
- The solution is random, intermittent rewards, like a slot machine. After goal work, flip a coin: heads = reward, tails = no reward.
- On a reward day, use positive self-talk for 30-60 seconds to reinforce the neural circuits associated with internal motivation.
- Treat yourself to a physical reward from time to time, such as watching a movie or eating a food you enjoy.

chunks.heading: The middle problem
chunks.text:
- People tend to be highly motivated to start and finish a goal, but motivation often declines in the middle.
- To overcome it:
  1. Acknowledge this is a normal phenomenon.
  2. Use time chunking: break the middle portion into 3-4 smaller time segments.

chunks.heading: Timing goal work to circadian rhythms
chunks.text:
- Andrew cites Dr. Pablo Valdez's description of three peak times each day when attention and focus are highest.
- As a rough guide, 30 minutes, 3 hours and 11 hours after waking are great times for hard work.
- This arises from the body's circadian rhythm (sleep-wake cycle) and the rhythmicity of body temperature and associated neurochemicals.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman's newsletter explains how to cut jet lag by pre-shifting your circadian clock before travel and timing light, meals, exercise and caffeine at the destination. The key tool is timing bright light relative to your home-time temperature minimum, roughly two hours before usual wake-up.

chunks.heading: Why eastward travel is harder, and how to prep
chunks.text:
- Andrew says most people find it easier to stay up later than to fall asleep earlier, so eastward travel is harder. Westward gives more time to get the right light signals.
- Jet lag worsens with age. The degree depends on the person and the number of time zones crossed.
- Prep for eastward travel starting two days before departure with three levers (light, caffeine, exercise):
  - Wake 30 to 45 minutes earlier than usual and view bright sunlight or bright artificial light immediately.
  - Drink caffeine early in the day to promote early alertness.
  - Move within 60 minutes of the new earlier wake-up time, even light jogging if a full workout isn't possible.
- Example given: California to New York.

chunks.heading: Prepping before westward travel
chunks.text:
- Westward travel is easier, but Andrew still recommends pre-adjusting with light, caffeine and exercise, shifted 30 to 45 minutes later instead of earlier.
- Wake a bit later, take caffeine a bit later (still avoiding caffeine in the 8 to 10 hours before bedtime), and exercise a bit later, even by just 45 minutes.
- Get bright artificial light to the eyes in the one to two hours after sunset, to prepare to stay up later.

chunks.heading: Temperature minimum: the power tool for shifting the clock
chunks.text:
- The temperature minimum is the lowest body temperature of each 24-hour cycle. It occurs about two hours before usual wake-up time, so no measurement is needed. For a 7 a.m. riser it is roughly 4:30 to 5:30 a.m.
- Use typical wake time, whether or not an alarm is used.
- Bright light to the eyes in the one to two hours after the temperature minimum shifts the clock earlier (sleep earlier, wake earlier). This suits eastward travel.
- Bright light in the one to two hours before the temperature minimum shifts the clock later (sleep later, wake later). This suits westward travel.
- Andrew stresses that the temperature minimum must be calculated on your home time before you leave. "Get it right and you'll shift fast across time zones. Get it wrong and it can be a mess."

chunks.heading: Common mistake: morning sun on arrival going east
chunks.text:
- Example: San Francisco to London (+8 hours). Landing to London morning sunlight, for the first two to three days, equals a giant blast of light at midnight San Francisco time to the brain's clock.
- That pushes the body toward later bedtimes and wake times, the opposite of what is wanted. Many people sleep well the first night, see sunlight, and then have a bad second night.
- Fix: wear dark sunglasses for the two to three hours before your (home-based) temperature minimum for the first two days. Get sunlight in the eyes in the London afternoon, which falls one to two hours after the temperature minimum.
- London is only an example; work out the timing from your own trip.

chunks.heading: Eating, fasting and exercise at the destination
chunks.text:
- Eating is a strong entraining signal. Eat breakfast, lunch and dinner at local times, even if not hungry, and start as early as possible.
- Many people fast 14 to 16 hours before local breakfast time to adopt the new schedule.
- Andrew personally skips this because he dislikes eating when not hungry and it lands in his subjective middle of the night. He acknowledges it is known to work.
- Keep a consistent early-in-the-day exercise routine on local time. It can be light aerobic activity like walking or more engaged, depending on fitness and degree of jet lag.

chunks.heading: Light tools: portable lights, cloud cover and red lenses
chunks.text:
- If it's cloudy or you land at night, travel with a portable bright light device of 5,000 to 10,000 lux.
- Even through cloud cover, sunlight is almost always far brighter than artificial lighting, so go outside at the correct times. Once shifted, return to standard "view sunlight in the (local) morning and (local) afternoon."
- In the evening, reduce bright light, especially short-wavelength blue and green light. All LEDs are rich in these.
- Andrew wears red-lens glasses after sundown to adjust to the local sleep schedule. He says this protects against the melatonin-reducing and cortisol-increasing effects of bright light. (He helped ROKA design the Wind Down lens, and ROKA sponsors the podcast.)

chunks.heading: Short trips
chunks.text: - For trips under three days, staying on the home schedule may minimize circadian disruption.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman lays out five foundations to re-up every 24 hours (sleep, nutrients, movement, light, relationships), then details his weekly training split, sleep and performance supplements, gut and fertility tips, and his changed stance on supervised psychedelics.

chunks.heading: Daily foundations: the five things to re-up every 24 hours
chunks.text:
Andrew argues that your state of mind and body at any moment is strongly set by what you did in the preceding hours and days. Sleep architecture works this way: the REM share of a 90-minute sleep bout depends on the slow wave to REM ratio of the previous bout. Focus works this way too, since it is "not a square wave function" you can drop into on demand. He says there is no real "optimization" until five foundations are handled, and each needs to be re-upped every 24 hours:

- **Sleep.** Quality sleep brings gain of function, not just avoided loss.
- **Nutrients.** Macronutrients, micronutrients and hydration. Roughly 80% or more of food should be unprocessed or minimally processed. Supplements like Ashwagandha, Shilajit, tongkat ali and Fadogia agrestis are things you "won't get from food."
- **Movement.** Both cardiovascular exercise and resistance training.
- **Light.** Sunlight early and through the day, and less bright artificial light in the evening and at night.
- **Relationships.** This includes your relationship to yourself.

His take: "nothing else really happens for very long unless those five things are tended to." Before asking which focus supplement to take, he steps back through all five. He adds that this is not about being soft; it makes you resilient and effective.

chunks.heading: Andrew's weekly training split: one adaptation per day
chunks.text:
Andy Galpin's research convinced Andrew that concurrent training works. You can build endurance and strength at the same time, because the body has only a small set of core adaptations and many methods for triggering them. He assigns each day one target:

- **Sunday, endurance.** A 75-90 minute slow jog with hills, wearing an 8-10 lb weight vest and nasal breathing. With others, he does a 3-5 hour loaded hike instead. The first 10-30 minutes feel bad, then central pattern generators take over repetitive movement without conscious attention, and effort feels easier.
- **Monday, legs.** About 10 minutes of warmup, then about 55 minutes of work. Each exercise gets 2-4 hard sets to failure with tight form, and he rests 2-5 minutes between sets.
- **Tuesday, heat and cold.** The leg recovery day. No cold immersion in the six hours after hypertrophy training, because it can blunt the adaptation.
- **Wednesday, short run.** Five minutes of warmup, then 25-30 minutes of steady running.
- **Thursday, "torso."** Overhead press, ring dips or dips, and neck work.
- **Friday, VO2 max.** Three minutes of warmup and about 12 minutes of work.
- **Saturday, small muscles.** Biceps, triceps, rear delts, and a lighter tib and calf session.

Other rules he follows:
- He keeps resistance sessions under 60 minutes, because beyond that cortisol rises and recovery suffers.
- He trains no later than about 11 a.m.
- He tracks sessions in a handwritten journal and adds a rep, a set or weight each time.
- He rates sessions subjectively from level 1 to 10.
- He plays low-stakes sports (e.g. badminton) about an hour a week.

He is 47 and says he is still getting stronger.

chunks.heading: Leg day, tib raises and why legs matter
chunks.text:
Andrew's Monday leg session in order:

1. Tibialis raises as a warmup: a couple of warmup sets, then 3 sets of 6-10 reps. Alternatively, lean back against a wall at an angle with heels on the floor and lift the toes for 25-30 reps.
2. Standing or sled calf raises, 2-4 sets of 5-10 reps.
3. Lying leg curls on a machine, 2 warmups then 2-4 working sets.
4. Glute-ham raises, 3-4 slow sets (a deadlift rotated 90 degrees, ending in a leg curl). Nordic curls are a substitute.
5. Leg extensions, 2-3 sets.
6. Hack squats, heavy, 2-3 sets after a warmup. Back squats give him hip pain. Weighted sissy squats are an alternative.

On tib raises (from Ben Patrick, "Knees Over Toes Guy"): Andrew credits them with getting rid of his right-side sciatica, improving posture, and making him able to "run like a beast" with no knee, back or shoulder pain. They also made his calf work more effective, and fixed his shin splints. He had believed his problem was flat feet, but it was weak tibialis muscles. He also says the idea that knees can't pass the toes is "silly" (see skateboarders and Olympic lifters).

Leg training has outsized value:
- Cognitive gains from resistance training come from big lower-body work, not "bicep curls."
- Legs create a "systemic anabolic effect."
- Protein synthesis peaks around 48 hours after training and stays elevated for a couple more days, so Friday's sprints and jumps indirectly keep the legs online.

If he could pick only three exercises, they would be glute-ham raise or Nordic curl, ring dips, and sprinting.

chunks.heading: Heat, cold, neck training and the soleus push-up
chunks.text:
**Tuesday heat and cold protocol.**
- 20 minutes in a very hot sauna (he works up to about 260°F).
- 3-5 minutes in a cold plunge up to the neck.
- Repeat for three sauna rounds and three plunges.
- He uses the time to listen to books.

**Sperm and heat.** Because he hopes to have children, he wears shorts in the sauna and puts a cold pack at his groin.

**Neck training.** Andrew says to do it for spinal strength and injury protection, and because it changes posture and presence. He stands more upright and finds it easier to look people in the eye.
- Lie on your side on a bench holding a towel-wrapped plate against your head, 10-15 reps, with one light warmup and three work sets.
- Then lie on your stomach with the plate behind your head and do head raises.
- Tim adds that manual resistance from a partner, done very slowly, also works.
- For women who don't want a larger neck, use lighter weight or hand resistance. He says women who want to avoid rounded shoulders should also go easy on upper-trap work.

**Soleus push-up.** A University of Houston study had people do seated calf raises (toe down, raising the heel every few seconds) for a couple of hours. They showed a meaningful improvement in insulin sensitivity. The soleus is about 1% of body musculature but can account for at least 15% of daily energy expenditure. It is not a replacement for exercise. Andrew's line: "if you're unwilling to try that, then your bar for entry is just way too high."

chunks.heading: Sleep stack, morning vs. evening, and hydration timing
chunks.text:
**Sleep stack.**
- Magnesium threonate, theanine, apigenin (a concentrated chamomile extract), and sometimes 900 mg of myo-inositol.
- If limited to two: magnesium threonate and apigenin.
- Theanine can make dreams more vivid, so people with intense dreams or nightmares should be wary of it.
- The myo-inositol helps him fall back asleep after waking to urinate. It is a mild sedative that is also studied for insulin sensitivity and depression.
- He tracks sleep on an Eight Sleep. He says wristbands and rings (WHOOP, Oura) can misread limb movement.

**Hydration timing.**
- Gulp fluids in the morning. The kidney is a different organ in the morning than at night.
- Sip, don't gulp, your last drink of the day. Rapid fluid intake sends a fast signal to the bladder, so slower intake means fewer 3 a.m. bathroom trips.

**Early day vs. late day.**
- Get sunlight (or bright artificial light), caffeine, hydration and movement early. Sunlight raises cortisol about 50% above baseline. You want cortisol and catecholamines (dopamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine) high early and low late.
- Late-shifted cortisol is associated with depression and immune problems.
- High-intensity interval training early, or cycling, appears to improve sleep stages, including REM, which is when emotions from the previous day get unpacked.

chunks.heading: Omega-3s, gut-brain sensing and fermented foods
chunks.text:
**Omega-3 dosing.**
- Minimum 1 g of EPA per day, sometimes more. Up to about 3 g per day has antidepressant effects in clinical trials.
- His routine: three capsules with his big midday meal, plus a tablespoon of Carlson's lemon-flavored liquid fish oil that he stirs into oatmeal with salt.
- He recommends refrigerating liquid fish oil after opening.
- Tim's problem: nausea after 5-7 days at about 2 g in capsules. Andrew suggested trying liquid, because the capsules themselves might be the issue.

**Two mechanisms for mood.**
- EPA is a structural lipid in neuronal membranes, including those of neurons that release serotonin and dopamine.
- Gut "neuropod cells" sense sugar, essential fatty acids and essential amino acids, and signal via the vagus nerve to the brain's dopamine centers (work from Diego Bohorquez at Duke and Charles Zuker at Columbia).
- Nutrient-poor but highly palatable food gives a dopamine hit without that matching nutrient signal.
- Getting enough omega-3s or small amounts of L-glutamine reduces sugar cravings. Quality BCAA or essential amino acid powder can too.

**Fermented foods.** One serving a day is not enough. He says to aim for three or four servings of low-sugar fermented foods, such as nattō, sauerkraut, kimchi and sour Bulgarian yogurt. Since few people manage that, he notes AG1 as a convenient option, and he does not have high-dose probiotics as a first choice because they are expensive and need refrigeration.

chunks.heading: Rhodiola, Ashwagandha, tongkat ali and Fadogia agrestis
chunks.text:
**Rhodiola rosea.**
- 200 mg, 30-60 minutes before training. Effects last about four hours.
- It reduces perceived effort and allows more power and endurance output, and it reduces the post-workout energy dip.
- It does not work by suppressing cortisol. His guess is it blunts adrenaline's energy-depleting trough.
- He takes it before hard, high-intensity or hike sessions, not before every leg day.
- He avoids taking it all day every day, because studies suggest its effects taper.
- If it doesn't work the first time, he'd try a slightly higher dose.
- He calls it "probably the best addition to my kind of physical performance stack" in a long time.

**Ashwagandha.**
- It suppresses cortisol.
- Take it late in the day, not early, and not in high doses (400-600 mg) before exercise, because the cortisol spike drives adaptation.
- Low doses (25-50 mg) can be taken continuously.
- For higher doses, take at least two weeks off after about two weeks.

**Tongkat ali.**
- Use the Indonesian variety.
- Typically 400 mg a day, single or divided, taken before noon or 2 p.m. because it can increase energy.
- It lowers sex hormone-binding globulin, freeing testosterone. He cringes at doses of a gram a day, since high-dose herbals risk immune reactions.

**Fadogia agrestis.**
- 300-600 mg a day, with or without food, any time of day.
- It raises luteinizing hormone, and so testosterone in men and estrogen in women. It can increase testicular size and density.
- Rat data suggest testicular toxicity only at very high doses.
- He does not cycle tongkat ali or Fadogia, and he does blood work including liver enzymes twice a year.

**Estrogen in men.** He notes estrogen matters in men too: crashing it hurts libido and cognition, and estrogen is cardioprotective.

**Testosterone range.** He prefers the high end of normal (about 600-900 ng/dL) over exogenous testosterone, which suppresses endogenous production.

If limited to two across these and omegas, he would pick omegas and tongkat ali.

chunks.heading: Fertility, sperm and egg health: dos and don'ts
chunks.text:
Andrew spent a year researching this, and he has monitored and frozen his own sperm. He treats fertility as a proxy for vitality. He defines vitality as the ability to wake with energy, move between driven and relaxed, and feel good doing it.

**Do:**
- Get quality sleep, sunlight, low stress and good relationships.
- Get enough omega-3s.
- Take L-carnitine. It improves egg and sperm health, including forward motility. Injectable (about 1 mL a day) needs a prescription. Oral capsules need 4-5 g a day, which can raise TMAO. He says to offset that with about 600 mg of garlic (allicin).
- Get 20 minutes of sun on bare skin (shirt off, or tank top and shorts) three times a week. An Israeli study found this raised free testosterone, estrogen and libido, with afternoon sun.
- Consider banking eggs or sperm. In California, eggs can generally be frozen up to about 42 (after that only embryos), and he suggests sperm banking before about 45.

**Don't:**
- Smoke or vape anything, including cannabis.
- Carry a phone in your front pocket. A meta-analysis found it lowers sperm quality, motility and testosterone, and even short durations matter. Use a back pocket, a bag, or a shoulder pocket.
- Drink more than two or three drinks a week (women), which reduces egg quality. He says negative health effects begin past about two drinks a week for men and women.
- Handle printed receipts, which he calls a major BPA source, and avoid airborne pesticide exposure (rural areas, per Shanna Swan's work).

Tim reports his own sperm quality is better now than 10 years ago after L-carnitine, maca and other changes.

chunks.heading: Cannabis and psychedelics: Andrew's stance
chunks.text:
**Cannabis.**
- Smoking or vaping is worse than edibles or tinctures.
- Very high-THC cannabis in teens and young adults carries about a 4x higher chance of later psychotic episodes that don't reverse.
- Low-dose edibles in adults past the critical period of brain plasticity (older than about 25) are very unlikely to be a problem. 2.5 mg is a sub-perceptible dose.
- Pure CBD cannabis (Charlotte's Web) is a powerful anti-epileptic with essentially no psychoactive effect.
- Tim notes THC at about 2.5 mg helps his onset insomnia caused by rumination.

**Psychedelics and MDMA.**
- His view has changed completely in the last 24 months.
- He took LSD recreationally in high school and regrets it.
- He has done three physician-guided MAPS-style MDMA sessions for trauma, and says they were immensely beneficial.
- Session one was somatic and left him comfortable in his body and emotions. Session two brought deep acceptance and forgiveness of old resentments. Session three, at a higher dose with the booster, gave him boundaries between his emotions and others'.
- He says the benefits have held for years.
- Psilocybin trials for intractable depression show 60-70% of patients getting substantial, ongoing relief.
- Eye masks and music appear key to the introspective effect.

**Safety.** Street drugs are often laced with fentanyl. Tim recommends DanceSafe test kits. Sourcing MDMA through MAPS is the clean route. He also continues psychotherapy "like going to the gym."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Huberman describes his Dorian Yates-style low-volume, high-intensity split plus cardio, and explains the cortisol principle of high morning and low night levels. He reviews peptide categories (GLPs, GH secretagogues, BPC-157, pinealon) with a skeptical, risk-aware lens, and shares his MDMA plus psilocybin experience.

chunks.heading: Peptides: categories, what the evidence supports, and sourcing
chunks.text:
- Andrew defines peptides as short amino-acid chains the body already makes (insulin is one). Following Dr. Abud Bakri, he frames the trend as "mining the body for medicines" instead of plants.
- He splits them into weight-loss (GLP), growth hormone secretagogues, tissue repair, and miscellaneous.
- **GLPs:** drugs that raise GLP about a thousandfold produce robust weight loss, including some muscle loss. Retatrutide (Lilly, not yet released) hits GLP, GIP and glucagon.
  - It is already sold on the gray market, since it is easy to synthesize.
  - Some people take roughly a tenth of the prescribed dose and report similar effects with less nausea.
  - He has never used a GLP himself.
  - He says people should resistance train regardless.
- **Gray market risk:** "for research purposes only" products carry contamination risk (e.g., lipopolysaccharide) and may not contain what the label says.
- **Compounding pharmacies:** these are cleaner than the gray market, and he names Tailor Made, Upstate and Revive Pharmacy as better known. A doctor must write the script.
- **Bottom-line view:** he says "you do you" on risk, but be logical about it.
  - He expects few robust effects beyond GLPs and, anecdotally, pinealon.
  - He thinks the big opportunity is clean, American-made, verified-supply peptides.
- Women are a massive peptide market, e.g., low-dose tirzepatide or reta, NAD, and GHK-Cu (with red light or sun, for wrinkles).

chunks.heading: Growth hormone secretagogues vs. real GH
chunks.text:
- This category covers sermorelin, ipamorelin, tesamorelin, CJC and MK677, which stimulate nighttime GH release. Typical increase is three to eightfold in GH and IGF-1.
- Some, like MK677, stimulate appetite. CJC variants can cause some insulin resistance.
- He tried sermorelin briefly:
  - It dramatically increased slow wave deep sleep and "nuked" REM.
  - It spiked his PSA, which returned to normal after stopping. No one could give him a mechanism.
  - He saw no notable fat loss or strength gain.
- He doesn't find secretagogues worth it. If someone can get a legitimate script, he prefers pharma-grade somatropin or omnitrope.
  - Trial dosing is typically 1 to 2 IU, five nights per week.
  - Bodybuilders use about 8 IU a day.
  - Effects people report: more deep sleep, better recovery and tissue repair, joints that feel good, general well-being. It is less anabolic than testosterone.
- He is not telling people to run out and do GH, but sees a low-dose script as better than unknown secretagogue peptides.

chunks.heading: BPC-157 and tissue repair peptides
chunks.text:
- BPC-157 ("Body Protection Compound") is an amino acid chain found in gastric juice. Original use was gut issues (high-dose enemas in one trial).
- Animal data are impressive (cartilage regrowth, fibroblast migration, angiogenesis, nerve regrowth), but there is "not a single published human trial," and he doesn't expect one: trials are expensive and nobody will fund them.
- His experience: after a strain, recovery feels faster, but he can't run a control because it goes systemic. He keeps some in the fridge and injects it for strains only.
- Capsule forms are claimed to work equally well; he doesn't know. Pentadecapeptide is another form.
- Angiogenesis caveat: it could vascularize a tumor, though it isn't mutagenic.
- He would not take it ongoing or without an injury. For recovery, he says sleep (or low-dose GH) does more.
- TB-500 plus BPC is the "Wolverine Stack." He hasn't tried TB-500.
- Tim Ferriss notes he took the Wolverine Stack after elbow surgery and has no idea whether it helped.

chunks.heading: Pinealon, epitalon and other peptides
chunks.text:
- **Pinealon** (despite the name) comes from the neocortex, not the pineal. Epitalon does come from the pineal.
  - He uses pinealon only occasionally, by subcutaneous injection (oral forms exist), via a compounded script.
  - Effect: about three hours of REM for him, with slow wave sleep intact, and it carries over to following nights. Few things increase REM; most drugs deplete it.
  - Some people use it in the daytime for cognition; one songwriter likes the hypnotic state it induces.
- **Epitalon:** proposed to preserve histone and DNA structure; vague evidence. Some animal data on visual repair in retinitis pigmentosa models.
  - He tried a capsule form plus morning sunlight for jet lag and it seemed to shift his clock faster, but he won't repeat it because he isn't sure.
- **Melanotan:** causes tanning, can cause priapism and greatly increases libido. Vyleesi is an FDA-approved drug for female hyposexuality.
- **Safety framing:** there are no reported adverse events tracked to non-FDA peptides, but Tim's point is that absence of reporting isn't evidence of safety. Andrew says to use good injection hygiene: alcohol swabs, never reuse needles, and don't dip back into a vial with a used needle.

chunks.heading: Sleep tools: REM, DORAs and meditation
chunks.text:
- **More REM without drugs:** heat the sleeping environment in the final two hours (credit: Matt Walker). Cool at the start, cold mid-night, warm toward morning, e.g., a heated blanket, socks or a wool cap if he wakes to use the bathroom.
- **Late workouts:** to avoid caffeine, take 900 mg alpha-GPC. He says it lets you sleep and likely increases REM.
- Intense weight training can triple or quadruple cortisol. Ice baths raise it trivially by comparison.
- **DORAs:** Tim takes Belsomra, partly because Alzheimer's runs in his family, and cycles on and off due to morning grogginess. Andrew tried Quviviq once and got "zombie sleep" (woke in the same position, unrested), so he avoids prescription sleep tools.
- Supplement stack he likes: magnesium threonate, apigenin, theanine. Try light and caffeine management first, before pinealon.
- A PNAS paper shows short meditations increase glymphatic clearance in the daytime, with more clearance in that night's sleep.
- To raise nighttime HRV, do exhale-emphasized breathing during the day, even a few deliberate exhales.
- **Jet lag:** fasting may shift peripheral clocks (liver, gut). Tim reports fasting on long flights helped him.
- **Sleep induction:** a bed-rocking study shows faster sleep onset and deeper sleep. An MIT-linked sleep mask stimulates behind the ears to drive eye movements and induce sleep in under six minutes; Andrew has no relationship to the company.

chunks.heading: Resistance training: the Dorian Yates approach and Andrew's current split
chunks.text:
- After training with Dorian Yates (six-time Mr. Olympia), Andrew says the peer-reviewed data caught up to low-volume, high-intensity training.
- Dorian's structure: a couple of warmups, then two all-out sets to failure, or one set plus assisted reps, a drop set or rest-pause. Do 2 to 3 exercises per major body part, about 4 to 8 work sets per body part, in the 5 to 12 rep range.
  - Each body part is trained directly once a week and indirectly a second time.
  - Take a lighter or off week about every 6 to 8 weeks.
  - Mike Mentzer's single set was probably too little for most people.
